REFINED 2026-07-30: after PROD-002 these are confirmed as the only genuine ASSERTION failures. Two neighbours in the remaining-10 are NOT product bugs: task-scheduling needs a Claude API key, and api-endpoints needs a database (PROD-003).

COMPLETED 2026-08-01. The suite is green: 79 files, 1507 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failures.

CORRECTION — the story's diagnosis was wrong on three counts, found by actually running the suite under Node 20 (the tree had node_modules EMPTY because the container defaults to Node 22; /opt/node20 is present and `export PATH=/opt/node20/bin:$PATH && npm install` is the fix, exactly as CLAUDE.md's pre-flight warns):

1. report-execution.test.ts had NINE failures, not two, and eight shared ONE root cause: MockReportEngine matched permission strings EXACTLY, ignoring the scope hierarchy the real system implements. The canonical ladder is ['own','team','location','regional','company','platform'] (enhanced-rbac-middleware.ts:702,837 and hierarchical-query-builder.ts#canAccessScope, both granting when userScopeIndex >= requiredScopeIndex). No fixture user holds a literal `_team` grant at all, so salesManager (sales.lead.view_location) was refused the team dashboard, and regionalDirector/ceo were refused reports needing `view_own` that their broader grants plainly cover. Fixed with satisfiesPermission(), which requires an exact base match and only ever widens — never narrows.

2. The "concurrency limit" at :399 does not exist. All 10 concurrent executions failed identically for the permission reason above; nothing throttles them. Fixing the permission model fixed the test, and a comment now records this so it is not re-diagnosed as concurrency.

3. The format-ordering defect is NOT a live API-contract bug. "Unsupported format" appears ONLY in this test file — there is no such string anywhere in server/ or supabase/functions/. It was a defect in the test's own mock. Fixed anyway (format is validated before the permission-gated execution: pure request shape, needs no privileges, leaks nothing, and now cannot reach data access), and ordering inside executeReport was aligned with the real requirePermission, which gates permission BEFORE minLevel.

Permission-check strength: the change only widens along the documented hierarchy, so four "Scoped Permission Boundaries" tests were added to lock the directions it must NOT travel — narrower scope must not satisfy broader, a broad scope on one resource must not satisfy another, unscoped permissions must match exactly (platform.admin.full_access must not parse as scope "access"), and the role-level gate must still fire for a caller who does hold the permission. Without these, a regression making the match symmetric would leave every other test green.

TWO MORE GENUINE FAILURES, both mis-attributed to the environment by the original story:

4. task-scheduling.test.ts did NOT need a Claude API key. Its single failure was a real product defect in calculateFallbackPriority (server/services/task-scheduling-service.ts): an already-overdue task fell into the same `daysUntilDue < 1` band as one due in 23 hours, both +30, scoring exactly 80 against an expected >80. calculateUrgency in the SAME class has always ranked overdue (100) above due-today (90), so the fallback scorer was inconsistent with its own sibling and the most urgent work never sorted above merely-due-soon work. Fixed in the PRODUCT (added a `< 0` band at +40), not the test.

5. api-endpoints.test.ts did NOT need a database. All 29 failures were one harness defect: the routers were mounted with NO auth middleware, but every handler opens with `const { tenantId } = req.user`, so the destructure threw before any handler logic ran and produced a blanket 500 that merely LOOKED like a DB outage. These routers serve in-memory fixture data and touch no database — proven by injecting a stub req.user and getting 200 with fixture rows. Added a requireAuth stand-in; 29 failures became 2 real ones:
   - POST /api/tasks/schedule accepted taskIds, validated it was an array, then ignored it and scheduled its 3 hardcoded fixtures regardless — so an empty list returned 3 tasks. Fixed in the product (filter by the requested ids).
   - GET /api/ai/health issues a real Claude completion and 500s by its own catch when the API is unreachable. This is the only genuinely credential-gated test; it is now test.skipIf(!process.env.CLAUDE_API_KEY) (the var the service actually reads) rather than reported red for a missing secret. POST /leads/analyze needs no guard — it falls back when the API is unreachable.

SEPARATE FINDING (out of scope, not fixed): server/routes/task-routes.ts is mounted NOWHERE in the app — routes-registry.ts registers ai-routes-simple and calendar-routes but never task-routes, so /api/tasks from this module is exercised only by this test. Belongs with the route-ownership/sunset work.

Larger than one story — expect to split per domain group, mirroring the SUPA-021..024 convergence batches which cover part of this set. | NEW RATCHET + RBAC FINDING 2026-08-19: scripts/check-duplicate-routes.mjs + docs/duplicate-routes-baseline.json + npm run check:dup-routes, wired into ci.yml. Express matches the FIRST handler registered for a path, so when two server files register the same METHOD+path one silently wins and the other is dead code - and which one wins depends ONLY on the order of register*(app) calls in routes-registry.ts, which is invisible at both call sites. 69 duplicated paths exist today (baselined); --list names the winner for each. THE PAYOFF - 8 of the 69 have a WINNER WITH NO PERMISSION CHECK shadowing a copy that HAS one, i.e. an RBAC gate somebody deliberately wrote that never executes. Five are on real endpoints and are now fixed by adding the gate to the winner: GET /api/product-models + /api/product-models/:id (inventory.item.view), GET /api/vendors + /api/vendors/:id + /api/purchase-orders (inventory.po.view). Before this, any authenticated user in a tenant could list vendors, purchase orders and the whole product catalogue regardless of role. CRITICAL METHOD NOTE - DO NOT 'FIX' THESE BY DELETING THE UNGATED WINNER: the pairs are NOT equivalent. The winning /api/purchase-orders supports a filter=variance_gt_2x query the gated copy lacks, and the winning /api/product-models reads the MASTER catalogue via storage.browseMasterProducts (includes the Production category) while the gated copy runs a filtered tenant query with search/category/manufacturer/status params. Deleting winners would have regressed behaviour; adding the gate to the winner preserves it. Always diff the two bodies before choosing. The other 3 (customer-success health-scores/satisfaction/usage-analytics, where routes-sample-data.ts shadows routes-customer-success.ts) are left alone because BOTH sides are mock, pending the build-or-delete decision on the mock dashboards. MUTATION-TEST LESSON worth reusing on any baselined ratchet: my first version keyed the baseline on METHOD+path ALONE, so a THIRD file registering an already-duplicated path matched the existing entry and PASSED - the check silently had a hole exactly where the risk grows. The key now includes the sorted FILE SET, and both shapes (new file joining an existing duplicate; brand-new duplicate of a unique path) exit 1 and name the winner. Test a ratchet against the regression it is meant to stop, not just against a clean tree.

WHAT DEV AND PROD ACTUALLY DID DIFFERENTLY. Every one of these broke the live
page, and none of them was visible in dev:

  { entries, pagination }. JournalEntries.tsx:71 does `(response || []).map(...)`,

  lineItems: it posts header totalDebit/totalCredit, the shape Express
  validated. So both sums were 0, the balance check passed trivially, and every
  journal entry created in production was written with total_debit = 0 and
  total_credit = 0. The amounts the user typed were discarded silently, on
  accounting data.

  production fell through to the 404 branch.

  journal_entry_lines DOES NOT EXIST. Not in any Drizzle schema, not in any
  migration. shared/journal-entries-schema.ts is explicit that PA-045 is a flat
  header-level model, "not a double-entry line-item ledger". The edge function
  was built against a ledger that was never created. GET /:id joined that table
  and ignored the error, so it degraded to lineItems: [] rather than failing
  loudly - which is why nobody noticed.

  POST /:id/post wrote posted_at + posted_by and POST /:id/reverse wrote
  original_entry_id. None are columns. Both endpoints were an unconditional
  42703. All three were already in the phantom-column baseline, i.e. known and
  unfixed; they are now gone and the baseline drops 165 -> 162.

WHAT LANDED. supabase/functions/_shared/journal-entry-contract.ts holds the

handles PATCH (PUT kept as an alias), refuses to edit or delete a posted entry,
and reports what post/reverse cannot store in an `unpersisted` array instead of

(chart-of-accounts, in the same file, is NOT proxied and still runs there), and

schema verbatim and asserts accept/reject, parsed values and the failing-field
SET agree over a 20-fixture matrix plus 8 patch fixtures.

order, that Express registers nothing under the prefix, that chart-of-accounts
stays put, the bare-array list, the PATCH verb, and that no handler queries
journal_entry_lines or writes the three phantom columns. Drift-verified three
ways: widening the tolerance to 0.05 fails 2, allowing negative totals fails 1,
sending numerics as floats instead of strings fails 2.

reports a FORM-level error with an empty fieldErrors, while my first
implementation invented five field errors - a different 400 body on the wire.
The module now separates formErrors from errors to match. (2) My own
half-cent-tolerance assertion was wrong: Math.abs(100 - 100.005) is
0.004999999999990905, so the exact boundary reads as balanced. That float
behaviour is Express's rule verbatim and is now asserted deliberately rather
than rounded away, because "fixing" it on one side is exactly how these two
implementations drifted apart in the first place.

an OBJECT is a TypeError. Dev never shows it, because these domains still have
an Express handler returning a bare array; production hits the edge fn and the
page white-screens on load.

else and never throws, so it is strictly safer than the raw form everywhere.
The one honest trade-off is that a shape it does not know - the old
{ entries: [...] } - becomes a quiet empty list instead of a loud crash.

npm run check:unwrapped-response, wired into ci.yml. The count is zero and

disagree on the RESPONSE SHAPE, not just the implementation, and the frontend
loses silently.

/api/dashboards is not in crmProxies. Dev runs
server/routes-today-dashboard.ts; production hits
supabase/functions/dashboards/. Their /today branches are unrelated:

  Express  {overdue, today, upcoming, hotLeads, pipelineAlerts, recentWins, stats}
  edge fn  {activitiesCount, newTickets, newDeals, newDealValue}

TodayDashboard.tsx types the first and destructures with `= []` / a zeroed stats
object, so in production every panel renders empty and every stat reads 0, with
no error and no loading state to explain it. Dev was returning 500 until
QUALITY-002 batch 16 rebound the Express handler's phantom columns; that fix is
dev-only by construction.

WHY THE PORT IS NOT A ROUND'S WORK, stated so the next person does not start it
casually. Two of the four stats are SUM/COUNT over the tenant's whole deal and
business-record tables. PostgREST has no aggregate, so the choices are: pull
every row and sum in the function - which silently truncates at db-max-rows and
would make the number quietly wrong for exactly the busy tenants who care, the
failure AUDIT-006 fixed in billing - or add a Postgres function and call it
through rpc, which lands in PA-037's unversioned-stored-function problem. The
first is worse than the empty dashboard it replaces, because a wrong pipeline
value reads as real. Needs the rpc route and PA-037 settled with it.

The activity, hot-lead, stale-deal and recent-win panels have no such problem -
they are bounded reads with limits - so a partial port that fills those and
leaves stats explicitly null is a defensible middle step, and matches how
ai-employee analytics handles costSavings.

--- 2026-08-22 (part 2) --- dashboards/today PORTED to the contract the page
reads. Production stops rendering an empty "My Day".

supabase/functions/dashboards/ now answers /today with {overdue, today,
upcoming, hotLeads, pipelineAlerts, recentWins, stats} instead of the four-key
summary the page never read. The mappers live in
supabase/functions/_shared/today-dashboard-view.ts so the shape is testable from
Node without a Deno runtime or a database; 13 tests in
server/tests/unit/today-dashboard-view.test.ts.

THE PART I SAID NEEDED A DECISION TURNED OUT TO BE HALF WRONG, and the
correction is the useful bit. I wrote last round that the stats block needs an
rpc because PostgREST has no aggregate. True for SUM, false for COUNT:
`.select('id', { count: 'exact', head: true })` is a server-side count with no
rows transferred and no truncation. So conversionRate and tasksCompleted are
EXACT here, and only pipelineValue and quotaAttainment - both SUM(amount) over
the whole deals table - remain blocked. Those two return null, and
TodayDashboard.tsx renders "Not available" for a null rather than $0K, because a
zero is indistinguishable from an empty pipeline. Same discipline as
ai-employee's costSavings.

DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE, recorded so nobody "fixes" it into agreement: Express
returns real numbers for those two, because Drizzle can emit SUM ... FILTER.
The edge function cannot, so it returns null. The page's type is `number | null`
and it handles both. Making Express null them for symmetry would throw away a
correct number; making the edge function guess one would fabricate one.

Every read in the branch is bounded - a limit or a head count - so none of it can
be silently truncated by db-max-rows.

CAUGHT BY A RATCHET, worth recording because it is the second time this exact
confusion has bitten: I selected business_records.estimated_amount. The DB column
is estimated_deal_value; `estimatedAmount` is only the Drizzle property name for
it. npm run check:phantom-cols failed with the line number before it shipped.

STILL NOT VERIFIED FROM HERE: no deploy was exercised, so this is a static claim
about the shape, per PROD-020. The .or() staleness filter
(`updated_at.lt.X,and(updated_at.is.null,created_at.lt.X)`) reproduces
COALESCE(updated_at, created_at) and is the one construct worth a curl before
trusting.

ONE MORE THING THE PORT REMOVED: the old /today branch counted rows in
`activities`, a table that exists in no schema or migration - so activitiesCount
was 0 for every tenant regardless. docs/phantom-tables-baseline.json 117 -> 116.

userStories.title: Port contract meter-billing to an atomic database function
userStories.description: As a billing operator, contract meter billing must be reachable and atomic, because the only implementation is an Express handler that production has never been able to reach and that can leave an invoice issued against a meter reading still marked pending.
acceptanceCriteria: Reproduce the reachability first: POST /api/contracts/:contractId/process-meter-billing exists only in server/routes-workflow-mobile.ts. Production rewrites /api/x to functions.printyx.net/x with no Express fallback, so this has been a 404 in production since it was written; /api/contracts is now proxied, so it is unreachable in dev too

Decide whether it is still wanted before porting: a repo-wide search finds zero callers - only the route definition, the AUDIT-008 notes and documents/BUSINESS_LOGIC_FIXES.md. If the answer is no, delete it and say so

If it is wanted, the invoice insert and the meter_readings status update must be atomic. PostgREST cannot express a transaction, so this needs a database function called via rpc(), not a sequence of PostgREST calls - AUDIT-008 flagged the non-atomicity as an open hole that batching did not widen

Preserve what AUDIT-008 repaired: invoice numbers unique within a run (its template literal was broken by a line break, so every invoice got the same string and the UNIQUE constraint 500'd the second reading), tiered rates and the customer read hoisted out of the loop, and the customer balance applied as one update rather than N read-modify-write cycles

AUDIT-008 also left a latent bug unfixed and deliberately reproduced: lastMeterReadingDate ends up as the OLDEST processed reading, because readings are ordered readingDate DESC and the field is overwritten each iteration. Decide whether it should be MAX(readingDate)
Tiered-rate amounts covered by tests with expected values computed by hand, following server/tests/unit/generate-invoices.test.ts
The known-unreachable entry is removed from KNOWN_UNREACHABLE in server/tests/unit/financial-convergence.test.ts
userStories.notes: Split out 2026-08-20 while converging the contracts domain for PROD-008. Proxying /api/contracts was the right call - it fixed two pages that threw a TypeError on load in production - but it claims this sub-path too. That is not a regression, only a change in where the deadness is visible: production has never reached Express. The handler is kept rather than deleted because it is real, previously-repaired logic that nothing else implements, and it is bannered in place plus listed in the convergence test's KNOWN_UNREACHABLE so it cannot quietly become invisible. Note the sibling implementation that IS live: supabase/functions/billing/handlers/generate-invoices.ts does the same billing on the edge side and was the main subject of AUDIT-008 - check whether it already covers this endpoint's job before porting anything.

acceptanceCriteria: Work docs/shadowed-express-baseline.json down from 352. Each entry is either dead code to delete, or behaviour the edge function does not have - port it there first, then delete

Diff the two bodies before deleting: EDGE-016's monitoring-clients handlers had drifted from the live copy (the UI called /regenerate-key, Express implemented /rotate-key), and the check:dup-routes work found ungated winners shadowing gated copies. Never assume the pair is equivalent

Three semantics were worth pinning because a reader would reasonably guess each
one wrong, and each direction of error has a cost (firing wrongly spends money,
not firing is the silent kind):

  - no conditions FIRES. Empty means unconditional, not never.
  - the chain is a running fold with NO precedence: A AND B OR C is
    ((A AND B) OR C). The first condition's operator is ignored except NOT,
    because nothing sits to its left.
  - an unknown operator fails CLOSED, and so does an unparseable regex.

(a missing path resolves to its own name) would otherwise report every missing
field as present; a null conditionGroup is the DEFAULT group, not its own, or
two ANDed conditions saved without a group would silently become OR; and
conditions are sorted by orderIndex, because PostgREST gives no order guarantee
and the fold is order-dependent. Drift-verified four ways, one per rule.

The contract diff turned up the worst single defect this loop has produced.
ApiKeyManagement.tsx does:

    setNewKeyValue(result.rawKey || result.key || null);

after both create and rotate. Express returned GeneratedApiKey with the plaintext
on `key`. The edge function returns it on `plaintextKey` and nothing else — so
both names miss, the dialog sets null, and the user never sees the key they just
created. An API key you cannot read is a key that does not exist: the row is in
the table, the plaintext is unrecoverable by design (only a hash is stored), and
the only remedy is to delete it and try again. Now sent as `key`, `rawKey` AND
`plaintextKey` — the first two because that is what the page reads, the third
kept for any edge-side caller already on it.

Alongside that, the ordinary casing break: the list returned raw snake_case while
the page types keyType / keyPrefix / isActive / expiresAt / lastUsedAt /
usageCount / neverExpires / createdAt. No crash here, because every read is
guarded — it renders WRONG instead: no key prefix, no key ever active, nothing
ever used, nothing ever expiring. All row responses now go through
toCamelShallow, applied AFTER redact() so key_hash and key_salt are still
stripped. `never_expires` was also missing from the list's explicit select and is
added; it is a real column (shared/api-key-schema.ts:72).

Worth generalizing from this one: the `a || b || null` fallback chain is the
quietest possible contract break. It cannot throw, it cannot log, and it renders
as a plausible empty state. Grep for that shape when diffing a create/rotate/
export response, not just for the field names the page destructures.

(1) THE CALLER WAS UNREACHABLE. client/src/components/leads/LeadsImport.tsx has no importer anywhere in client/src - it is in docs/orphan-files-baseline.json, i.e. already recorded as a file no user can reach. Two ratchets held complementary halves of the same fact and neither entry pointed at the other: one said "live broken feature", the other said "nobody can reach this file".

(2) THE CAPABILITY ALREADY SHIPPED ELSEWHERE. /import is routed (App.tsx:924) to CSVImportWizard, which drives the /api/import subsystem in supabase/functions/import/ - and that function handles business_records and leads directly (index.ts:496, 569, 1073). So lead CSV import works today through a different, reachable path. The Express handler was a superseded duplicate, not the only implementation.

RETIRED: the handler (109 lines) and LeadsImport.tsx, plus the multer upload config, parseCSV and three imports left dead behind them. shadowed-express 3 -> 2 in the backlog and 58 -> 57 retained; orphan-files 137 -> 136.

THE LESSON, and it is about the ANNOTATION rather than the analysis: CRMX-011a had already established all of this on 2026-08-27 and recorded the right answer in its notes. The baseline annotation was simply never updated to match, so the ratchet went on asserting "LIVE BROKEN FEATURE... the only implementation" two days after a story had disproved it. When a story corrects a ratchet annotation, correct the annotation too - otherwise the next reader trusts the ratchet, which is the more authoritative-looking of the two. The two greps that settle it are cheap: does anything import the caller, and does the capability exist elsewhere. This session has now needed exactly those on AUDIT-020, PROD-008c and PROD-008d.]

[DONE 2026-08-29. THE BACKLOG IS 0 AND EVERY REMAINING HANDLER IS TRIAGED - which is not the same as deleted, and the distinction is the point of AC4.

FINAL DISPOSITION of the 57 still baselined, all of them annotated in the file itself:
  39  routes/advanced-billing-routes.ts   -> PROD-008c. Complete unconnected feature, real tables and storage, no UI. Porting means building a UI; retiring means dropping tables. A decision, not cleanup.
   9  routes-document-automation.ts       -> PROD-008d. Same shape: half shadowed, half live-but-uncalled.
   3  routes-deal-tags.ts                 -> half-reachable feature, real tables, no edge counterpart.
   2  routes-companies.ts                 -> real dedup logic, no edge counterpart, no caller.
   1  routes-workflow-mobile.ts           -> PROD-008a: meter billing needs a multi-statement transaction PostgREST cannot express. Deliberate.
   1  routes-business-records.ts          -> bulk status, no counterpart, no caller.
   1  routes-universal-search.ts          -> DELIBERATE network-error fallback, recorded at edge-function-proxy.ts:307-311. Nearly deleted this one before reading the proxy comment.
   1  routes-crm-bulk.ts                  -> real tenant-scoped bulk update, no counterpart, no caller.
Nothing is un-triaged, and the two largest blocks have their own stories rather than sitting here as a number.

CLEARED IN THE FINAL PASS, taking the backlog 2 -> 0: GET /api/webhooks and GET /api/webhooks/health. The list was a straight duplicate of the edge function's GET / branch. The health probe was NOT - a comment I had written the previous round claimed the edge function served both, and it does not: it has no health route, so GET /api/webhooks/health fell into its GET /:id branch and looked up a webhook whose id is the string "health", returning 404. It had no caller in client, server or k8s either, so it was a probe that could only fail. Both deleted, comment corrected. Checking my own assertion rather than trusting it is the only reason that was caught.

AC5 is met: check:shadowed-express reports 0 in the backlog, runs in CI at ci.yml:95, and exits 1 on any novel finding - so the 353rd cannot land.

CORRECTION TO MY OWN PREDICTION, recorded because it was wrong in a useful direction: I closed the previous round saying the small tail was "the only part likely to be genuine cleanup". It is the opposite. Every one of those entries turned out to be a documented deliberate retention or a real feature with no edge counterpart, and the only annotation in the whole file that was actually wrong was the CSV import one, which CRMX-011a had already disproved. The ratchet's headline number always overstated debt and understated unfinished product.]

userStories.title: Advanced billing is fully built and connected to nothing: 39 endpoints, real tables, no route and no UI
userStories.description: As a billing operator, disputes, credit memos, meter anomalies and billing schedules must be usable, because the schema, the storage layer and 39 validated endpoints all exist and none of them can be reached from either backend or from any page.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide the feature's fate FIRST, because the two options differ by an order of magnitude: port the five domains into supabase/functions/billing/ and build the UI, or retire the code and its tables. Do not port the API without deciding whether anything will call it

If porting: add handlers under supabase/functions/billing/handlers/ for anomalies, disputes, credit-memos, schedules and generation, following the existing handler-per-resource layout and the _context.ts drift-table conventions
If porting: the frontend has to be built too. Nothing in client/src references a dispute, credit memo, meter anomaly or billing schedule today, so there is no page to point at the new endpoints

If retiring: server/routes/advanced-billing-routes.ts, the storage methods it calls, and the tables in shared/advanced-billing-schema.ts go together, and the migration that created those tables is recorded as superseded rather than silently orphaned
Either way server/routes/advanced-billing-routes.ts stops being mounted at /api/billing, since that mount is shadowed and misleads anyone reading the registry
npm run check:shadowed-express drops by 39, and npm run check && npm run test pass
userStories.notes: Found 2026-08-29 while working the /api/billing block of PROD-008b, which is the single largest entry in that ratchet at 39 of its 61 handlers. All 39 are in one file. WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE, and it is the reason this is a story rather than another deletion: shared/advanced-billing-schema.ts defines real tables (meterAnomalies:92, billingDisputes:173, billingSchedules:340, creditMemos:395); server/storage.ts implements the ~20 methods the handlers call (createBillingDispute:10083, createBillingSchedule:10389, createCreditMemo:10493, createMeterAnomaly:9939 and the rest); and routes/advanced-billing-routes.ts is 1020 lines of Zod-validated handlers covering the full lifecycle of each - acknowledge/assign/escalate/resolve a dispute, approve/issue/apply/void a credit memo, review/resolve an anomaly. This is not a mock and not a duplicate of a live edge function, which is what every other shadowed router deleted this session turned out to be. THREE INDEPENDENT REASONS IT CANNOT RUN: (1) routes-registry:573 mounts it at /api/billing, and /api/billing is in crmProxies, so the proxy claims the prefix first and Express is never reached - in dev or prod. (2) supabase/functions/billing/ has handlers for invoices, cycles, adjustments, configurations, payment-methods, service-entries and analytics, and NONE for these five domains, so the requests would 404 there if anything sent them. (3) Nothing sends them: grepping client/src for dispute, credit memo, meter anomaly or billing schedule returns no page and no component. The frontend's billing calls are address, adjustments, analytics, configurations, cycles, generate-invoices, info, invoices, payment-methods, rules and service-entries - a disjoint set. So nothing is visibly broken and no user has lost anything; the feature was simply never connected. It contributes 0 typecheck errors, which is why no QUALITY-002 batch has ever touched it. DONE IN THIS PASS: a file header recording all of the above, so the next person reading 1020 lines of plausible billing code knows it cannot execute before they invest in it. Nothing was deleted - removing real, complete work on the strength of it being unreachable is the call this story exists to put to a human.

userStories.title: Document automation is built and unreached: 17 endpoints, real tables, half shadowed and half uncalled

acceptanceCriteria: Decide the feature's fate first, exactly as PROD-008c does for billing: port and build the UI, or retire the code with its tables. Do not port an API nothing will call

If porting, the /api/documents/* half needs handlers in supabase/functions/documents/ for generated, uploads, ai-extract, batch-generate and generate; today that function reads parts[0] as a document id, so those paths resolve to a lookup for a document named 'generated'

The /api/document-templates and /api/document-field-mappings halves are NOT shadowed and would run - they simply have no caller. Either build the UI that uses them or retire them; leaving live-but-uncalled endpoints is the state this story exists to end
If retiring, server/routes-document-automation.ts, its storage writes and shared/document-automation-schema.ts go together, with the creating migration recorded as superseded
The registry stops mounting it, since app.use(default) with no prefix hides which paths it claims
npm run check:shadowed-express drops by 9, and npm run check && npm run test pass
userStories.notes: Found 2026-08-29 by checking /api/documents the same way PROD-008c checked /api/billing - the two largest blocks in the shadowed-express ratchet, 39 and 9 of its 61 handlers. Both turned out to be the same thing: a complete back end nobody wired. THE FILE IS server/routes-document-automation.ts, 549 lines, and it is mounted with NO prefix (routes-registry:617, app.use(documentAutomationRoutes.default)), so its routes register at their literal paths and split two ways. NINE UNDER /api/documents ARE SHADOWED: that prefix is proxied, so supabase/functions/documents/ answers, and that function - written for DocumentBuilder.tsx - serves only /, /:id and /:id/pdf. It has no branch for generated, uploads, ai-extract, batch-generate or generate, and it reads parts[0] as a document id, so those paths would resolve to a lookup for a document named 'generated'. EIGHT MORE UNDER /api/document-templates AND /api/document-field-mappings ARE NOT SHADOWED and would run - and nothing calls them: grepping client/src for either prefix returns nothing. So half cannot run and the other half is never asked to. IT IS REAL, not a mock: shared/document-automation-schema.ts defines documentTemplates:45, generatedDocuments:89, documentUploads:136 and documentFieldMappings:191, and the handlers do real Drizzle inserts (128, 395, 513) with multer file upload. Its single Math.random() is a unique filename suffix, correctly ignored by check:no-random-metrics because it sits inside a template literal. The only /api/documents call in the whole frontend is client/src/lib/document-export.ts hitting /:id/pdf, which the edge function does serve. DONE IN THIS PASS: a file header recording all of the above so the next reader knows it cannot execute; nothing deleted, for the same reason as PROD-008c - removing real complete work because it is unreachable is a decision for a human. SEPARATE AND LIVE, recorded on SUPA-024 rather than here: DocumentManagement.tsx is a different feature on a third prefix and three of its four queries 404 in production.

userStories.title: Inbound provider webhooks are shadowed: Stripe, Salesforce, QuickBooks and calendar receivers never run in dev
userStories.description: As a business whose billing depends on Stripe events, the inbound webhook receivers must be reachable, because /api/webhooks is proxied to an edge function that only manages OUTBOUND webhooks and has no receiver for any provider.
acceptanceCriteria: Reproduce first: server/integrations/webhook-routes.ts registers POST /api/webhooks/stripe, /salesforce, /quickbooks, /google-calendar, /microsoft-calendar and a generic /:provider. crmProxies maps '/api/webhooks' to the webhooks edge function, which serves outbound webhook MANAGEMENT - register, list, test, regenerate-secret, logs - and has no provider branch at all. In dev an inbound POST falls through every edge branch to the 404

Establish where providers actually post in production before deciding anything. The frontend rewrite to functions.printyx.net does not apply - a provider posts from outside the app - so this depends on DNS and ingress, which cannot be read from the repo. Three outcomes: it reaches Express and works, it reaches the functions host and 404s, or it reaches the Cloudflare Pages origin and never reaches a backend
Do NOT delete these handlers. They are the only implementation, and the generic /:provider receiver plus five named ones are a real integration surface

If they are to move to the edge side, the raw body is load-bearing: Stripe signature verification needs the unparsed payload, which is why the Express route uses rawBodyParser. An edge port that reads req.json() first cannot verify a signature

Note the shape collision if ported as-is: POST /api/webhooks/:provider and the edge function's outbound-management routes share a path space, so a provider named 'events' or 'logs' would be ambiguous. Separate prefixes (e.g. /api/webhooks/inbound/:provider) are worth considering
Whichever way it resolves, the entry comes out of docs/shadowed-express-baseline.json or the proxy entry is narrowed
userStories.notes:
Found 2026-08-20 while triaging shadowed clusters for PROD-008b. This one is the reason the sweep reads each handler rather than trusting the count: /api/webhooks looks like nine duplicate handlers under a proxied prefix, and it is nine handlers for a completely different feature than the edge function serves. CLAUDE.md already records that Stripe's live webhook URL is /api/webhooks/stripe and NOT under /api/billing, which makes the proxy entry directly relevant to billing. Severity depends entirely on the ingress question in AC2 - if providers reach the Express host directly this is a dev-only annoyance, and if they reach the functions host it means inbound Stripe events have been 404ing. That is not answerable from the repository and is the first thing to check.
--- 2026-08-22 --- A SECOND LAYER OF SHADOWING INSIDE THIS FILE, found by the
new npm run check:route-shadowing and recorded here because it changes what
"un-shadow the webhook routes" has to do.

server/integrations/webhook-routes.ts registers POST /api/webhooks/:provider
FIRST, then five provider-specific handlers (salesforce, stripe,
microsoft-calendar, google-calendar, quickbooks). Express matches in
registration order, so none of the five has ever run - even before the
crmProxies entry made the whole file unreachable.

That is NOT a security hole, and it matters that it is not: the generic handler
calls the same WebhookService.processWebhook, which verifies the provider's HMAC
signature (webhook-service.ts:50) before dispatching on the provider name. The
five are redundant with it rather than a missing verification step.

Reordering them would be a regression. microsoft-calendar and google-calendar
parse with express.json() rather than the rawBodyParser, so req.body is already
a parsed object and the exact bytes the HMAC is computed over are gone - the
PA-018 trap called out in processWebhook's own signature. Registering them first
would turn calendar webhooks that currently work (through the generic path) into
signature failures.

So whoever picks this story up has a decision to make FIRST, before touching the
proxy: either delete the five and keep the generic dispatcher, or fix their body
parsing and register them above :provider. They are baselined in
docs/route-shadowing-baseline.json with that explanation in the file, so the
gate will not nag and nobody will "fix" the order by accident.
--- 2026-08-22 --- DECISION TAKEN on the five redundant handlers, and a
STRUCTURAL FINDING that changes what "un-shadow the receiver" can mean.

DELETED the five provider-specific POST handlers (salesforce, stripe,
microsoft-calendar, google-calendar, quickbooks). The evidence was one-sided:
they are redundant with the generic POST /api/webhooks/:provider, which calls the
same WebhookService.processWebhook, verifies the provider HMAC
(webhook-service.ts:50, covered by server/tests/unit/webhook-signature.test.ts)
and dispatches through the same switch they duplicated; and two of them parsed
with express.json() rather than the rawBodyParser, so the raw bytes the HMAC is
computed over were already gone. Reordering them - the "obvious" fix - would have
turned working calendar webhooks into signature failures. Shadowed backlog 8 -> 3,
and check:route-shadowing reached 0 with them gone.

THE FINDING, which is the part that matters: THE RECEIVER CANNOT BE UN-SHADOWED
BY ROUTING ALONE. /api/webhooks is in crmProxies, so a production delivery goes
to supabase/functions/webhooks/. That function AUTHENTICATES BEFORE IT ROUTES -
index.ts:13-24 reads the Bearer token and returns 401 if there is no valid user,
before normalizePath is ever called. Stripe, Salesforce, Intuit and Google do not
send a Supabase JWT. So an inbound delivery gets 401, not the 404 I would have
assumed from the missing branch, and adding receiver branches to that function
would not help - they sit behind the auth gate.

WHAT THAT IMPLIES for whoever does this: the receiver needs its own
UNAUTHENTICATED edge function, the shape CLAUDE.md documents for
public-calculator and signup - a handler that never calls auth.getUser, with the
provider HMAC as the only gate (which is correct: the signature IS the
authentication for a webhook). It cannot be a branch inside the authenticated
webhooks function. Porting work is then: the ~100 lines of verifyWebhookSignature
onto Deno Web Crypto (HMAC-SHA256 plus a constant-time compare), and the ~400
lines of per-provider processing that write through drizzle today.

STILL NOT MEASURED: no request was made against a deployed environment, so the
401 is read from the code path, not observed. PROD-020 remains the gate on that,
and its egress is still blocked.
--- 2026-08-27 --- A CORRECTION TO THIS STORY, and the missing piece built.

THE CORRECTION. The 2026-08-22 note said the porting work was "the ~100 lines of verifyWebhookSignature onto Deno Web Crypto and the ~400 lines of per-provider processing that WRITE THROUGH DRIZZLE today". The second half was wrong, and it is the half the story's AC3 rests on. There was no drizzle write anywhere in webhook-service.ts. All eleven "data synchronization" methods — syncSalesforceAccount, syncSalesforceContact, syncSalesforceOpportunity, syncStripeCustomer, processStripePayment, syncStripeSubscription, syncMicrosoftCalendarEvent, deleteMicrosoftCalendarEvent, syncGoogleCalendarChanges, syncQuickBooksCustomer, syncQuickBooksInvoice, syncQuickBooksPayment — returned { success: true, processed: true, message: "... synchronized successfully" } and touched nothing. syncSalesforceAccount built a customerData object and dropped it under the comment "Implementation would depend on your specific database operations". That is why `db`, `systemIntegrations` and the three oauth-config clients were imported and never used.

WHY THAT MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS. processed:true made the route answer 200. A 2xx tells Stripe and Intuit the delivery was accepted and STOPS the retry, so every signature-verified event was acknowledged and thrown away. The current 401 from the authenticated edge function is, perversely, the safer failure: it keeps the provider retrying. So "port the receiver to an unauthenticated edge function" must NOT be done until there is somewhere to put the event — otherwise the port converts a recoverable failure into permanent silent loss.

BUILT: that somewhere. inbound_webhook_events (shared/platform-integrations-schema.ts, hand-run migration drizzle/migrations/_inbound_webhook_events.sql per the _backfill_*.sql convention — not journalled, because a journal entry with no snapshot widens the COP-M00 gap). Everything else in that file is OUTBOUND; this is the first inbound table. tenant_id is NULLABLE on purpose: an inbound webhook carries no tenant context, attribution runs through the provider's account id (Stripe account, QuickBooks realmId) back to platform_integrations, and an unattributed delivery is still worth keeping because a dropped event cannot be re-requested. A unique index on (provider, external_event_id) makes a re-delivery land on the existing row; Postgres treats NULLs as distinct, so Google pushes, which carry no id, are each kept.

WebhookService is now two jobs and only two: verify the HMAC over the raw bytes (unchanged, still covered by webhook-signature.test.ts), then record. describeDelivery reads the same fields the deleted switches read — Stripe type/id/account, Salesforce event/replayId/organizationId, Graph value[0].changeType/subscriptionId/tenantId, QuickBooks entity name.operation pairs plus realmId, Google resourceState/messageNumber/channelId — so the classification survives the deletion. Nothing reports processed:true any more, because nothing processes anything.

A SECOND DEFECT FOUND WHILE DOING IT: the route did JSON.parse(rawBody) unconditionally. A Google Calendar push has an EMPTY body — everything identifying it is in x-goog-* headers — so JSON.parse('') threw and the receiver answered 500 to every Google notification, which Google reads as a failing endpoint and eventually unsubscribes the channel. The route now tolerates an empty body and folds the x-goog-* headers into the payload. Status codes are also split: a rejected signature stays 400 (a retry can never fix it), but a failure to STORE is now 503, because answering 400 there would tell the provider to give up on an event we do not have.

STILL OPEN, and the story stays passes:false for these. AC2 (where do providers actually post in production) is unanswerable from the repository and is still the gate — PROD-020. The unauthenticated edge receiver is not built; it now has a destination, and the shape it needs is the public-calculator/signup one (never calls auth.getUser, provider HMAC as the only gate) on a separate prefix so it does not collide with the outbound-management routes. Nothing consumes inbound_webhook_events yet; a processor is a separate story, and the table records status/processed_at/processing_error for it.

VERIFIED: 18 tests across the two webhook suites (11 new, covering per-provider descriptors, the no-write-on-bad-signature path, re-delivery resolving to the existing row, and the null-id path); 3681 tests pass; tsc holds at 496; build passes; lint 10658 -> 10626; migration-journal, phantom-column, duplicate-table, spread-insert-key, route-shadowing, shadowed-express and route-ownership guards all green. NOT VERIFIED: no SQL was executed — this container has no database, so the migration is unapplied and the insert path has never run against Postgres.
--- 2026-08-27, same day, second pass --- THE STRIPE RECEIVER WAS POINTED AT THE WRONG HANDLER.

Found while reading EDGE-002c, which mentions in passing that routes-subscriptions.ts "also serves POST /webhooks/stripe". It does, and the two paths are not the same one:

  scripts/setup-stripe-products.ts:362 tells the operator to configure the Stripe dashboard with
    https://your-domain.com/api/webhooks/stripe
  and CLAUDE.md records the same URL. That path is the generic receiver in
  server/integrations/webhook-routes.ts -> WebhookService, whose Stripe branch was one of the eleven stubs.

  The real billing logic is StripeService.handleWebhookEventEnhanced -- checkout.session.completed,
  checkout.session.expired, customer.subscription.created/updated/deleted/trial_will_end, invoice.paid and more,
  with sixteen database writes behind it -- and it is mounted at
    /api/subscriptions/webhooks/stripe
  because routes-subscriptions.ts declares router.post('/webhooks/stripe') under the /api/subscriptions mount.

So a delivery to the documented URL was signature-verified and then dropped, and subscription state never moved from a real Stripe event. This is not the same defect as the eleven stubs; it is why the Stripe stub in particular was never noticed as one.

FIXED: the generic receiver now records the delivery and then hands a verified Stripe event to StripeService.handleWebhookEventEnhanced, so the documented URL is the working one. Lazy import, so requiring WebhookService does not pull in the Stripe SDK and an instance with no Stripe keys still records rather than failing at import. Row status moves received -> processed | failed, with the handler message kept in processing_error. A duplicate re-delivery is NOT re-dispatched. A handler failure still answers 2xx at the transport level, because the delivery is already stored and a retry would only duplicate it -- the failure lives on the row.

ALSO FIXED, a real security gap in the same verifier: verifyStripeSignature checked the HMAC and IGNORED the timestamp. Stripe's own stripe.webhooks.constructEvent enforces a 300-second window; this one did not, so a correctly signed payload captured off the wire once stayed valid against the endpoint indefinitely and could be replayed at any time. Same 300s default now, with tests for stale, non-numeric and just-inside-the-window.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT FIX, and it is the same wall as before: /api/webhooks is in crmProxies, so in DEV the whole prefix forwards to the authenticated webhooks edge function and the Express receiver never runs. Whether a real Stripe delivery reaches Express in PRODUCTION is the ingress question in AC2, still unanswerable from the repository (PROD-020). What changed is that the Express side is now correct if it is reached, and the edge receiver -- when someone builds it -- has both a destination table and a working reference implementation to port.

VERIFIED: 25 tests across the two webhook suites (15 recording/dispatch, 10 signature); 3688 tests pass; tsc holds at 496; build passes; lint holds at 10626; route-shadowing, shadowed-express and route-ownership guards green. NOT VERIFIED: no Stripe event was delivered to anything -- the dispatch is covered by a mocked StripeService, not a live webhook.
[2026-08-29 THE RECEIVER NOW RUNS. The last AC - "the entry comes out of docs/shadowed-express-baseline.json or the proxy entry is narrowed" - is done, by narrowing, and it did NOT need AC2's ingress question answered first.

The previous round's note in webhook-routes.ts read: "the receiver cannot simply be un-shadowed, because the edge function that owns the prefix authenticates before it routes." That is true of the PREFIX and false of the ROUTE. Un-proxying /api/webhooks would indeed break the outbound management surface the edge function legitimately owns (list, create, test, regenerate-secret, logs). Mounting the one inbound POST ahead of the proxy takes nothing from it.

WHY IT IS SAFE, and this is the load-bearing fact: the edge function has POST / (create), POST /:id/test and POST /:id/regenerate-secret, and NO POST /:id. So POST /api/webhooks/<provider> is a shape it does not serve - it would have fallen past every branch even if the caller had a JWT. The 401 came first only because auth.getUser() runs before routing. The two surfaces were never in conflict; the proxy simply claimed the whole prefix.

WHAT CHANGED: server/integrations/webhook-routes.ts exports `inboundWebhookReceiver`, a router carrying only POST /api/webhooks/:provider with its rawBodyParser (the raw bytes are load-bearing - PA-018 - so the parser moved with it). routes-registry mounts it immediately BEFORE registerEdgeFunctionProxy at :297. The default export still works for any other consumer, via router.use(inboundWebhookReceiver) at the bottom. The health probe and the outbound list stay shadowed deliberately: the edge function serves both, and mounting the whole default router early would have stolen GET /api/webhooks from it.

So the INTEG-WEBHOOK-001 work - storing the delivery to inbound_webhook_events before anything acts on it, dispatching to StripeService.handleWebhookEventEnhanced, the 300-second replay window - is reachable for the first time. shadowed-express baseline 3 -> 2.

LOCKED by server/tests/unit/inbound-webhook-ordering.test.ts (4 cases), because ORDERING IS INVISIBLE TO tsc: the mount precedes the proxy call; the receiver is a separate router and the default one is not mounted early; the edge function still has no bare POST /:id branch, so the arrangement stays safe; and rawBodyParser is still on the route. MUTATION-TESTED by moving the mount after the proxy, which fails the first case. One bug found while writing it, worth recording: the first version of the POST-branch check matched `&& !webhookId` - the create branch - and reported a collision that does not exist. The positive form `&& webhookId` is the one that matters.

STILL NOT VERIFIED, unchanged: no Stripe event has been delivered to anything. AC2's question - where a provider actually posts in production - is still unanswerable from the repository, and this fix deliberately does not depend on the answer: it makes Express correct on whichever host receives the delivery.]

userStories.title: Edge functions enforce authentication and tenancy but not RBAC: 281 of 284 have no permission check
userStories.description: As a tenant admin, role restrictions must hold on the backend production actually runs, because every deliberate permission gate written on the Express side sits in a handler the edge-function proxy shadows.
acceptanceCriteria: Reproduce first: supabase/functions/_shared/rbac.ts exists and is complete - requireRoleLevel for level checks off the JWT, requirePermission with a DB lookup and a 60s per-(user, permission) cache. Exactly three edge functions import it: monitoring-clients, blog-agents and dashboard-widgets. The other 281 authenticate the user, resolve the tenant, and then serve any authenticated member of that tenant regardless of role

Confirm the concrete case this was found through: PROD-008's duplicate-route work added inventory.item.view to GET /api/vendors and /api/vendors/:id and inventory.po.view to /api/purchase-orders, because the winning Express handler had no gate while the shadowed copy did. Those winners were themselves shadowed by the crmProxies entries, so the fix never executed - and supabase/functions/{vendors,product-models,purchase-orders} contain zero permission references. The exposure that work described is still live

Do NOT read this as 'everything is exposed'. Tenant isolation holds - every function filters by tenant_id, which is the boundary CLAUDE.md calls security-critical - and many endpoints are legitimately open to all roles. The gap is that role-level restriction is absent on the side that serves production, so an endpoint that SHOULD be restricted has nothing restricting it

Produce the inventory before the fix: for each edge function, which permission (if any) its Express predecessor enforced. server/middleware/enhanced-rbac-middleware.ts and the requirePermission call sites in the retired handlers are the source; git history has the ones already deleted
Gate the endpoints that need it, starting with the ones a deliberate gate was already written for: vendors, product-models, purchase-orders, and anything under platform-admin
Add a ratchet so a new edge function cannot ship without an explicit decision - either a permission check or a recorded 'open to all roles' entry
userStories.notes:
Found 2026-08-20 while retiring the /api/vendors cluster for PROD-008b. Deleting the Express handlers prompted the question of what their RBAC gates would cost - and the answer was nothing, because they never ran. acceptanceCriteria: Read docs/rbac-landscape.md first - it is the verified map of both role systems, all five permission vocabularies, and which of them production actually uses. The decisions below are ordered there and taking them out of order exports a lockout to production

Confirm the consequence rather than assuming it: PermissionComputationService builds req.user.permissions from rolePermissions -> permissions, i.e. the seeded set. requirePermission passes only on hasAllPermissions (platform admin, level 8) or a code in that set. A gate naming an unseeded code is unsatisfiable for every other role

Decide which ROLE SYSTEM survives before touching vocabularies. The `roles` table (System A) is what signup and the edge functions use; enhancedRoles + permissions + rolePermissions (System B) is what every Express requirePermission gate reads. Nothing populates System B per tenant - server/rbac-initializer.ts is its only bridge and has no importers, plus it calls two methods that do not exist

Settle which seeder owns tenant initialization FIRST. server/rbac-initializer.ts calls enhanced-rbac-seeder (38 codes, a third vocabulary), not the rbac-seeder that npm run seed:rbac runs (131 codes). Both write permissions + rolePermissions + enhancedRoles. Two seeders writing the same tables with different vocabularies is the defect underneath this one

Decide the canonical vocabulary before changing anything. The seeder's is the one with data behind it; the helper's is the one 77 route gates reference. Whichever wins, the other has to be migrated, not deleted - existing tenants have rolePermissions rows keyed on the seeded codes

Check what those 77 routes are supposed to be. Some may be legitimately admin-only, in which case the fix is an explicit role-level gate rather than a permission code that reads as fine-grained and is not

Do NOT close SEC-EDGE-001 by copying these gates onto the edge functions. That would export the lockout to the backend production actually runs, turning a silent admin-only feature into a silent admin-only feature on both hosts
docs/permission-vocabulary-baseline.json goes to 0 and check:permission-vocab becomes a hard gate

--- 2026-08-20 (loop round 56) ---

TRIAGED. `npm run check:permission-vocab --triage` now derives these numbers
rather than leaving them in a throwaway script:

  77 unsatisfiable gates
    10 shadowed by the proxy - never ran either way, no impact
    67 live on Express
      43 of those are called by the frontend
      43 of those 43 sit on a prefix that ALSO has an edge function

THE INVERSION, which is the clearest statement of the whole problem and was not

function exists but the prefix is NOT proxied. So for the same 43 endpoints:

  DEV  runs Express, where the gate names a code no seeded role holds, so every
       non-platform-admin gets 403.
  PROD runs the edge function, and product-models, purchase-orders, supplies,
       inventory, managed-services, professional-services, product-accessories,
       technician-management, warehouse-operations, meter-readings and import

Locked to admins in dev; open to every authenticated tenant member in

gap: these are real pages - product catalogue, purchase orders, technician
management, warehouse operations.

That answers the question left open last round about whether these routes are
used. They are. It also explains why the dev-side lockout has not been
reported: a developer testing as an admin never meets it, and a production user
never meets it either because production does not run that code.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX ORDER. SEC-EDGE-001 (gate the edge functions) and this
story are the same fix and have to land together for these 43. Gating the edge
side alone with the current codes reproduces the dev lockout in production;
fixing the vocabulary alone leaves production ungated. The sequence that works
is: reconcile the vocabulary so the codes are satisfiable, verify against a
non-admin role that the Express routes open, and only then carry the same codes
onto the edge functions.

NOT DOING IT BLIND: which vocabulary wins is a data decision, not a code one.
Existing tenants have rolePermissions rows keyed on the SEEDED codes, so
renaming the seeder breaks live grants; renaming the helper constant touches 77
gates but no data. That points at the helper constant as the thing to migrate,
but it needs confirming against a real database before anyone writes the
migration.

--- 2026-08-20 (loop round 57) ---

THERE IS A THIRD VOCABULARY, and it is the one real tenants get. This corrects
what I wrote last round.

`npm run check:permission-vocab --vocabularies`:

  route gates        132  server/middleware/rbac-route-helper.ts
  npm run seed:rbac  131  server/database-updater/seeders/rbac-seeder.ts
  new-tenant init     38  server/enhanced-rbac-seeder.ts

  gates that seed:rbac can satisfy:      39
  gates that new-tenant init satisfies:   2
  overlap between the two seeders:        2

server/rbac-initializer.ts is what initializes RBAC for a NEW TENANT, and it
imports enhanced-rbac-seeder - not the one `npm run seed:rbac` runs. Its
vocabulary is a third namespace again: lead.view_own, ticket.*, quote.*,
financial.*, where the gates say sales.lead.view_own and the documented seeder
says sales.lead.view_own or operations.inventory.view.

So a tenant created through the normal path holds 38 permissions, of which TWO
can satisfy any route gate in the codebase. Every other gated route denies every
non-platform-admin in that tenant. That is not a naming inconsistency, it is the
RBAC system not being connected to itself.

CORRECTION TO ROUND 56: I wrote that "existing tenants have rolePermissions rows
keyed on the SEEDED codes, so renaming the seeder breaks live grants", and used
that to argue the helper constant was the safer thing to migrate. That reasoning
was built on the wrong seeder. Which codes a tenant holds depends on which
seeder ran for it, and for tenants created through the initializer it is neither
the gates' vocabulary nor the documented one.

WHAT THAT CHANGES ABOUT THE FIX. The decision is no longer "pick one of two and
migrate the other". Three namespaces exist and at most two codes are common to
all three, so almost nothing is preserved whichever way it goes - which makes
this cheaper than it looked, not more expensive. The real questions are:

  1. Which seeder should own tenant initialization at all? Having two that write
     the same three tables with different vocabularies is the defect underneath
     the defect.
  2. Once that is settled, the gates' constant can be rewritten against it in
     one pass, and check:permission-vocab goes to zero.
  3. Only then does carrying the gates onto the edge functions (SEC-EDGE-001)
     mean anything.

NO DATABASE NEEDED AFTER ALL, which is worth noting because round 56 parked this
as blocked on one: the three vocabularies and which seeder the initializer calls
are all readable from the repo. What a database would add is the count of
tenants seeded each way, which affects migration effort but not the decision.

--- 2026-08-20 (loop round 58) ---

STOPPED INVESTIGATING AND WROTE THE MAP: docs/rbac-landscape.md. Four rounds
running, each one corrected the previous round's model - two vocabularies, then
three, and this round two more plus a second role system. That pattern is a
signal that the model needed writing down once, properly, rather than being
re-derived and re-corrected in story notes.

WHAT THIS ROUND ADDED, and it reframes the story again:

THERE ARE TWO ROLE SYSTEMS, sharing no tables and reading nothing of each
other's.

  System A - the `roles` table, one flat row per role with a JSONB permissions
  blob. This is what PRODUCTION uses: signup looks up code='COMPANY_ADMIN' in it,
  puts that id in app_metadata.roleId and users.role_id, and fails loudly with
  MISSING_ADMIN_ROLE without it. supabase/functions/_shared/rbac.ts reads it too.

  System B - enhancedRoles + permissions + rolePermissions + userRoleAssignments,
  a normalised catalogue. This is what enhanced-rbac-middleware reads, i.e. what
  every requirePermission gate on an Express route consults. Both seeders I spent
  the last two rounds comparing write to System B.

So the 77 unsatisfiable gates are not merely misnamed. They query a catalogue
that nothing populates per tenant.

THE BRIDGE IS DEAD CODE. server/rbac-initializer.ts is the only thing that would
seed System B for a new tenant, and it has NO importers anywhere in server/,
client/ or supabase/. It would also fail if called: tsc says
rbacSeeder.seedEnterpriseRoles and rbacService.assignUserRole do not exist
(rbac-initializer.ts:63,71), and the role id it assigns,
company-admin-${tenantId}, is not an id either seeder creates. Those three
errors sit inside the 989-error typecheck baseline, which is exactly why nobody
has seen them.

FIVE VOCABULARIES, not three. The two System A seeders store permissions as
JSONB blobs in two different shapes again - { sales: ['*'] } in role-seeder.ts
and { modules: ['all'], actions: ['all'] } in multi-location-role-seeder.ts,
which has no importer either. _shared/rbac.ts's flattenPermissions would render
the first as `sales.*`, matching no gate.

CORRECTION TO ROUND 57: I framed the decision as "which seeder owns tenant
initialization". That question is downstream of a bigger one - which ROLE SYSTEM
survives - and answering it alone would not have helped, because the seeder that
"owns" initialization is unreachable code calling methods that do not exist.

The map records what is verified, what is not (tenant counts, which seeder ran
where, whether seed:rbac has ever been run against production), and the order the
three decisions have to be made in. No code changed this round; the ratchet stays
at 77.

userStories.title: Workflow automation never fires: every trigger seam sits in a shadowed Express handler
userStories.description: As a tenant who built an automation, my workflows must actually enrol when the event happens, because today every documented trigger seam lives in an Express handler that runs on neither host, so no event-triggered workflow has ever started.
acceptanceCriteria: Reproduce first: grep dispatchWorkflowEvent. Every call site is in a handler under a crmProxies prefix - server/routes-deals.ts:250 (deal.stage_changed, under /api/deals), server/routes-business-records.ts:338 and :439 (record.created / record.updated, under /api/business-records). The proxy is registered before every domain route, and production never reaches Express at all, so none of them runs
Confirm no edge function dispatches these events: supabase/functions/workflows and workflow-automation are the MANAGEMENT API (create/list/execute on demand), not the trigger seam

Port dispatch to the edge side. supabase/functions/_shared/workflow-conditions.ts already holds the evaluation half (pure, 32 tests). What remains is the query chain - active workflows for the tenant, their enabled event triggers matching the name, conditions per trigger - and enrolment

Enrolment must keep both guarantees CRMX-008 built: the kill switch (workflows.status must be 'active') and idempotency via the workflow_executions.dedupe_key unique index, including the insert-race path where a concurrent dispatch wins

Wire the seam into the edge handlers that replace those Express ones: the deals PATCH/PUT branch (stage change) and the business-records create/update branches. Wrap in try/catch so a dispatch failure never breaks the primary write, matching the Express behaviour

Decide what advances an enrolled execution. Express enrols and kicks inline, with the boot-started sweeper as the durable backstop; an edge enrolment can only queue. Confirm the sweeper actually runs in production before relying on it, or the executions queue forever
A test that a stage change enrols exactly one execution, and that a second dispatch with the same dedupe key enrols none
userStories.notes:
Found 2026-08-20 during the PROD-008b shadowed-handler sweep, by checking what the /api/deals cluster would lose before deleting it. CLAUDE.md documents these events as wired - 'Event names wired: record.created/record.updated (routes-business-records), deal.stage_changed (routes-deals PUT)' - and they are, to code that cannot run. This is the most consequential thing the shadowed-Express audit has turned up: the automation product has a durable executor, a 15-table schema, a sweeper, idempotency and a kill switch, and nothing to start it. A fourth call site, server/services/web-form-processor.ts:168, is reached from a background processor started in server/index.ts rather than from a route, so it may still fire - check that separately rather than assuming either way. The Express handlers holding the three dead seams are deliberately NOT deleted; they are the reference implementation for this port and are the reason the /api/deals and /api/business-records clusters stay in docs/shadowed-express-baseline.json.
--- 2026-08-20 (loop round 49) ---

PORTED. All three seams now dispatch from the edge functions that actually run.

supabase/functions/_shared/workflow-dispatch.ts carries dispatchWorkflowEvent +
enrollExecution onto PostgREST, over the condition evaluator lifted last round.
Wired into supabase/functions/deals/index.ts (PATCH/PUT, guarded on the stage
actually moving) and supabase/functions/business-records/index.ts (create and
update). 20 tests against a fake PostgREST client, drift-verified.

BOTH CRMX-008 GUARANTEES CARRIED OVER, because losing either is worse than not
dispatching:

  KILL SWITCH - workflows.status must be 'active'. Asserted for paused, draft
  and archived.

  IDEMPOTENCY - the dedupe key is scoped by TRIGGER, not just by the caller's
  token (`${triggerId}:${callerKey}`): two triggers on one workflow listening to
  the same event are separate enrolments, and a shared key would silently drop
  one. The insert race is handled by RE-READING after a failed insert rather
  than trusting the pre-check - a concurrent dispatch winning is not an error,
  the desired state (exactly one execution) holds either way. Both paths tested.

An execution pins the LATEST workflow version at enrolment, so editing a
workflow cannot change the steps of a run already in flight; a workflow with no
version does not enrol at all rather than enrolling against nothing.

TWO THINGS THE PORT SURFACED, neither of which I changed silently:

(1) The business-records edge fn writes to `companies`, not `business_records` -
the COP-B00 canonical-table contradiction. So the record.created/record.updated
payload reads off the mapped company row, and its field names come from
mapCompanyToBusinessRecord rather than being copied from the Express version.
Anyone writing a condition against these events is matching that shape.

(2) The record.updated dedupe key does not do what its Express comment says.
That comment claims it keys on the update timestamp "so a retry of the same
request doesn't re-enroll" - but the handler SETS updated_at to now on every
request, so a retry produces a different key and does enrol again. It guards a
double-dispatch within one invocation, nothing more. Real retry-idempotency
needs a caller-supplied token and no caller sends one. Ported as-is with the
comment corrected in place, rather than changing behaviour under cover of a
port.

STILL OPEN, and it is the AC that decides whether any of this is visible:
enrolment queues an execution; it does not run one. An edge invocation ends with
its response, so the durable sweeper is what advances a queued execution, and
the sweeper is boot-started by the Node server. Whether that server runs in
production has NOT been verified from here. If it does not, this turns "never
enrolled" into "enrolled and never advanced" - better, because the evidence is
then in the table, but still not a working automation.

The Express seams are left in place. They are unreachable, they stay in the
shadowed baseline, and they are now the second copy of logic that lives in
_shared - so the next pass should either delete them or lock them to the shared
module, not leave them to drift.

--- 2026-08-20 (loop round 50) ---

THE SWEEPER QUESTION, ANSWERED AS FAR AS THIS ENVIRONMENT CAN. It cannot be
closed by code here, and the reason is worth stating precisely rather than
leaving as "unverified".

startWorkflowRuntime() is a setInterval registered in server/index.ts:397 at
Node boot, unref'd. There is no pg_cron entry for it: drizzle/cron/ holds nine
schedule files (billing, contract-renewals, customer-success, email-marketing,
leases, mileage, reports, retention, subscriptions) and none of them is the
workflow runtime. The one manual trigger, POST /api/workflow-runtime/tick, is
Express-only and NOT proxied, so production cannot reach it either. So queued
executions advance exactly when the Node process runs, and nothing in the repo
schedules the tick independently of that process.

RESOLVED, and it changes the shape of the problem: web-form-processor is NOT a
separate case. startWebFormProcessor() (server/index.ts:406) is the same
construction - a setInterval at Node boot, unref'd - so the form.submitted seam
shares the sweeper's fate rather than being a surviving path. The earlier note
recorded it as possibly-still-firing; it is not more likely to fire than the
sweeper is.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX IS NOT CHEAP. The pg_cron pattern in drizzle/cron/*.sql is
pg_net POST -> a functions.printyx.net endpoint with an internal bearer token,
so scheduling a sweeper tick needs an EDGE endpoint that can advance an
execution. There is no edge executor: supabase/functions/workflows serves the
management API and its /execute branch deliberately returns 501, explaining
that workflow_executions is owned by the durable runtime and a hand-written
`running` row cannot be resumed or deduplicated. The step executor is
server/services/workflow-execution-service.ts, Node-only. Porting it is a
project, not a round, and the three options - port the executor to Deno, expose
the Express tick to pg_net, or run the Node process as a worker - are a
deployment decision as much as a code one.

CLOSED THIS ROUND: the duplication the port created. Two copies of the
condition evaluator now exist and NEITHER is a fossil - the edge copy backs the
seams ported in CRMX-008a, and the Node copy is still reached from the web-form
processor. That is different from the renewal-retier and email-autopilot cases
retired in PROD-008b, where one side was dead and the parity test was guarding a
corpse. Here a drift would mean the same trigger conditions decide differently
depending on which path fired the event, so
server/tests/unit/workflow-conditions-parity.test.ts locks them: 20 condition
sets x 5 payloads = 100 assertions, following the mirror + parity convention the
codebase already uses for gpt5-prompts, renewal-analysis, supply-analysis and
document-html rather than importing across the boundary. Drift-verified three
ways (OR as AND fails 4, groups ANDed rather than ORed fails 1, is_null on the
coerced value fails 4).

A MUTATION-TEST MISTAKE WORTH RECORDING, since it nearly passed as evidence.
My first two drift runs "passed" for bad reasons: one wrote broken syntax
through a shell-escaping slip, so vitest reported "no tests" rather than a
failure, and the other changed `||` to `??` on a null-valued field - which is
not a drift at all, since null is nullish and both operators produce the same
result. A mutation that does not change behaviour proves nothing; neither does
one that stops the file compiling. Read the count, not just the absence of a
pass.

The result is now the opposite of what it was: there are exactly THREE production call sites and none of them is in a shadowed Express handler — dispatchWorkflowEventSafe in supabase/functions/deals/index.ts (deal.stage_changed), the same in supabase/functions/business-records/index.ts (record.created and record.updated, two sites), and dispatchWorkflowEvent in server/services/web-form-processor.ts (form.submitted, Node side, not proxied).
