userStories.title: Calendar OAuth: no authorize flow production can reach, and two connection stores
userStories.description: As a user, connecting my Google or Microsoft calendar must work in production and land where the events code reads it.
acceptanceCriteria: Add an authorize + callback pair in the edge tree that requests CALENDAR scopes, distinct from oauth-proxy which requests sign-in scopes.
Write the resulting tokens into calendar_connections, the table supabase/functions/meetings/handlers/events.ts reads for push propagation.
Decide and record whether system_integrations or calendar_connections is canonical for a calendar connection; today the Express OAuth flow writes one and the events code reads the other.
Reuse refreshAccessToken/withAutoRefresh from _shared/google.ts rather than growing a second refresh path.
CalendarProvider.connectProvider replaces its placeholder toast with the real redirect.
Do not add /api/integrations to crmProxies as part of this - the edge integrations function has no OAuth handlers and proxying would 404 the dev consent flow.
userStories.notes:
[ROUTING/MEDIUM] Opened 2026-09-01 by PA-052, which pointed CalendarProvider at
the calendar surface that works and could not make Connect do anything.

There is no OAuth authorize flow for CALENDAR scopes that production can reach.
POST /api/meetings/calendar/connections accepts an access token and a refresh
token and stores them; it does not obtain them. The two authorize flows that
exist are neither of them this:

  supabase/functions/oauth-proxy  requests openid/email/profile for SIGN-IN.
                                  Wrong scopes, wrong purpose, and its callback
                                  creates a Supabase session.
  server/integrations/routes.ts   POST /api/integrations/oauth/init and
                                  GET /api/integrations/:provider/callback, the
                                  real Google/Microsoft calendar consent flow -
                                  Express-only, and the browser cannot reach
                                  Express in production because getApiUrl sends
                                  /api/* to the functions host. It also writes to
                                  `system_integrations`, a DIFFERENT store from
                                  the `calendar_connections` the meetings
                                  function reads.

So a user can never connect a calendar in production, and in dev the connection
lands in a table the events code does not read.

The work: an authorize + callback pair in the edge tree requesting calendar
scopes, writing the resulting tokens into `calendar_connections` so
/api/meetings/calendar/events can use them. Two things to settle rather than
discover: which of the two stores is canonical for a calendar connection (the
events handler and its push propagation read calendar_connections, so that is the
answer unless something argues otherwise), and where the refresh happens -
_shared/google.ts already exports refreshAccessToken and withAutoRefresh, so the
callback should not grow its own.

Do NOT resolve this by adding /api/integrations to crmProxies: the edge
integrations function has no OAuth handlers, so proxying would take the dev
calendar consent flow to 404 as well.

Already done by PA-052, do not redo: CalendarProvider reads its provider list
from /api/meetings/calendar/connections rather than from two hardcoded entries
with isConnected permanently false, its create/update/delete call
/api/meetings/calendar/events[/:id], its disconnect calls DELETE on the real
connection instead of only mutating local state, and /api/meetings/calendar is
proxied per-path so dev and prod agree.

DONE 2026-09-01, commit 5d18827. supabase/functions/calendar-oauth/ serves
/authorize (JWT) and /callback (none), writing calendar_connections.

AC3 ANSWERED: calendar_connections is canonical. The events handler and its push
propagation read it, it holds the token columns, and it already carries
UNIQUE (tenant_id, user_id, provider, calendar_id) - so reconnecting replaces
tokens rather than stacking a row. system_integrations stays the generic
third-party connection registry the ERP flows use.

TWO HALVES, TWO AUTH MODELS, AND THAT IS WHY IT IS ITS OWN FUNCTION rather than a
branch of `meetings`: /authorize needs a JWT because that is where the tenant and
user come from, and /callback has none because it is a redirect the PROVIDER
makes. Everything the callback writes a connection under therefore comes from
`state` - so the state is HMAC-SHA256 signed, ten-minute bounded, compared
without an early return per byte, and rejected if any identity field is missing.
Unsigned, it would let anyone attach a connection with live tokens to any tenant
they can name. The secret has no default: signing with a constant is
indistinguishable from not signing at all.

WORTH KNOWING: calendar_connections and calendar_events are DRIFT TABLES. They
are created by migrations/calendar-integration-migration.sql and
drizzle/rls/meetings-tables.sql, both hand-run, and appear in no Drizzle schema
and no journaled migration - so check:phantom-cols is blind to them and that DDL
is the only source of truth for their columns. Same class as the meeting_* tables
CLAUDE.md records. Not fixed here; it wants its own story alongside PA-031.

A REFRESH TOKEN IS PART OF THE CONNECTION, not an optimisation. A connection
stored without one works until the first expiry and then fails silently, and
neither the page nor the sweeper can tell why - so the callback refuses it,
rather than storing something that will stop working. access_type=offline and
prompt=consent are set for the same reason.

Only /authorize is proxied. The provider's redirect lands on the functions host
directly: it carries no JWT, and dev has no public URL a provider could call back
to, so proxying it would be theatre.

userStories.title: Delete the unreferenced onboarding-checklists edge function (duplicate of the live onboarding fn)
userStories.description: As a maintainer, a dead copy of a live function must not sit in the tree carrying annotations that read as findings about the live one.
acceptanceCriteria: Confirm supabase/functions/onboarding/ covers every path OnboardingDashboard.tsx and OnboardingDetails.tsx call, porting anything missing onto equipment_onboarding_checklists and onboarding_dynamic_sections.
Delete supabase/functions/onboarding-checklists/ and remove its entry from docs/unreferenced-edge-fns-baseline.json.
Do not carry COP-M01's 501 CHECKLIST_MODEL_MISMATCH branch across - its premise is a table this feature was never about.
Re-run check:unreferenced-edge-fns and check:edge-coverage; neither may grow.
userStories.notes:
[CLEANUP/LOW] Opened 2026-09-01 by PA-052.

CORRECTED BEFORE IT WAS EVER TRUE. This was first written as a HIGH severity
claim that the live onboarding surface queried the wrong table. It does not.
`supabase/functions/onboarding/` - the function segment 0 actually resolves to,
and the one the frontend reaches - queries `equipment_onboarding_checklists` and
`onboarding_dynamic_sections` correctly throughout.

The file I had read was `supabase/functions/onboarding-checklists/`, a SECOND
directory that no client tree, alias or cron reaches; it is already recorded in

`onboarding_checklists` (the user lifecycle progress record - user_id,

which are not columns on it, and embed `sections:onboarding_sections`, a relation
in no schema at all. All of that is real, and all of it is unreachable, so the
severity is cleanup rather than an outage.

Worth keeping because of what it nearly caused: COP-M01 annotated that dead
function's create branch with a 501 CHECKLIST_MODEL_MISMATCH and an argument that
the CALLER's model was wrong - name / description / status / customer_id /
assigned_to / due_date. Every one of those except template_id maps cleanly onto
equipment_onboarding_checklists, which the live function uses. A carefully
reasoned note on a dead file reads exactly like a carefully reasoned note on a
live one, and I filed a HIGH bug off it before checking which directory the
router resolves.

The work: delete supabase/functions/onboarding-checklists/ and its baseline entry,
after confirming the live function covers every path the two callers use
(OnboardingDashboard.tsx and OnboardingDetails.tsx). If anything is missing, port
it first - but port it onto the correct tables, not the ones the dead copy names.

DONE 2026-09-01, commit c89cf71. supabase/functions/onboarding-checklists/ is
deleted; unreferenced-edge-fns 84 -> 83.

Confirmed before deleting rather than assumed: the live `onboarding` function is
a strict SUPERSET of the dead one (list, single, create, update, delete, sections

generate-pdf), and OnboardingDashboard.tsx and OnboardingDetails.tsx call only

still baselined gaps, but they come from useOnboarding.ts, SetupWizard.tsx and
EnhancedOnboardingForm.tsx and were never part of this story.

phantom-columns 158 -> 152: the dead file's two entries, the demos fix from
f944348, and three stale entries naming customer-metrics/, fleet-dashboard/ and
fleet-devices/ - files that no longer exist. Worth knowing the baseline carries
entries for deleted files until something re-runs --update-baseline.

Also renamed the PDF bucket default from 'onboarding-checklists' to
'onboarding-checklist-pdfs': a bucket sharing a name with a deleted function
directory is a false trail for the next grep.

userStories.title: The team-collaboration router answers seven paths from mocks, over tables that already exist
userStories.description:
The team-collaboration router is mounted at the /api root and every one of its
remaining handlers is a mock with no database call: GET /api/teams, GET
/api/teams/:teamId, POST /api/teams, POST /api/teams/:teamId/members, GET
/api/projects/:projectId, GET /api/collaboration/templates and GET
/api/collaboration/analytics. The file has zero `db.` references. Its service,
server/services/team-collaboration-service.ts, has the same shape below the
capacity analysis AUDIT-021 rewrote: getTeamProjects returns a hardcoded "Q4
Sales Campaign" at 75% complete, and createProject/getTeamProjects touch no
table.

Real tables exist for all of it. `teams` is in shared/schema.ts with tenant_id,
department, manager_id and parent_team_id; membership is users.team_id, which
AUDIT-021 already wired into getTeamMembers; `projects` and `tasks` are in
shared/task-schema.ts. So this is a data-contract rewrite over tables that are
already there, not a feature to design.

Two things make it worth doing rather than deleting. supabase/functions/projects/
already reads the real projects table and serves production, so dev and prod
disagree about what a project is for every path this router still answers. And
`projects` is declared TWICE - shared/schema.ts:5692 and shared/task-schema.ts:82 -
which is a check:dup-tables case that has to be settled before either half can be
trusted; check:phantom-cols skips tables declared twice with different shapes, so
neither declaration is currently checked against anything.

The two paths a live page depends on are already safe: GET and POST /api/projects
were deleted in the AUDIT-021 follow-up because server/routes-tasks.ts registers
the same paths first over the real table, so TaskHub and TemplatesView have always
been served real rows. Nothing else in any client tree calls /api/teams or
/api/collaboration.
acceptanceCriteria: Settle the duplicate `projects` declaration first (shared/schema.ts vs shared/task-schema.ts) - check:dup-tables lists it, and check:phantom-cols skips a table declared twice, so nothing verifies either shape today
For each remaining handler: read the real table, or delete the handler. Do not port a mock (PROD-011's rule), and do not ship a shape no caller can consume (AUDIT-030's rule)

Whatever survives must agree with supabase/functions/projects/, which already serves production over the real projects table - a dev-only answer of a different shape is the defect this story exists to close

getTeamProjects and createProject in server/services/team-collaboration-service.ts go the same way; the file's capacity analysis is already real after AUDIT-021 and is the pattern to follow, including its unbacked array

Every query filters by tenant_id. analyzeTeamCapacity took a teamId straight off the URL with no tenant until AUDIT-021 threaded one; the remaining handlers have the same gap and it stops being latent the moment they read a table
npm run check && npm run test pass, and check:dup-routes stays at its baseline
userStories.notes:
Filed 2026-09-01 while closing AUDIT-021. Found by extending check:dup-routes to resolve mount prefixes: the guard could only see literals starting with /api/, and a router mounted under a prefix declares its paths without one, so all nine root-mounted routers were invisible to it. That exposed GET/POST /api/projects here as dead mocks behind the real handler, and the rest of the file came with the reading.
--- 2026-09-01: AC1 done, and it found a live defect in the quote engine ---

AC1 asked for the duplicate `projects` declaration to be settled first, because
check:dup-tables lists it. It did not list it. The guard EXCLUDED
shared/schema.ts from its scan, on the reasoning that it is the aggregator that
re-exports the others and so is not itself a declaration site. Half true: it
re-exports plenty, and it also declares 129 tables of its own. Excluding it hid
every collision between it and another schema file, which is most of them - the
list went 3 to 14. Re-exports were never a hazard for that scan, since
`export { x } from './y'` is not a pgTable call.

WHAT SETTLES A DUPLICATE, which the story did not know: shared/drizzle-schema.ts
is the single entry point drizzle-kit reads, and it picks ONE declaration per
table and SKIPS the other BY NAME, with a comment saying so. So the skipped
shape has no migration behind it, and code written against it writes to columns
that do not exist. That answers AC1 for all fourteen without a product decision:
the exported declaration owns the table.

THE DEFECT THIS EXPOSED, three tables over from `projects`.
quote-proposal-schema.ts's proposalLineItems is one of the six SKIPPED
declarations, and it is the shape the quote engine is written against -
shared/quote-math.ts and the proposals edge function both use `discount`,
`is_recurring`, `recurring_frequency` and `recurring_duration`. Migration 0000
created all four; 0002 dropped all four; 0047 restored `discount` by hand when
the builder started sending it, and nobody restored the other three.

So a recurring quote line has never been storable. It did not error: the
proposals edge function catches PGRST204 and retries with CORE_LINE_ITEM_COLUMNS
only, none of which is a recurring column, so the line saved with its recurrence
stripped - a monthly charge persisted as a one-time amount, with a warning in
the log and a wrong total on the quote. That is QUOTE-017's whole feature.

Verified against a real Postgres 16, not inferred: the journal chain applied to
a fresh database has `discount` and none of the other three, exactly as read.

Migration 0064 restores all four, written in the 0046/0047 idiom rather than as
drizzle-kit emitted it - ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS inside a table guard, because
real databases already have `discount` and a plain ADD would fail on precisely
the databases that matter. Proven by applying it twice to a database that had
`discount` (the first run skipped that column and added three, the second
skipped all four) and by replaying the whole chain on a fresh database: 0 errors,
all four present. The four columns are added to schema.ts's declaration too -
the one drizzle-kit diffs - so the snapshot stops omitting them and the next
db:generate does not emit a DROP for `discount`.

STILL OPEN: this story's own subject, the seven mock handlers in the
team-collaboration router. AC1 is now answered - `projects` is owned by
schema.ts, since drizzle-schema.ts skips task-schema's copy - so the rewrite can
proceed against that shape. The other thirteen duplicates are recorded in
docs/duplicate-tables-baseline.json with the ownership rule in its note; each is
worth the same check, because a skipped declaration with code written against it
is a silent write to nowhere.

--- 2026-09-01, later: the other thirteen duplicates, checked against a real database ---

Last pass established the ownership rule and fixed proposal_line_items. Applying
the same check to all fourteen, with the migration chain replayed on Postgres 16
and each SKIPPED declaration's columns compared against what the table really
has:

  proposals             15 columns missing (customer_needs, proposed_solution,
                        implementation_plan, equipment_package_id, custom_equipment,
                        payment_terms, delivery_terms, warranty_terms, service_terms,
                        e_signature_* x4, time_spent_viewing, customer_feedback)
  proposal_templates    10 missing
  dashboard_layouts      8 missing
  location_history       8 missing
  proposal_approvals     7 missing
  proposal_line_items    5 missing (after 0064)
  equipment_packages     3 missing
  proposal_analytics     3 missing
  proposal_comments      2 missing
  projects, tasks        0 - the skipped declaration is a SUBSET, so nothing breaks
  blog_posts, purchase_orders, purchase_order_items
                        neither declaration is marked SKIPPED in drizzle-schema.ts,
                        which is worth its own look: drizzle-kit sees the table twice

A missing column only matters where code names it, so the next question was which
of these are live. proposal_templates is, and badly.

PROPOSAL TEMPLATES COULD NOT BE CREATED, EVER. The proposals edge function was
written against the skipped shape and named ten columns the table does not have.
POST /proposals/proposal-templates spread template_name, template_type,
header_content, cover_page_template, executive_summary_template,
proposal_body_template, terms_conditions_template, footer_template,
branding_colors and font_settings into the insert, so it answered 500 every
time. GET with ?templateType= filtered on a missing column and 500'd too. The
default-clearing UPDATE filtered on the same column and swallowed the error, so
"set as default" silently did nothing. And four client files - ProposalTemplates,
ProposalTemplateEditor, ProposalBuilder and GenerateProposalDialog - rendered
{t.template_name}, which is blank on every row.

The table really holds name, description, category, template_content, styling,
access_level, team_id, is_active, is_default. All four clients and the edge
function are bound to those now. The five body sections and two styling blocks
have no columns of their own, so rather than dropping them the normalizer FOLDS
them into template_content and styling, which are real jsonb columns - a caller
sending the richer shape keeps its content, and an explicit template_content in
the body still wins.

WHY NO GUARD SAW IT: check:phantom-cols SKIPS a table declared twice with
different shapes, on the reasoning that it cannot tell which shape applies. With
the ownership rule that ambiguity is now resolvable - drizzle-schema.ts names the
winner - so teaching that guard to resolve these fourteen would close the blind
spot this defect lived in. That is the next piece of work here, and it is worth
more than the remaining mock handlers.

CORRECTION to the table above, found by making the guard resolve these rather
than reading the SKIPPED comments by hand: `projects` and `tasks` are owned by
schema.ts, NOT task-schema.ts. drizzle-schema.ts says so explicitly
("tasks — SKIPPED: defined in schema.ts"), and my script matched the comment
against the wrong side because both declarations use the same identifier. So the
skipped declaration for those two is a SUPERSET, not a subset, and the entry
saying "0 missing, nothing breaks" was backwards: parent_task_id, dependencies,
time_tracked, assignee_id, project_manager_id, tags and template_id are all
written by live edge functions and none of them is a column. They are in
AUDIT-037 with the rest.

The lesson is the one this session keeps repeating in a new place: a hand-read
of a comment is not evidence. The guard resolves the export now, so the answer
comes from the same module drizzle-kit loads.

userStories.title: Seventeen foreign-key columns cannot hold the key they name
userStories.description:
Seventeen foreign-key columns are declared `integer` against a target whose
primary key is a varchar uuid. An integer column cannot hold a uuid, so a row
referencing a real record cannot be written and a filtered read cannot match:
the read is 22P02, the write is 42804 - both reproduced for the tenant_id
version of this defect on Postgres 16 under AUDIT-032.

This is AUDIT-032 one column family over. That story found 21 tables declaring
`tenant_id integer` against a varchar `tenants.id`, converted them in migration
0062, and stopped at that column name. The foreign keys on the SAME tables were
never looked at, and they break the same three features AUDIT-032's own note
names: auto-supply replenishment, contract renewal and document automation.

  contract_renewal_tracking.contract_id -> contracts.id
  renewal_proposals.contract_id         -> contracts.id
  supply_monitoring.equipment_id        -> equipment.id
  supply_usage_history.equipment_id     -> equipment.id
  auto_supply_orders.equipment_id       -> equipment.id
  generated_documents.{workflow,task,business_record,quote,deal,service_call}_id
  document_uploads.{workflow,task}_id
  document_workflow_actions.workflow_id
  document_notifications.{document,workflow,task}_id

Confirmed on both sides independently: the Drizzle declarations, which are what
db:generate diffs, and the migration chain replayed in journal order. The two
agree exactly, which is what makes this a schema fact rather than a reading of
one file.

The consequence is the same silent one AUDIT-032 documents. The routed
/contract-renewal-autopilot dashboard analyses contracts it structurally cannot
join to, and `contract_renewal_tracking` sits in
docs/unwritten-tables-baseline.json as a table nothing writes to - when the
truth is again that nothing COULD.

npm run check:fk-id-types now gates this at 34 baselined entries (17 columns,
seen once per side). The guard is written and CI-wired by this story; what
remains is the conversion.
acceptanceCriteria: Convert all 17 columns to varchar in one migration, following the shape of 0062_round_sway.sql: idempotent, USING clauses, and generated through npm run db:generate so the journal and snapshot stay consistent (SUPA-005, COP-M00)

PROVE it against a real Postgres before claiming it works. COP-M07 records that this container ships PostgreSQL 16 at /usr/lib/postgresql/16/bin and how to bring one up; apply the chain in journal order and then apply the new migration twice, as AUDIT-032 did

Check the columns the name-based rule cannot see. contract_renewal_tracking.customer_id is integer and the real customer is business_records.id, a varchar uuid, but no `customers` pgTable exists so the guard does not resolve it - walk the three affected schema files by hand for the same shape
Drive docs/fk-id-types-baseline.json to 0 and keep the guard at a hard gate, the way check:tenant-id-types is gated

Re-check docs/unwritten-tables-baseline.json afterwards: entries that were unwritable rather than unwritten need re-reading, since the question 'who fills this in' has a different answer once the column can hold a key
npm run check && npm run test pass
userStories.notes: Filed 2026-09-01 while triaging AUDIT-026. The renewal model comparison turned on which of the two schemas could actually reference a contract, and the live one could not - contract_renewal_tracking.contract_id is integer against a uuid contracts.id. Scanning the rest of shared/ for the same shape found sixteen more. The guard landed with the story because the finding is only useful if it cannot grow while the conversion waits.
userStories.closure_note:
Closed 2026-09-01. check:fk-id-types is a hard gate at 0.

Migration 0063_abandoned_the_phantom.sql converts 31 columns across the three
schema families. PROVEN against a real Postgres 16 in this container rather than
asserted, following AUDIT-032's standard:

  1. The whole journal chain applied to a fresh database, statement-tolerantly
     per COP-M07 (db:migrate itself still dies in 0000, PA-032): 0 errors,
     668 tables.
  2. BOTH failures reproduced BEFORE the fix, on the real schema:
       select ... where contract_id = '<uuid>'  -> 22P02 invalid input syntax
       insert ... values ('<uuid>')             -> same, on the write path
  3. 0063 applied: the same insert then failed on contract_number NOT NULL, i.e.
     the complaint moved past the type to a real constraint. Filled in, the row
     writes and the tenant-scoped read by contract_id returns it.
  4. 0063 applied a SECOND time: exit 0, row intact.
  5. The full chain including 0063 replayed on a second fresh database: 0 errors,
     and 0 integer FK columns left across the ten affected tables.

WHAT THE GUARD COULD NOT FIND, which is why AC3 asked for the files to be read by
hand: it resolves a target by column NAME, so it found 17 of the 31.
assigned_sales_rep_id, sent_by_user_id, reviewed_by, uploaded_by, generated_by,
created_by, recipient_user_id, target_entity_id and supplier_id all point at a
uuid-keyed table and none is named for it. That limit is in the guard's header
rather than left to be rediscovered.

ONE REPORTED COLUMN WAS A FALSE POSITIVE and is NOT converted.
document_notifications.document_id is integer and correct: its sibling
document_type selects between generated_documents and document_uploads, both
integer-keyed. A polymorphic <x>_id beside an <x>_type names no single table, so
the guard now skips that shape BY RULE. Baselining it would have put a known
non-defect in the list, which is where a real one hides.

Internal foreign keys were deliberately left alone - contract_renewal_tracking_id,
renewal_proposal_id, supply_monitoring_id, template_id, parent_template_id and
field_mapping_id all point at integer-keyed tables in the same schema and are
internally consistent.

AC5, re-reading the unwritten-tables baseline: six of its entries were unwritable
rather than unwritten, and the note now says so. The question that file asks -
who fills this in? - is a real one for them now instead of a symptom. A seventh
entry appeared while checking, platform_bant_qualification, which is the clean
version of the shape: the PA-052 read in supabase/functions/platform-deals/ is
correct, the table is real, and nothing inserts a row, so the BANT tab is
honestly empty. Recorded, not fixed - building the writer is a feature.

Two tests that asserted the DEBT (that both sides report the same 17 columns,
and that the baseline names contract_renewal_tracking.contract_id) are rewritten
to assert the outcome. That is the third time this session a debt-floor
assertion has failed on its own story's success.

Verified: 4,274 tests pass, npm run build succeeds, check-types holds at 319,
check:migrations, check:tenant-id-types, check:spread-insert-keys and
check:unwritten-tables all clean.

userStories.title: 128 column references were hidden behind a guard that skipped ambiguous tables
userStories.description:
check:phantom-cols used to skip any table declared twice with different shapes,
because it could not tell which shape was live. AUDIT-035 established that it
can: shared/drizzle-schema.ts is the single entry point drizzle-kit reads and it
resolves every collision by hand, so whatever it exports is the shape the
migrations built. Teaching the guard to use that took the ambiguous count to
zero and surfaced 128 references that were already broken - each one a 42703 the
moment its code path runs.

They fall into three clusters, and the first is a decision rather than a fix.

BLOG_POSTS, 95 references. shared/schema.ts re-exports content-marketing-schema's
declaration, not blog-schema's, and an explicit named re-export beats a later
`export *` - so drizzle-kit has only ever seen the content-marketing shape and
every migration reflects it. The US-BLOG subsystem is written against the other
one: body_markdown, body_html, deleted_at, canonical_url, brief_id, cluster_id,
brand_voice_id, cms_post_url and more. Reads return nothing; an INSERT cannot
work at all, because the physical table has content NOT NULL and the blog code
never sets it. PROD-013's notes recorded all of this on 2026-08-19 and it has sat
since. _backfill_blog_tables.sql creates the blog shape with CREATE TABLE IF NOT
EXISTS, which is a silent no-op on any database that already has the table, so
running the backfills does not fix it either. Renaming the US-BLOG table is the
smaller change - the content-marketing one is what physically exists and what
migration 0000 creates - but it touches 28 tables' foreign keys and every blog-*
edge function. Do not resolve this by editing a declaration: only one shape can
exist, and whichever loses takes its rows with it.

PURCHASE_ORDERS AND PURCHASE_ORDER_ITEMS, 17 references, and this one is a
straightforward fix. supabase/functions/purchase-orders/ writes submitted_at,
submitted_by, approved_at, approval_notes, rejected_at, rejected_by,
rejection_reason, received_by, last_receipt_date and receipt_notes - so submit,
approve, reject and receive each 42703. The search filter names notes and
reference_number, which do not exist either, so search 500s. auto-supply-
replenishment inserts supplier_id, source_rule_id and order_type onto the same
table. equipment-schema.ts's declaration is the skipped one and has those
columns; schema.ts's, which drizzle-kit reads, does not.

THE REST, 16 references. proposals (total_dealer_cost on a select,
total_margin_percentage, share_token, share_expires_at, customer_feedback),
proposal_comments (comment, user_id on an insert - so a comment cannot be
posted), proposal_analytics (visitor_id), tasks (parent_task_id, dependencies,
time_tracked, assignee_id), projects (project_manager_id, tags, template_id) and
location_history (customer_id, device_id, ticket_id). All the same shape: code
written against the declaration drizzle-schema.ts skips.
acceptanceCriteria: Settle blog_posts FIRST and separately - it is 95 of the 128 and it is an ownership decision with data at stake, not a rebinding. PROD-013's notes carry the evidence; the smaller change is renaming the US-BLOG table, and it touches 28 tables' foreign keys

Rebind supabase/functions/purchase-orders/ and the auto-supply-replenishment insert to the columns schema.ts declares, the way AUDIT-035 rebound proposal templates - or add the missing columns in a migration if the workflow genuinely needs them, proven against a real Postgres

Fix the remaining sixteen the same way, checking per column whether the right answer is to rebind the code or to add the column: proposal_comments cannot accept a comment at all, which suggests the column is wanted
Every fix shrinks docs/phantom-columns-baseline.json. Never shrink it by re-widening the ambiguous skip - that is what hid all of this
npm run check && npm run test pass
userStories.notes:
Filed 2026-09-01 on closing the check:phantom-cols blind spot. The guard change is shipped and the baseline records why it grew; this story is the backlog it exposed. Worth knowing the order it was found in: AUDIT-035 fixed proposal_line_items and proposal_templates by hand, one at a time, before anyone asked why the guard had never mentioned them.
--- 2026-09-01: the purchase_orders cluster, and a bigger one behind it ---

All 17 references are gone; the baseline is 280 -> 262.

Two different fixes, chosen per column rather than in bulk. Names that already
had a home were REBOUND: approved_at -> approved_date, supplier_id -> vendor_id
in the validate function, and the search's reference_number/notes -> po_number/
description. Genuine workflow state with nowhere to live got columns in
migration 0065 - submitted_at, approval_notes, rejected_at, rejected_by,
rejection_reason, received_by, last_receipt_date, receipt_notes - because the
function already implements submit, approve, reject and receive end to end, and
dropping them would mean a rejection with no reason and a receipt with no
receiver. Idempotent and table-guarded in the 0046/0047/0064 idiom; proven on
Postgres 16 by replaying the chain fresh (0 errors), applying 0065 a second time
(all eight skipped) and round-tripping a rejection with a reason and a partial
receipt.

AUTO-SUPPLY REPLENISHMENT'S TRIGGER IS A 501 NOW, and it deserved worse than a
rename. It filtered supply_replenishment_rules on is_active, auto_order and
product_id; that table is ONE ROW of per-tenant settings - thresholds, budgets,
notification preferences - with none of those columns and no reorder_point,
warehouse_id or reorder_quantity either, so there is no per-product rule model to
iterate. It then inserted a purchase order naming three phantom columns while
omitting six NOT NULL ones, and destructured the result as `{ data: order }`
with NO error, so every failure was swallowed and the endpoint answered 200 with
`ordersCreated: 0`. A replenishment run that ordered nothing looked exactly like
a run with nothing to order. Building it is a feature - a per-product rule table,
PO numbering, supplier-to-vendor resolution, a priced line - so it says that.

A BIGGER CLUSTER SITS BEHIND THIS ONE, and it is not fixed. purchase-orders'
CREATE and UPDATE build their payload as a NAMED VARIABLE (`poData`,
`updateData`), which check:phantom-cols cannot resolve - it reads inline object
literals only, and its header says so. Inside them: reference_number,
expected_delivery_date, ship_to_address, ship_to_city, ship_to_state,
ship_to_zip, shipping_method, payment_terms and internal_notes, none of which is
a column. So creating a purchase order fails too, not just the workflow steps,
and the guard reported none of it. The table has delivery_address and
special_instructions, so part of that is a rebind and part is a decision about
whether a PO carries a structured ship-to address. Left for a focused pass
rather than rushed alongside the rest - the honest count for this cluster is
larger than 17 and the guard cannot tell us by how much.

--- 2026-09-02: the named-payload blind spot is closed; 121 more references ---

Last pass fixed the seventeen purchase-order references the guard could see and
recorded that a bigger cluster sat behind them, invisible because the create and
update handlers build their payload as a named variable. Rather than rebind that
one file by hand, the guard now resolves named payloads - and the same shape
turned up 121 times across the edge tree. Baseline 262 -> 383.

Two confirmed true positives, to show the class is real rather than a scanner
artefact. Creating a user through supabase/functions/admin/ writes phone,
job_title and department, which CLAUDE.md already records as columns `users`
does not have - so the admin user-creation form has never worked. And the
purchase-order create writes reference_number, expected_delivery_date, four
ship_to_* fields, shipping_method, payment_terms and internal_notes, so a
purchase order cannot be created either, which is what last pass predicted
without being able to count.

THE RESOLUTION RULE MATTERS AND TWO LOOSER ONES WERE WRONG. Pooling declarations
by name across a file attributed one table's payload to another table's insert:
`row`, `payload` and `updateData` are reused constantly, and it reported 39
phantom columns on a ten-key location_history insert. Narrowing to the nearest
preceding LITERAL then reached past `const insertRow = normalizeLineItem(...)`
to an unrelated older literal of the same name and invented eighteen on
proposal_line_items - a table this session had just finished fixing, which is
how the false positive got noticed. The rule that survives collects EVERY
binding of a name, takes the nearest preceding one, and uses it only if it is an
object literal; a later bare re-assignment invalidates it too.

ALSO FIXED, because it bit twice: --update-baseline rewrites the file wholesale,
so prose added to the baseline JSON by hand was silently dropped on the next
regeneration - both times taking the explanation of why the list had grown. The
note now lives in the script as BASELINE_NOTE and is written on every
regeneration.

What is still unresolvable is now stated accurately in the header: a payload
whose keys are assembled at runtime - a spread, a camel-to-snake field map,
Object.assign.

--- 2026-09-02, later: two forms that could never have worked ---

Baseline 383 -> 361. Both fixes were in the class the guard had just started
seeing, and both are the same failure: one column that is not there makes the
whole write a 42703, so the feature reports a server error and saves nothing.

INVITING A USER. supabase/functions/admin/ created the auth account, then
inserted phone, job_title and department into `users`, which has none of them.
The insert failed, the cleanup branch deleted the auth account again, and the
caller got "Failed to create user record" - so inviting a colleague has never
worked. Those three live on user_settings, which is exactly the correction
COP-M01 made to the user and users-team functions; the same three plus timezone
and locale were in the UPDATE payload too, so ANY edit touching one lost the
whole update, including a role change in the same request. They upsert onto
user_settings now (locale -> language, the column that exists), and a failure
there is logged rather than raised: the account works without a job title, and
undoing the invitation would not be an improvement.

CREATING A PURCHASE ORDER. The page and the function did not share a vocabulary
at all. client/src/pages/PurchaseOrders.tsx posts poNumber, vendorId,
requestedBy, orderDate, expectedDate, description, deliveryAddress and
specialInstructions - the real column names - and the function read
referenceNumber, expectedDeliveryDate, four shipTo* parts, notes and
internalNotes, none of which is a column. It also never set requested_by, which
is NOT NULL, so it would have failed even with every name right.

Both handlers speak the page's vocabulary now. FOUR FIELDS ARE DROPPED RATHER
THAN GIVEN COLUMNS - reference_number, currency, shipping_method, payment_terms:
the page sends none of them, the PO number is the reference, and a vendor
already carries its payment terms. Adding columns for input nothing supplies is
how this file got into that state. The six that ARE genuine workflow state -
submitted_by and the order and cancel steps with their reason - are in migration
0066, completing 0065's set, idempotent and table-guarded, proven on Postgres 16
by a fresh chain replay, a second apply that skipped all six, and a full
create-then-cancel round trip.

A FOURTH DEBT ASSERTION FAILED ON ITS OWN STORY'S SUCCESS. Two tests asserted
that purchase_orders.submitted_by and users.job_title were still IN the phantom
baseline. Both went red the hour those columns were fixed. They assert the
opposite now - that a fixed entry leaves the list - and the evidence for why the
class was real moved into the note, which is where it belongs.

--- 2026-09-02: the CRM core, 361 -> 339 ---

CLAUDE.md has recorded for months that `deals` is queried as deal_value, stage,
value, name and closed_at by eight edge functions. The real columns are amount,
stage_id, title, actual_close_date and owner_id, so each of those reads was a
42703 and the surface above it showed nothing or zero - indistinguishable from a
quiet day. All of them are fixed:

  today-dashboard  today's revenue summed a column that does not exist, so it
                   was always 0 on a dashboard that prints it as a figure
  pipeline         every per-stage stat was computed over an empty array; the
                   join is on stage_id, which holds a legacy deal_stages.id
  sales-reports    two queries, both empty; nothing stores a weighted value, so
                   it is computed as amount x probability rather than read
  user-assignments the assignment page showed no deals for anyone
  opportunities    the iOS list showed no contact details, and CREATE 42703'd -
                   the columns are primary_contact_email/_phone

`business_records` had the same problem from the other direction. A record there
is a COMPANY and the person lives in primary_contact_*; code written as if it
were a person wrote first_name, last_name, email, job_title and linkedin_url.
The Chrome extension's contact import failed on every attempt, and so did its
duplicate check - which means the extension could not have detected a duplicate
even if the import had worked. THE LINKEDIN MATCH IS REMOVED RATHER THAN
APPROXIMATED: there is no linkedin_url anywhere on the table, and matching a
profile against a company name would merge two different people at the same
employer. The customers function wrote lead_source, estimated_amount and tags;
the columns are source and estimated_deal_value, and tags does not exist at all,
so creating a customer failed and any edit that sent tags lost the whole update.

TWO OF MY OWN ASSERTIONS WERE TOO BROAD and are scoped now. `assigned_to_id` is
a real column on `leads` and on the assignment table, so a whole-file absence
assertion was wrong; it checks the deals chain. And the files now EXPLAIN the old
column names in prose, so both sides strip comments - otherwise the test reads
its own explanation as the defect, which is the trap this repo has hit five times.

--- 2026-09-02: the blog_posts collision is one-sided, and the dead half is gone ---

97 of the 339 remaining references are on blog_posts, and the story said to
settle that first because it is an ownership decision with data at stake. It is
a much smaller decision than it looked, and the reason is worth recording.

shared/drizzle-schema.ts resolves the collision in favour of
content-marketing-schema, so that is the shape migration 0000 built and the shape
every database has. The OTHER declaration, blog-schema's, is what 37 blog-* edge
functions and the platform-admin blog UI read - hence the 97.

PROD-013 framed this as "which system owns the name", a contest between two live
systems. It is not one. server/routes-content-marketing.ts was the ONLY consumer
of the winning shape anywhere in the tree, and its twelve endpoints under
/api/content have no caller in any of the seven client trees, no edge function
behind them and no proxy entry. PROD-013 had already deleted the single beacon
that used to reach the prefix and called retiring the router routine cleanup;
nobody did it, so the collision kept reading as balanced.

Deleted: 863 lines, its export from server/domains/content.ts, its mount, and
its entry in a fix-script's file list. The typecheck ratchet drops 319 -> 315.

WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT SETTLE. The 97 references stay in the baseline,
because resolving them means altering a table two subsystems name and that is
the owner's call. What is gone is the reason it looked like a trade-off. On one
side: 37 edge functions, an admin UI, 28 tables' foreign keys. On the other:
nothing at all. The shape difference is 22 columns blog-schema has and the table
does not, plus `content NOT NULL`, which is what makes a US-BLOG insert
impossible rather than merely lossy.

The additive half of the fix - ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS for the 22, and dropping
the NOT NULL on `content` - would unblock the live subsystem without removing
anything, and is reversible. I did not do it: it is still a schema change to a
shared table on the strength of an inference about intent, and the story asks for
the decision to be recorded in docs/ by whoever owns it.

--- 2026-09-02: the deal desk, and how to order what is left ---

THE BACKLOG IS HALF NOISE, IN A SPECIFIC AND CHECKABLE WAY. Crossing the phantom
baseline against docs/unreferenced-edge-fns-baseline.json: 166 of the 339
references sit in edge functions that NOTHING CALLS, where a phantom column
cannot hurt anyone and fixing it is building for a caller that does not exist.
156 are in reachable functions and are live 42703s under a screen somebody
opens. That ordering is now in the guard's note, because working this list
top-down would have spent the effort on the wrong half.

DEAL DESK, the largest reachable cluster at 18, is fixed. The eighteen split
evenly and the split is the finding: creating an approval RULE 42703'd, and so
did submitting a REQUEST. The deal desk had nothing to match against and nowhere
to put a submission - the entire feature was inert, over a table set
(shared/deal-desk-schema.ts) that is real and detailed.

Rules: rule_name, comparison_operator, approval_chain_type,
escalate_to_role_id. approver_role_ids folded into approvers, which is the same
jsonb list under a second name.

Requests: original_price, proposed_price, business_justification,
current_approval_level, sla_deadline, final_decision_comments.

FOUR FIELDS DROPPED, each for a reason rather than in bulk.
auto_approve_below_threshold has no home and is a POLICY that would silently
approve discounts if it were ever honoured - inventing a column for it would be
inventing the behaviour. requires_justification is the same shape:
business_justification is nullable, so nothing enforces it, and a flag no code
reads is worse than an absent one. A request has no priority - that is a
property of the RULE that matched it. And total_steps is derived from
approval_chain's length now: storing a count beside the list it counts is how
the two come to disagree, and the decision handler compared them on every
approval.

Callers that send the dropped rule fields get them back in an `ignored` array
rather than silently losing them.

--- 2026-09-02: the proposals cluster, and a pattern worth naming ---

Ten references, and eight of them were not phantoms at all. The columns EXIST on
every database; the DECLARATION did not know:

  customer_feedback                            migration 0000
  total_dealer_cost, total_margin_percentage   0042
  share_token, share_expires_at                0045
  discount_reason, discount_reason_note        0047

Four hand-written migrations, each added when a feature needed the column, and
not one of them came back to shared/schema.ts. THE PATTERN IS THE FINDING: a
column added by hand is invisible to everything that reads the declaration, which
is every tool here - drizzle-kit's snapshot, check:phantom-cols, and tsc. It is
also the same shape as the `discount` column AUDIT-035 found on
proposal_line_items, so this is now four migrations and two tables with the same
history. Worth checking the other hand-written migrations against their
declarations; 0042, 0045, 0046, 0047, 0064, 0065 and 0066 are all of this kind,
and the later ones were declared because I wrote them that way, not because the
process caught it.

No DROP risk, to be accurate about the consequence: a column that was never in
the declaration was never in the snapshot either, so db:generate does not know to
remove it. The cost is that the tooling is blind to it, not that it is at risk.

TWO WERE GENUINE. Posting a comment on a proposal wrote `comment` and `user_id`;
the table has content and author_id - and author_id was already being set right
beside the duplicate, which is how the row managed to look plausible. Recording
an accept or an open wrote visitor_id to proposal_analytics, which has no such
column, so the public share link's analytics never recorded anything. The
anonymous cookie goes into event_details now, the jsonb the rest of the row
already uses: a column for a value that identifies nobody is not worth adding.

Baseline 321 -> 311.

--- 2026-09-02: the drift class, measured and then closed ---

Last pass named a pattern - a hand-written migration adds a column and the
declaration never hears about it - and said it was worth checking the others.
Checked: by replaying the journal and diffing every table against
shared/drizzle-schema.ts, exactly ONE column was left undeclared across 668
tables, proposal_templates.template_content. So the class was almost entirely
the proposals cluster; there is no systematic backlog behind it. That negative
result is worth as much as the fix, because the alternative was assuming a
sweep was needed.

template_content is declared now - it is the jsonb the template body lives in,
which is where AUDIT-035 folded the five body-section fields the edge function
used to name.

npm run check:declared-cols is the guard, CI-wired: it replays the journal and
fails on a column the migrations create that no pgTable declares. It earns its
place because this drift produced a FALSE ACCUSATION rather than a silent gap -
eight correct reads on `proposals` were reported as phantom columns, and I spent
part of a pass proving the code was right. A guard that manufactures defects is
worse than no guard, and nothing else here would have caught it: every other
tool reads the same declaration.

The header is careful about the consequence, because overstating it would be its
own error. There is NO DROP RISK: a column that was never in the declaration was
never in the snapshot either, so db:generate does not know to remove it. The cost
is blindness, not danger.

--- 2026-09-02: technicians, 311 -> 303 ---

Eight references breaking three separate things: creating a technician,
recording availability, and the performance panel.

Create wrote skill_set, certification_level, employment_status and hire_date;
the columns are skills, certifications and is_active. certification_level was a
single string and certifications is a list, so one level becomes a one-element
list rather than being dropped. hire_date is not written at all - the table
records what a technician can do, not their employment history, and inventing a
column for it would be inventing the feature. The ?status= and ?skillSet=
filters were querying the same absent columns, so the list was empty whenever
either was used.

AVAILABILITY IS THE ONE WORTH STATING. The code sent is_available; the column is
is_booked, which is its INVERSE. Had the name been right and the sense wrong, a
free slot would have been stored as booked and the scheduler would have hidden
every available technician. It was saved from that by being broken outright: the
insert 42703'd, so no availability was ever recorded. The mapping now negates.
`notes` has no column and is dropped.

THE PERFORMANCE PANEL AVERAGED A COLUMN THAT DOES NOT EXIST. service_tickets
records no first_response_time, so avgResponseTime was always 0 - printed as a
response time on a technician's record, which is a claim about a person's work.
What the table carries is created_at and resolved_at, and that is a RESOLUTION
time, not a response time; reporting one as the other would be a different wrong
number. So avgResolutionHours is reported under its own name, null when nothing
has been resolved, and avgResponseTime is named in an `unbacked` array. Also
service_tickets.completed_at is resolved_at.

--- 2026-09-02: document-management, and the third table called "document" ---

303 -> 291, and the twelve went by deletion rather than repair. That needs the
reasoning, because deleting a routed page listed in the sidebar is not the
default move.

/api/document-management was a routed page (level 3 in navigation-permissions,
an entry in both the desktop sidebar and the mobile drawer) calling four paths,
and not one of them worked on either host. In PRODUCTION all four 404'd:
supabase/functions/document-management/ read parts[0] as a document id, so
/library was a lookup for a document whose id is the string "library", and
/workflows, /search and /upload had no branch at all. That is exactly the hazard
SUPA-024 recorded and docs/edge-path-coverage-baseline.json had already listed
those three segments as gaps - nobody had connected the baseline entry to the
page. In DEV two fixtures in routes-sample-data.ts answered /library and
/workflows with 2,847 documents, 12 categories, 4.2 GB of 50 GB used, 23 pending
approval and a 96.5% COMPLIANCE SCORE. /search and /upload had no live handler
either: server/routes-document-management.ts implements them over real Drizzle
queries and is registered nowhere.

THE TWELVE COLUMNS WERE THE SMALLEST PART OF IT. `documents` is a purchase
agreement and service contract - agreement_number, buyer_name, black_rate,
monthly_base, five NOT NULL columns the edge function's insert never set - and
supabase/functions/documents/ already owns it correctly for DocumentBuilder
(PROD-013). The file-library columns the deleted code read off it are not a
rebind away from anything; document_folders, which two of those files queried,
is in no schema and no migration either.

And repairing the columns would not have been enough. The page's own Document
interface wants per-document permissions.{view,edit,approve}, a workflow with a
current stage and an assignee, a checksumMD5, a retention policy and a
compliance status. No table in this repo stores any of that. Making the four
calls succeed would have meant inventing the twelve columns and then inventing
the rest - which is how PROD-010 describes BusinessProcessOptimization, and the
rule LEGAL-010 set is that a claim with no backing data is deleted, not
relabelled. A compliance score is the specific example.

Deleted: the 919-line page and its route, lazy import, nav-permissions entry and
two sidebar entries; the 828-line unregistered router; the 225-line edge
function; both fixtures.

WHERE A REAL DOCUMENT LIBRARY WOULD GO, since the absence is the useful half of
this. document_uploads (shared/document-automation-schema.ts) holds actual file
metadata, OCR text and confidence, AI-extracted fields, a review trail and an
archive flag, alongside document_templates and generated_documents. Real tables,
real inserts, and nothing reaches them - PROD-008d's unconnected feature.
Building the library means connecting that, not adding columns to `documents`.
docs/document-surfaces.md maps all four "document" prefixes so the next search
does not have to work it out again, and
server/tests/unit/document-surfaces.test.ts locks both the removal and the two
tables' meanings - including that a future file model goes on document_uploads,
because giving `documents` two meanings is how this happened.

Six ratchets moved on one deletion, which is itself worth noting about how this
debt is distributed: phantom-cols 303 -> 291, phantom-tables -1, dup-routes -2
(the two fixtures duplicated the unregistered router), edge-path-coverage -3,
edge-rbac -1, route-ownership -1, server-orphans -1. docs/route-parity-matrix.md
and route-divergence.json are regenerated; the matrix had gone badly stale
(missing-edge 4 -> 0, both-divergent 68 -> 53) from earlier deletions nobody
regenerated it after, so most of that diff is catch-up rather than this change.

--- 2026-09-02: client-metrics, 291 -> 281, and a gate nothing ever passed ---

The next reachable cluster after document-management was
supabase/functions/client-metrics/ at ten. It is deleted, and the ten columns
were the least of it.

THE FUNCTION COULD NOT AUTHENTICATE ANYONE. It read the key from an `x-api-key`
header and compared that raw value against monitoring_clients.api_key, which
stores a SHA-256 hash - the live Express handler in routes-client-monitoring.ts
hashes before comparing, and the schema comment says "Hashed API key". The agent
sends `Authorization: Bearer <key>` and no x-api-key at all, so the request 401'd
on the missing header before the comparison it would also have failed. Nothing
behind that gate has ever run, in any environment.

WHAT WAS BEHIND IT IS WHY THE DIRECTORY WENT RATHER THAN GETTING A MATCHING AUTH
FIX. All four write paths discard the PostgREST error and answer 200:

  /submit     ten phantom columns on device_metrics - the agent posts a generic
              { metricType, value, unit } triple and the table is a fixed-shape
              meter snapshot with impression counters. COP-M01 had already
              written that in a comment and left it, correctly, as a product
              decision. `if (!error && data)` means the answer is
              { success: true, received: 12, processed: 0 }.
  /alerts     three more on device_alerts, same swallow, same shape of answer.
  /devices    queries `discovered_devices`; the table is client_discovered_devices.
              check:phantom-tables did not report it, because its rule needs a
              handler that TESTS for 42P01 - one that discards the error entirely
              slips past. Worth knowing as a blind spot in that guard.
  /heartbeat  the same key twice in one object literal:
              `{ last_heartbeat: <iso string>, last_heartbeat: { timestamp,
              version, device_count, status } }`. The second wins, so it writes
              an OBJECT into a timestamp column. No error check at all here, not
              even a discarded one. No guard in this repo sees a duplicate key
              in an object literal - both names are the same real column, so
              check:phantom-cols is satisfied, and eslint's no-dupe-keys does not
              run on supabase/functions (deno, no deno.json).

Its own header asked for deletion once nothing routed to it. That condition is
unsatisfiable as written - the Coolify dispatcher resolves segment 0 to the
directory name, so functions.printyx.net/client-metrics/* reaches it by
construction, with no DNS rule to remove. The stronger fact settles it instead:
the auth gate rejects every caller, so deleting it cannot break a caller that
does not exist. And 404 beats a 200 that reports success and stores nothing.

scripts/lib/route-parity.mjs keeps `client-metrics` in EXPRESS_CANONICAL, now
annotated: it is the only implementation rather than the canonical one of two,
and the classifier still needs to know the agent ingest path is not a migration
gap. server/tests/unit/client-metrics-ingest.test.ts locks the removal and the
two facts that make it safe - Express still serves the prefix, and it still
hashes.

Ratchets: phantom-cols 291 -> 281, phantom-tables -1, edge-rbac -1.
(edge-path-coverage was unaffected - client-metrics was never in it. The 81 ->
77 drop belongs to the previous entry: three from document-management and one
unrelated resolution the regeneration absorbed.)

--- 2026-09-02: the duplicate-key blind spot is closed, and a bigger one is filed ---

npm run check:dupe-keys is a hard gate at zero over supabase/functions, using
the TypeScript parser rather than a regex - nesting, computed keys and spreads
are not something to pattern-match on a hard gate. It catches the client-metrics
heartbeat shape exactly: the same key twice in one object literal, where the
second silently wins.

THE REASON IT SCOPES TO THAT TREE IS WORTH RECORDING ON ITS OWN. Everything
under supabase/functions is checked by no typechecker and no linter.
tsconfig does not include it, eslint.config.js ignores 'supabase/functions/**'
outright - with a comment saying deno covers it - and `deno check` and
`deno lint` appear in no CI workflow and no npm script. So a grammar-level
mistake TS reports as TS1117 anywhere else survives indefinitely across 273 edge
functions that ARE the production backend. Every guard covering that tree is
bespoke, which is why a new one is usually the right answer there and a
lint rule is not.

Proven before wiring, on four cases in a throwaway probe directory: the real
client-metrics duplicate is caught; a legal `get x` / `set x` accessor pair is
not reported; computed keys are skipped, since [k] and [j] may or may not
collide and the parser cannot say; and a duplicate separated by a spread is
caught, because the second literal still wins.

AUDIT-038 IS FILED FOR THE BIGGER ONE. A first-cut scan counts 321 destructures
in that tree whose call chain contains insert/update/upsert/delete and whose
error is either absent from the binding or never surfaced - the shape behind
auto-supply-replenishment, all four client-metrics write paths, and a live one
in public-booking that silently discards a lead from a public page. The naive
rule is wrong in a specific way worth carrying into that story: a fixed line
window bleeds into the next statement, so a SELECT followed by an unrelated
update reads as a swallowed write. It needs the parser too.

--- 2026-09-02: email campaigns, 281 -> 270, and a page that could never enroll anyone ---

Eight of the eleven were on email_campaigns and the fix was deletion again, for
a reason stated in the tree: supabase/functions/email-marketing/'s header says
it absorbs the standalone email-templates/ and email-campaigns/ functions, and
that "they get deleted in PR 2 after 48h soak". PR 2 never landed. The
standalone that survived for months was the BROKEN copy.

WHAT IT GOT WRONG. It wrote name, from_name, from_email, reply_to, html_content,
text_content and scheduled_at; the columns are campaign_name, sender_name,
sender_email, reply_to_email and scheduled_date, and there is no html/text body
column at all - the body lives on a template or in sequence_steps. Create also
omitted four NOT NULLs (campaign_type, schedule_type, owner_id, created_by), so
it would have failed with every name right. Its /send read
customer_segment_members and wrote email_campaign_sends, and its /:id/stats read
the same send table - neither is declared in any schema or created by any
migration. So /send marked a campaign 'sending' with zero recipients (the
segment read is off a column that does not exist, so recipients was always
empty) and /:id/stats returned four zero percentages. The canonical handler uses
email_sends and email_events, which are real.

THE LIVE DAMAGE WAS ON THE FRONTEND AND IT WAS TOTAL. EmailSequencesPage filters
with ['drip','automated'].includes(c.campaignType). Every campaigns endpoint -
the deleted one and the canonical one alike - returns raw snake_case rows, so
campaignType was undefined on every row, the filter matched nothing, and the
page said "No drip or automated campaigns found" whatever the tenant had. The
routed /marketing/sequences admin could never select a campaign, so nobody has
ever been enrolled into a drip through the UI. The hook maps the row now, at the
boundary, and the page is unchanged.

Deleted: both standalone functions. The proxy entry moves from
/api/email-campaigns -> email-campaigns to /api/email-marketing ->
email-marketing, which shadows nothing (routes/email-marketing-routes.ts mounts
at the /api ROOT and owns /api/email-templates, /api/email-campaigns and five
more, not this prefix). That router's own header claimed /email-campaigns was
"the only one anything calls"; it is now zero of seven, and the header says so.

THREE FILES EACH HELD A PIECE AND NONE POINTED AT THE OTHERS - the canonical
function's header, the Express router's header, and the proxy's SEC-SESSION-001
comment. All three are corrected. The generalisable half is in the canonical
header: a superseding file that names its predecessor is only half the job, and
this is the fourth instance in this repo, so grep for the predecessor before
assuming the swap completed.

Ratchets: phantom-cols 281 -> 270, phantom-tables -2, unreferenced-edge-fns -1,
edge-rbac -2, shadowed-express retained 66 -> 58 (the eight email-campaigns
handlers are no longer shadowed - they are merely dead, as the whole file is).

A FIFTH DEBT ASSERTION FAILED ON ITS OWN STORY'S SUCCESS, in the same hour.
session-user-auth-annotations.test.ts asserted the email-marketing router's
header verbatim - that /email-campaigns was "the only one anything calls" and
was proxied to supabase/functions/email-campaigns/. Both sentences became false
the moment this landed. They assert the FACT now, by walking all eight client
trees for a caller of each of the seven prefixes, so the file's dead-ness no
longer depends on how its header is phrased. That rewrite immediately hit the
absence-assertion trap from the other side: the hook explains in prose that it
used to call /api/email-campaigns, and the scan read its own explanation as the
caller it was asserting was gone. Comments stripped, line comments first.

--- 2026-09-02: a comment recording a removal counted as a caller ---

270 -> 256, and the fourteen went by deleting two edge functions built on a
table that does not exist. `devices` is in no Drizzle schema and no migration;
supabase/functions/devices/ named it in five of its seven queries and
supabase/functions/order-toner/ in one, so a list, a detail read, a create, an
update and a delete were each a 42P01. order-toner's insert was also the exact
supply_orders defect AUDIT-031 had already found and fixed elsewhere - a second
copy, left behind.

AUDIT-028 recorded all of this on 2026-08-29 and left both as "belongs to
whoever takes the repoint". The repoint happened under other names and nobody
came back: PA-054 moved ManufacturerIntegrationDevices to /api/device-monitoring,
and AUDIT-031 rebuilt order-toner there over device_supply_orders. Both
originals survived, unreferenced, for four days.

THE GUARD SHOULD HAVE SAID SO AND DID NOT, in the sharpest version of a trap
this repo keeps hitting. check:unreferenced-edge-fns strips comments from the
proxy and the dispatcher but NOT from client sources, and
ManufacturerIntegrationDevices.tsx carries the line "PA-054: /api/devices is
proxied by neither host, so all three of this page's calls 404'd in production".
That comment - a note recording that the page STOPPED calling the prefix - was
the only thing keeping `devices` off the list. The explanation of the removal
faked the reference it was documenting.

It is the same guard CLAUDE.md already records being wrong about `fleet`, where
a MISTAKEN reference was the only thing making it pass. So it has now been wrong
in both directions on the same question, once because a reference was wrong and
once because a reference was not a reference. Comments are stripped now, and
that surfaced exactly one function: this one. The cost of the blind spot was one
entry, which is worth stating plainly rather than implying a sweep.

Not touched, and worth knowing: server/routes-manufacturer-integration.ts still
serves GET /api/devices, and unlike the edge function it is CORRECT - it joins
device_registrations to manufacturer_integrations. It has no caller either. It
stays because removing one handler from an otherwise coherent live router is a
different decision from deleting a dead function.

Ratchets: phantom-cols 270 -> 256, phantom-tables -2, unreferenced-edge-fns -1
(order-toner resolved; devices never made it onto the list).

--- 2026-09-02: onboarding, 256 -> 248, and the pages were the correct half ---

Eight references across two tables, and every one was in the HANDLER. Both
creator surfaces already spoke the real vocabulary; the edge function spoke
another one, and neither create had ever worked.

CHECKLIST CREATE wrote business_record_id, assigned_to, installation_date and
notes - none of them columns - while setting none of checklist_title,
installation_type, customer_data, site_information or equipment_details.
checklist_title and installation_type are NOT NULL with no default, so it was a
42703 that would have been a 23502 anyway. EnhancedOnboardingForm, routed at
both /onboarding/new and /onboarding/enhanced, builds exactly the real column
set in camelCase and even derives installationType correctly from whether any
equipment item is a replacement. The handler reads that payload now.

EQUIPMENT CREATE wrote model_number, installation_location, ip_address and
is_primary, and never set manufacturer or model, both NOT NULL. Of the nine
fields OnboardingDetails' dialog sends - manufacturer, model, serialNumber,
assetTag, buildingLocation, roomLocation, specificLocation, targetIpAddress,
hostname, all real column names - only serialNumber landed anywhere.

CHECKLIST UPDATE had a four-entry field map of which three named nothing, so any
edit touching one lost the whole update, including a status change sent in the
same request. It maps nineteen fields now and stamps last_modified_by, which the
old one never set.

is_primary is DROPPED rather than given a column and reported in `unpersisted`,
matching the idiom a previous pass established here for taskOrder: which of
several devices on a site is "primary" is not something this table records, and
a column for a flag nothing reads is inventing the behaviour. `notes` is
reported the same way - description and special_instructions both exist, and
guessing which one a caller meant would put customer text somewhere it may not
belong.

THE DASHBOARD'S QUICK CHECKLIST HAD TWO FAULTS OF ITS OWN, both behind the
42703. Its installation-type select offered new_site, equipment_upgrade,
relocation and expansion; the Postgres enum is new_installation, replacement,
relocation, upgrade. Only one of four overlapped, so three options were a 22P02
waiting to happen. And it collected a company NAME with no id, while
customer_id is NOT NULL and links to business_records - so that dialog could
never have satisfied the constraint however the handler was written. It has a
business-record selector now, and the four values are the enum's. The handler
answers 400 naming the missing field rather than letting a NOT NULL become a
500.

STILL OPEN, and it is a decision rather than a repair.
ComprehensiveOnboardingForm at /onboarding/original sends neither
installationType nor a customer link, so it 400s where it used to 500. It is
1,405 lines against EnhancedOnboardingForm's 2,378, and both /onboarding/new and
/onboarding/enhanced route to the Enhanced one, which has the auto-population
and replacement tracking the Comprehensive one lacks. That reads like AUDIT-018's
supersession shape, but confirming a strict superset across 1,405 lines of form
fields is work I did not do, so it is named here rather than asserted: either it
gets the same customer selector, or it is retired behind a LegacyRedirect. Do
not decide it from the line count.

--- 2026-09-02: field-service, 248 -> 241, and a trail that was always empty ---

Seven references over two tables, and no migration was needed for either.

GEOFENCE_ALERTS was a rename. The columns are is_acknowledged, is_resolved and
is_escalated; the handler used the names without the prefix, so acknowledging,
resolving and escalating an alert each 42703'd. The two stats counts read
`.count` off failed queries and rendered them through `?? 0`, so the alerts
panel reported zero unacknowledged alerts because the query failed, not because
there were none - the exact shape CLAUDE.md records for a dashboard of zeroes.

LOCATION_HISTORY IS A BARE GPS TRAIL and two separate inserts wrote ticket_id,
customer_id, device_id and activity_type onto it. The one that matters is in the
REAL-TIME PUT path, PUT /technicians/:id/location, and it discarded its error
entirely - so every ping since the file was written returned 200 and stored
nothing. The trail has never had a row from the path that produces pings. The
current ticket, customer and device belong on technician_locations, which the
same handler writes and which does have current_ticket_id, current_customer_id
and device_id.

NO COLUMN WAS ADDED FOR THE TICKET LINK, and this is the part worth reusing.
GET /tickets/:id/activity-timeline filtered location_history on ticket_id, so
the obvious fix was a migration. But the link already exists:
location_history.session_id references mobile_service_sessions, whose
service_ticket_id is NOT NULL. The timeline resolves ticket -> sessions ->
history now. That is the model the schema already expresses, and unlike a copied
ticket_id it cannot drift from the session's own ticket. Before adding a column
for a join, check whether the schema already joins.

A ping written by the real-time path carries no session unless the caller sends
one, so it will not appear in a timeline. That is stated in the handler rather
than fixed by a per-ping session lookup on a real-time path; sessionId is passed
through when supplied, and POST /location-history takes it explicitly.

REACHABILITY, STATED HONESTLY, because it qualifies the value of this pass.
NOTHING in any of the eight client trees calls /api/field-service. The mobile
app's own Field Service screen uses /api/mobile/*. The only caller is pg_cron,
at exactly one path - /field-service/mileage/auto-generate - so nine of this
function's ten handlers are unreached. check:unreferenced-edge-fns counts the
FUNCTION as reached because cron hits one endpoint, which means the
reachable/unreachable split this story has been ordering by is per-function and
coarser than it looks. Worth knowing before quoting "156 reachable" as though
each were behind a screen somebody opens.

I fixed it anyway because both were renames or joins over real, declared tables
with no migration and no invented behaviour - the cheap end. A caller with no
back end is a different story from a back end with no caller, and this is the
latter.

--- 2026-09-02: predictive maintenance, 241 -> 235, live on both hosts ---

The first cluster in a while that was reachable in the strong sense:
/predictive-maintenance-hub is routed, /api/predictive-maintenance is proxied,
and the page makes six calls. It has never worked on either host.

THE DASHBOARD 500'd ON EVERY REQUEST. Its equipment select named make, model,
location, current_meter_reading and status. The columns are manufacturer,
model_number, location_description and equipment_status, and equipment has NO
meter column at all - readings live in meter_readings. PostgREST rejects a whole
select on one bad name, so the error branch fired every time. parts-forecast
named three of the same five.

THE METER TERM NOW COMES FROM meter_readings, one batched pass ordered by
reading_date descending, first row per equipment_id. A device with no reading
gets null rather than 0: the health score has a "meter over 50,000 pages"
penalty, and defaulting an unread device to zero pages would silently score it
as healthy on evidence nobody collected.

SCHEDULING WAS WORSE THAN A RENAME. service_tickets has no ticket_type, and
customer_id, ticket_number and created_by are all NOT NULL - none of which the
insert set. So "schedule proactive service" was a 42703 that would have been a
23502 three times over. customer_id comes off the equipment row now, the ticket
number follows predictive-failure's PF- convention as PM-, and equipment with no
customer gets a 409 saying so rather than a ticket that cannot be raised.

FOUR HEADLINE FIGURES WERE DELETED, not repaired, and this is the PA-040 shape
again. preventableEmergencies was devicesAtRisk * 0.7. downtimePreventedHours
was that * 4. costSavings was that * 200. uptimeImprovement divided the third by
equipmentCount * 30 * 24. Every coefficient was typed in, and nothing in this
system records whether an at-risk device became an emergency, how long one
lasted, or what one cost - so the page's "Downtime Prevented" and "Cost Savings"
cards were a chain of constants wearing a derivation's clothes. Both cards are
gone and all four are named in the response's `unbacked` array. Worth noting
they would have shown as 0h and $0 today, since the endpoint they read 500'd -
the fabrication only becomes visible once the query is fixed, which is an
argument for checking the arithmetic while you are repairing the columns.

MY FIRST VERSION OF THE LOCK TEST CONTRADICTED ITSELF, and the shape is worth
recording next to the absence-assertion trap it resembles: it asserted the four
names were absent from the edge function AND that the same function names them
in `unbacked`. Both cannot hold. The fix is to assert absence of the
CALCULATION - `const <name> =` - rather than of the word, because the honest
half of this change is that the names survive as an admission.

--- 2026-09-02: billing rules, Apollo enrichment, and the guard accusing correct code ---

235 -> 223, and five of the twelve were never defects at all.

THE GUARD WAS RESOLVING A PAYLOAD ACROSS A FUNCTION BOUNDARY.
predictive-failure has `const updates = { … }` in its settings handler and, 340
lines later, `async function updatePrediction(admin, tenantId, id, updates)`
doing `.update(updates)` on a different table. The nearest-preceding-binding
rule matched the first, so five real columns of predictive_dispatch_settings -
agent_enabled, confidence_threshold, paused_at, paused_reason,
updated_by_user_id - were reported as phantom columns of
equipment_failure_predictions. Correct code accused, which is worse than a
missed finding and is the THIRD variant of this trap the script has hit; the
header now lists all three. Parameters are collected as keyless bindings, so the
existing rule stops at them.

A CRUDER FIX WAS TRIED FIRST AND WAS WRONG IN A WAY WORTH RECORDING. Rejecting
any resolution with a `function` keyword or arrow body between the declaration
and the call is simpler and looks conservative. It also dropped lead-scoring's
`updates`, which is separated from its
`.from('business_records').update(updates)` only by an unrelated
`const copy = (leadKey, apolloKey) => { … }` helper - and enriched_from_apollo /
apollo_enriched_at are genuine phantom columns. So "over-rejecting is the safe
direction" is FALSE when the over-rejection retires a true finding from the
baseline as though it were fixed. The rule has to name the actual shadow.

BILLING RULES COULD NOT BE CREATED. The handler wrote description, conditions,
actions, effective_from and effective_to - none of them columns - dropped the
twenty rate and rounding fields billing-rule-dialog.tsx collects, and never set
effective_start_date, which is NOT NULL. /billing-rules is routed and
/api/billing is proxied, so this was live on both hosts. The dialog was already
correct, the same as onboarding and purchase orders before it; the handler
speaks its vocabulary now, the update field map went from eleven entries (five
of them naming nothing) to thirty-three, and conditions/actions are reported in
`unpersisted` because billing_rules is a TYPED rule - rule_type picks the shape
and tiered_rates / volume_discounts / time_based_pricing / custom_calculation_-
formula carry it, so a generic condition/action pair would be a second rule
engine beside the one that exists.

APOLLO ENRICHMENT NEVER RAN PAST ITS FIRST GATE, and the two flagged columns
were downstream of that. `enrichFromApollo` tested `lead.email`, and
business_records has NO email column - a record there is a COMPANY and the
person lives in primary_contact_*. So every lead returned "no email to match
against" and the update was never reached. Below it, copy() wrote first_name,
last_name, job_title and linkedin_url, which is the same mistake CLAUDE.md
records for the Chrome extension's contact import. Fixed end to end: the match
is on primary_contact_email, Apollo's first and last name join into
primary_contact_name, title goes to primary_contact_title, the contact's phone
goes to primary_contact_phone rather than the company's `phone`, and the write
error is surfaced instead of discarded. linkedin_url and the two enrichment
stamps are dropped rather than given columns - the tenant_apollo_leads upsert
immediately below already records which Apollo contact matched and when, in the
table built to hold that.

WHY THE GUARD MISSED THE WORST OF IT: copy() assigns `updates[leadKey]`, a
COMPUTED key, and the assignment scan matches `name.key =` only. That blind spot
is already named in the header as "a payload whose keys are assembled at
runtime"; this is what it costs. Four wrong column names sat behind one wrong
gate, and the guard could see neither.

--- 2026-09-02: five handlers, a tenant leak, and a fourth accused-correct-code ---
