223 -> 212. Five reachable surfaces, each writing or reading names its table
does not have, and three findings beyond the renames.

A TENANT LEAK. quote-line-items' list filtered on quote_id ALONE, no tenant_id,
so any authenticated user holding a quote id could read another tenant's line
items and their prices. It only ever failed because the same select carried a
`product:product_id (…)` embed naming a foreign key that does not exist - an
accident, not a control. The table is minimal (quote_id, description, quantity,
unit_price, total_price); the rich model with discounts and line numbers is
proposal_line_items, behind the quote builder. The insert also omitted tenant_id
and total_price, both NOT NULL.

A DEFINITION-OF-DONE GATE THAT FAILED CLOSED ON ITS OWN QUERY. validate's
service-completion check selected technician_id, work_performed and time_spent;
the columns are assigned_technician_id, work_order_notes and labor_hours, so the
row came back null and the gate answered "Service ticket not found" for every
ticket that exists. DoDEnforcementButton and DoDValidationBanner both call it, so
completion was blocked on every ticket with a message saying the ticket was not
there. A gate that fails closed on a query error reads as a real finding, which
is why four missing fields hid one broken select.

PARTS ORDERS could not be created: parts, total_cost and ordered_by are not
columns, and service_ticket_id, order_number, vendor_name, order_date, subtotal
and total are all NOT NULL and none was set. The client was already right - its
form derives from insertPartsOrderSchema, and line items go separately to
/api/parts-orders/:id/items, which is why `parts` had nowhere to go. That is the
FOURTH page-was-right-handler-was-wrong in this story, after purchase orders,
onboarding and billing rules.

ACTIVITIES: description, not notes; call_duration, not duration_minutes; and no
priority column at all, so logging any activity was broken rather than just its
notes. priority is reported in `unpersisted` - the table records urgency as
due_date and follow_up_date, and a second quieter answer to the same question is
not an improvement.

AND A FOURTH INSTANCE OF THE GUARD ACCUSING CORRECT CODE, caught by my own lock
test before it shipped. I rebound supabase/functions/projects/ to schema.ts's
shape - budget, estimated_hours - and wrote a test comparing the result to
MIGRATION 0000. It failed: the physical table has project_manager,
estimated_budget, actual_budget, tags, color, template, workflow and
custom_fields, which is task-schema.ts's declaration, and drizzle-schema.ts
SKIPS that one in favour of schema.ts's. So three of the four reported columns
were real and estimated_budget really is an integer of cents, making the `* 100`
correct. Only project_manager_id was wrong. The change is reverted to that one
rename.

Filed as AUDIT-039, because it is bigger than a reporting error: the snapshot
drizzle-kit diffs against is the wrong shape for this table, so the next
generated migration would drop nine real columns. Note what caught it - a test
comparing code to the MIGRATION rather than to the declaration. Nothing that
reads drizzle-schema.ts could have, check:declared-cols included, because that
guard asks whether SOME pgTable declares a column and task-schema does.

The four projects entries stay in the phantom baseline meanwhile. They are known
non-defects, which is the thing I have twice said a baseline must not hold, so
AUDIT-039's criteria include removing them.

--- 2026-09-02: correcting the previous entry ---

The "fourth accused-correct-code" above is WRONG, and AUDIT-039 with it. I read
migration 0000, saw `projects` created in task-schema.ts's shape, and concluded
drizzle-schema.ts resolved the collision backwards. Migration 0002 converts the
table to schema.ts's shape - adds estimated_hours, actual_hours and budget,
drops project_manager, estimated_budget, actual_budget, tags and six more. So
the guard was right, the four reports were true positives, and I reverted a
correct fix on the strength of half the evidence.

npm run check:declared-cols told me so, in the same session, by replaying the
whole journal: it said the database has projects.budget, estimated_hours and
actual_hours while the schema does not. I read that output and did not act on
it. A guard that replays the chain outranks a person reading the first migration
that mentions the table.

The handler is now bound to the post-0002 shape, the lock test asserts against
0002's ALTER statements rather than 0000's CREATE, and AUDIT-039 is withdrawn
with the mistake recorded rather than deleted. Three of the four earlier
accused-correct-code findings in this story stand; this one does not.

userStories.title: 321 edge-function writes never look at the error PostgREST hands them
userStories.description:
A WRITE THAT REPORTS SUCCESS AND SAVES NOTHING IS THE COMMONEST SHAPE LEFT IN
THE EDGE TREE, and no guard here sees it. PostgREST returns `{ data, error }`
rather than throwing, so a handler that never looks at `error` carries on and
answers 200. Three instances found in two days, each independently:

  auto-supply-replenishment  destructured `{ data: order }` with no error at
                             all, so a replenishment run that ordered nothing
                             was indistinguishable from a run with nothing to
                             order (AUDIT-037, now a 501)
  client-metrics             all four write paths did `if (!error && data)` and
                             answered { success: true, received: 12,
                             processed: 0 } (AUDIT-037, deleted)
  public-booking             five steps in linkCrm, each inside a try/catch
                             that PostgREST can never trigger - it returns
                             { data, error } rather than throwing - so a linkage
                             failing on every booking looked exactly like a
                             booking with nothing to link. FIXED on filing:
                             errors are logged, best-effort is kept, and the
                             booking still must not fail because linkage did

MEASURED, not estimated: a first-cut scan over supabase/functions reports 321
destructures whose call chain contains insert/update/upsert/delete and whose
error is either absent from the binding or never surfaced. The blog functions
carry the bulk (blog-distribution-engine, blog-outreach and blog-platform-api at
17 each), and many of those are in docs/unreferenced-edge-fns-baseline.json, so
cross the two lists the way AUDIT-037 did before working the list top-down.

THE NAIVE RULE IS WRONG AND THE REASON MATTERS. A fixed line window after the
destructure bleeds into the NEXT statement: supabase/functions/import/index.ts:43
destructures `{ count }` off a SELECT and the following statement is an
`.update(...)`, so a window-based rule reports a read as a swallowed write. The
binding has to be attached to its OWN call chain. Use the TypeScript parser -
scripts/check-dupe-object-keys.mts already does, over the same tree - rather
than regex: find a VariableStatement whose initializer awaits a chain containing
a write method, read the binding pattern for an `error` element, then look for
that identifier in a surfacing position (thrown, returned, logged, or read for
.message/.code) inside the enclosing block.

WHAT COUNTS AS SURFACED IS A JUDGEMENT AND SHOULD BE STATED IN THE HEADER. A
read that falls back to [] is often deliberate - that is why this is scoped to
WRITES, where reporting success while failing is never right. A logged-and-
continued error inside a per-row loop is a real design (partial success), so it
should count as surfaced provided the RESPONSE distinguishes the failures; a
count of successes with no count of failures does not.

Related and cheap: check:phantom-tables' swallow rule keys on the 42P01/PGRST205
literal, so a handler that discards the error entirely slips past it. That is how
client-metrics' `discovered_devices` (the table is client_discovered_devices)
avoided the hard gate. Once the write guard exists, the two overlap and the
phantom-tables rule can point at it.
acceptanceCriteria: Build the guard with the TypeScript parser, not a line window - scripts/check-dupe-object-keys.mts is the working example over the same tree. A window-based first cut reported supabase/functions/import/index.ts:43, a SELECT followed by an unrelated update, so the binding must attach to its own call chain
Scope it to insert/update/upsert/delete. A read falling back to an empty list is frequently deliberate; a write reporting success while failing never is
State in the header what counts as surfaced, and why a logged-and-continued error in a per-row loop is only acceptable when the response reports the failure count

Sample at least ten baseline entries by hand before trusting the number, and cross the list against docs/unreferenced-edge-fns-baseline.json so the reachable ones are worked first - AUDIT-037 found 166 of 339 phantom columns sat in functions nothing calls

DONE on filing: public-booking's five linkCrm steps log their errors now. Its lesson generalises and belongs in the guard's header - a try/catch around a PostgREST call protects against nothing, because the failure comes back in `error` rather than being thrown, so a `catch { /* ignore */ }` reads as deliberate tolerance while tolerating something else entirely
check:phantom-tables notes the overlap - its swallow rule keys on the 42P01/PGRST205 literal, so a discarded error slips past it
npm run check && npm run test pass
userStories.notes:
Filed 2026-09-02 from AUDIT-037. The three named instances were each found by reading one file for another reason, which is the argument for a guard: nothing was looking.

2026-09-02: public-booking is done. The general form of its defect is worth carrying into the guard: a try/catch around a PostgREST call catches only a network fault, so five `catch { // ignore }` blocks read as considered tolerance while the real failure returned quietly in an error nobody destructured. Any rule built for this story should treat a surrounding try/catch as evidence of nothing.

userStories.title: WITHDRAWN: `projects` collision was resolved correctly all along
userStories.description:
shared/drizzle-schema.ts RESOLVES THE `projects` COLLISION THE WRONG WAY, and
unlike blog_posts this one is not a trade-off: the losing declaration is the
only one that describes a table that exists.

  drizzle-schema.ts:91   // projects — SKIPPED: defined in schema.ts
  migration 0000:6653    CREATE TABLE "projects" ( … "project_manager",
                         "estimated_budget" integer, "actual_budget" integer,
                         "color", "template", "workflow", "tags",
                         "custom_fields", "contract_id" … )

That is task-schema.ts's shape, verbatim. schema.ts's `projects` declares
estimated_hours, actual_hours and budget instead, and NONE of those three
columns exists in any migration. So the declaration drizzle-kit reads describes
a table that has never been built.

THREE CONSEQUENCES, in increasing order of cost.

1. check:phantom-cols accuses correct code. supabase/functions/projects/ writes
   estimated_budget, actual_budget and tags - all real - and the guard reports
   all three, because it trusts drizzle-schema.ts as the ownership authority
   (correctly; the authority is what is wrong). AUDIT-037 baselined them rather
   than "fixing" working code, which means the baseline currently holds four
   entries that are not defects, and a baseline holding known non-defects is
   where a real one hides.

2. check:declared-cols cannot see it. That guard asks whether SOME pgTable
   declares each column the migrations create, and task-schema.ts does - so
   estimated_budget passes even though the RESOLVED export does not have it.
   Checking the resolved export instead of any declaration is the fix, and it
   would likely surface more than this one table.

3. db:generate would try to reconcile the live table to the wrong shape. The
   snapshot drizzle-kit diffs against comes from drizzle-schema.ts, so the next
   generated migration for this table would DROP project_manager,
   estimated_budget, actual_budget, color, template, workflow, tags,
   custom_fields and contract_id and ADD estimated_hours, actual_hours and
   budget. That is real data loss sitting in the tooling, and COP-M00 already
   records how easily a snapshot problem here goes unnoticed.

THE SERVER IS ALREADY SPLIT ACROSS BOTH SHAPES, which is why this needs a
decision rather than a one-line swap. server/routes-enhanced-tasks.ts imports
`projects` from '../shared/task-schema.js' and reads projectManager and tags -
correct. server/storage.ts, routes-templates.ts and others import from
schema.ts and use its shape - those queries cannot work. Swapping the skip in
drizzle-schema.ts fixes the snapshot and the guard, and turns the schema.ts
callers from silently-wrong into tsc errors, which is an improvement but is a
visible one.

No data is at stake either way - schema.ts's shape exists nowhere - so this is
smaller than the blog_posts decision. It is filed rather than taken because it
changes what drizzle-kit believes about a table, and that belongs to whoever
runs the next migration.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide which declaration owns `projects` and make drizzle-schema.ts export it. Migration 0000 built task-schema.ts's shape, so that is the one the database has; schema.ts's estimated_hours / actual_hours / budget exist in no migration

Whichever way it goes, fix the server callers on the losing side rather than leaving them to fail at runtime: routes-enhanced-tasks.ts uses task-schema's shape, storage.ts and routes-templates.ts use schema.ts's
Re-run check:phantom-cols and remove the four supabase/functions/projects entries from the baseline - they are collision artefacts, not defects, and the story that baselined them says so

Teach check:declared-cols to compare against the RESOLVED export rather than any pgTable anywhere. It passes on estimated_budget today because task-schema declares it, which is exactly the column the resolved export lacks - so the guard cannot see the class it exists to catch
Prove the snapshot is right afterwards: run db:generate against a scratch Postgres per COP-M07 and confirm it emits nothing for `projects`
npm run check && npm run test pass
userStories.notes:
WITHDRAWN 2026-09-02, a few hours after filing. THE PREMISE WAS WRONG AND THE
MISTAKE IS THE USEFUL PART.

I read migration 0000, saw it create task-schema.ts's shape for `projects`, and
concluded that drizzle-schema.ts resolved the collision backwards. It does not.
Migration 0002 CONVERTED the table to schema.ts's shape - it adds
estimated_hours, actual_hours and budget and drops project_manager,
contract_id, estimated_budget, actual_budget, color, template, workflow, tags,
custom_fields and completed_at. So schema.ts's declaration is correct,
drizzle-kit's snapshot is correct, and the four phantom-column reports on
supabase/functions/projects/ were TRUE POSITIVES that I reverted a correct fix
for.

WHAT CAUGHT IT: npm run check:declared-cols, which replays the whole journal
rather than reading one file, said the database has projects.budget,
estimated_hours and actual_hours while the schema did not - the exact opposite
of my claim. I had it in front of me and dismissed it. A guard that replays the
chain outranks a human reading the first migration that mentions the table.

The handler is rebound to the post-0002 shape and
server/tests/unit/five-handler-rebinds.test.ts now asserts against 0002's
ALTER statements, so a future reader hits the conversion rather than the
creation.

TWO THINGS SURVIVE THIS STORY and are worth keeping, but neither is what it was
filed for:

1. supabase/functions/projects-enhanced/index.ts inserts projects.budget and
   was reported by check:phantom-cols mid-pass. That is worth a look on its own
   - it may be correct now.
2. check:declared-cols compares the migration chain against ANY pgTable rather
   than the resolved export. That blind spot is real even though this table was
   not an instance of it: task-schema still declares a `projects` with the
   pre-0002 columns, so a genuine drift on a duplicated table could still hide.

Leaving the story open would mean leaving a p1 that says something false about
the schema, so it is marked passing with this note as the record. If either
survivor above is picked up, file it fresh.

userStories.title: Decide which role system survives, and reopen RBAC-008 / RBAC-009
userStories.description: As the platform owner, I need one role system before any tier-scoping work starts, because docs/rbac-landscape.md records two (System A `roles` JSONB, which signup and /api/me use; System B `enhanced_roles` + `permissions`, which Express `requirePermission` reads and nothing seeds per tenant) and every scoping fix has to target one of them. Two closed stories misstate the current posture: RBAC-008 ("role-scoped API data filtering") is marked passing while its deliverable server/middleware/scope-middleware.ts has zero importers and sits in docs/server-orphans-baseline.json, and RBAC-009 (role-specific dashboards) is marked passing while RoleBasedDashboard never resolves a real role code (see WF-R-10).
acceptanceCriteria: A decision record in docs/ answers the three open questions in docs/rbac-landscape.md: which role table survives, which permission vocabulary is canonical, and the migration order for existing tenants.

prd.json RBAC-008 and RBAC-009 are set to passes:false with notes citing the evidence (scope-middleware.ts has no importers; RoleBasedDashboard.tsx effectiveRoleCode short-circuits on an always-truthy string).
docs/rbac-landscape.md gains a "Decision" section pointing at the record, so the next reader does not re-derive the landscape a fifth time.
No handler code changes in this story; it is decision and bookkeeping only, and it unblocks WF-R-02 through WF-R-08.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: docs/rbac-landscape.md; server/middleware/scope-middleware.ts:1-116 (no importers, docs/server-orphans-baseline.json:40); server/middleware/hierarchical-query-builder.ts (only importers are themselves orphans). Owner target: L1-2 own work, L3-4 team/location, L5-6 region, L7-8 company/platform. dependsOn: none. FILED 2026-09-02.
CLOSED 2026-09-02. Decision and bookkeeping only, as AC4 requires: the diff is
docs/rbac-decision.md, a Decision section on docs/rbac-landscape.md, prd.json, and
one test. No handler changed.

THE DECISION, in one line each - the reasoning is in docs/rbac-decision.md:

  WHICH TABLE SURVIVES: `roles` (System A). Not because it is better, but because
  it is the one production runs on and the alternative is populated by nothing.
  supabase/functions/signup/ requires it and fails MISSING_ADMIN_ROLE without it;
  its id is in app_metadata.roleId and users.role_id; _shared/rbac.ts resolves
  level and code from it. System B is populated only where somebody has hand-run
  npm run seed:rbac, and its bridge (server/rbac-initializer.ts) has no importers
  and would not compile if called. Choosing B means changing signup, the JWT and
  every consumer of _shared/rbac.ts in favour of a catalogue that mostly does not
  exist - a rewrite with a lockout in the middle, not a migration.

  WHICH VOCABULARY: three-segment `module.resource.action`, stored NESTED in
  roles.permissions. This is not a fresh choice - _shared/rbac.ts's
  flattenPermissions already produces exactly that shape, and
  navigation-permissions.ts and the 132 route gates already speak it. What has to
  change is the two System A seeders, which produce `{ sales: ['*'] }` and
  `{ modules: ['all'] }` - flattening to `sales.*` and `modules.all`, matching no
  gate, the second named after the shape of the blob rather than after anything.
  Wildcards are explicitly NOT in the vocabulary: they would turn every gate check
  into a pattern match and make "who can do X" unanswerable.

  MIGRATION ORDER: WF-R-02 (seed the surviving table automatically) -> WF-R-03
  (claims in the token) -> WF-R-04 (one scope helper on nine endpoints) ->
  WF-R-05/06/07 (sales, operations, service) -> WF-R-08 (org structure) ->
  WF-R-09 (close the /api/me fail-open) LAST, because it is the step that starts
  denying and should deny only once the claims exist and the org structure is
  there to read. Until WF-R-03, LEVEL is the enforcement primitive: a permission
  code copied onto an edge function before the codes are seeded denies everyone
  below platform admin, which is SEC-EDGE-002's finding.

System B is NOT deleted by this. rbac-seeder.ts holds the best-documented
131-code catalogue in the repository and is the source the surviving vocabulary is
drawn FROM. What it stops being is a runtime authority.

AC2 - RBAC-008 AND RBAC-009 ARE REOPENED, both verified rather than taken from the
audit:
  RBAC-008: scope-middleware.ts has zero importers across server/, client/ and
  supabase/ - confirmed by walking all three trees, not by grep on one - and is in
  docs/server-orphans-baseline.json. hierarchical-query-builder.ts is orphaned by
  transitivity (AUDIT-034: reachability is transitive and one-level grep gets it
  wrong in both directions).
  RBAC-009 is SHARPER than the story stated. usePermissions.ts:70 is
  `role?.code || role?.name || 'USER'` - never empty - so RoleBasedDashboard's
  `if (roleCode) return roleCode.toUpperCase()` ALWAYS returns and every fallback
  beneath it is unreachable: the four level tiers AND the sales/service department
  inference, written for exactly the case they can never see. A role row with no
  code and no name resolves to the literal 'USER', which is not one of the twelve
  seeded codes, so getDefaultLayout falls to DEFAULT. The general shape worth
  carrying: an always-truthy default in a hook can make a whole fallback chain in
  its consumer dead, and neither file looks wrong on its own.

A DECISION RECORD WITH NOTHING CHECKING IT DRIFTS, which is how this landscape came
to be derived four times. server/tests/unit/rbac-decision-evidence.test.ts pins the
facts the decision turns on: scope-middleware still has no importer, usePermissions
still returns a literal default, the short-circuit is still above the fallbacks, and
'USER' is still not a seeded layout. If one stops being true the test fails and the
record is re-read rather than quietly outlived.

userStories.title: Give the surviving roles table an automated seed path so signup works on a fresh database
userStories.description: As a new tenant, signup must succeed without a manual database insert. supabase/functions/signup/index.ts looks up `roles.code = COMPANY_ADMIN` and fails with MISSING_ADMIN_ROLE when the row is absent; the only files that create System A rows (server/role-seeder.ts, server/multi-location-role-seeder.ts, server/initialize-roles.ts) have no importer and no npm script, and `npm run seed:rbac` fills System B, which signup never reads. Whatever WF-R-01 picks, its seeder has to run by an automated path.
acceptanceCriteria: A fresh scratch Postgres (the COP-M07 recipe in CLAUDE.md) can complete POST /signup end to end with no hand-run seed step.
The chosen seeder is invoked from a migration, a documented setup script wired into the deployment runbook, or a lazy create-on-first-signup path; it is no longer a file with zero callers.
The superseded seeders are deleted or given the missing importer; docs/server-orphans-baseline.json shrinks accordingly.
All 34 role codes in server/database-updater/seeders/rbac-seeder.ts (or the surviving equivalent) exist for a newly created tenant, with their numeric level populated.
A unit test asserts every seeded role has a level in 1..8 and a unique code.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: supabase/functions/signup/index.ts (roles lookup, MISSING_ADMIN_ROLE); grep for role-seeder across the tree returns only the file itself. dependsOn: WF-R-01. FILED 2026-09-02.

DONE 2026-09-02 (WF-R-02). The role catalogue signup depends on is now seeded by a
journaled migration, drizzle/migrations/0072_seed_role_catalogue.sql (journal idx
55), 45 rows, ON CONFLICT (code) DO NOTHING.

WHY A MIGRATION AND NOT A SCRIPT. roles has NO tenant_id and code is UNIQUE, so the
catalogue is global - one row set for the whole deployment, not one per tenant. That
makes a one-time idempotent insert the right shape: it runs with db:migrate, needs
no runtime code on the signup path, and cannot double-insert. A lazy
create-on-first-signup would have had to invent a level for COMPANY_ADMIN inside a
request handler, which is where the level bug below came from in the first place.

TWO FINDINGS THAT DECIDED THE CONTENT, both checked rather than assumed:

(1) multi-location-role-seeder.ts's 33 codes DO NOT INCLUDE COMPANY_ADMIN. Wiring
that file up - the obvious reading of "give the seeder an importer" - would have
left signup failing with MISSING_ADMIN_ROLE exactly as before, and the seeder would
have looked like it worked.

(2) THE OLD SEEDERS CONTRADICTED THE GATES. role-seeder.ts put COMPANY_ADMIN at
level 5 and ROOT_ADMIN at 7; rbac-seeder.ts also puts COMPANY_ADMIN at 5.
supabase/functions/_shared/rbac.ts - which every edge-function gate reads - defines
COMPANY_ADMIN as 7 and PLATFORM_ADMIN as 8. A company admin seeded at 5 fails
requireRoleLevel(ctx, ROLE_LEVEL.COMPANY_ADMIN) on its own platform: it would have
signed up successfully and then been denied the admin surfaces. The ladder wins
because it is the side doing the enforcing, and this is the ONE code where the two
sources disagree - the test asserts that single disagreement by name, so a second
one cannot appear silently.

WHICH 45. The 35 ROLE_TEMPLATES in server/database-updater/seeders/rbac-seeder.ts
(the dealer org chart the repo already documents, CEO through CSR) plus every code a
live consumer names that the templates omit: the ROLE_LEVEL rungs and the
DEFAULT_ROLE_LAYOUTS keys in client/src/lib/dashboard-widget-registry.ts. Note on
AC4's premise: rbac-seeder.ts writes enhanced_roles, i.e. System B, which WF-R-01
retired - so its CODES carry over but its table does not, and `npm run seed:rbac`
is still not what signup reads. SERVICE_TECH is deliberately absent (the registry
and the ladder both say TECHNICIAN). permissions is '{}' on every row on purpose:
per docs/rbac-decision.md the vocabulary lands in WF-R-03, and authoring 45
permission sets here would be inventing authorization ahead of the story that
defines it. The 12 can_* flags ARE set, because supabase/functions/admin/ reads
can_manage_users to decide admin access today.

VERIFIED. The migration was applied TWICE to a real PostgreSQL 16 (COP-M07 recipe):
run 1 ok, run 2 ok, 45 rows / 45 distinct codes / levels 1..8, COMPANY_ADMIN at 7,
PLATFORM_ADMIN at 8, and the exact query signup runs - select id from roles where
code='COMPANY_ADMIN' limit 1 - returns a row. SCOPE OF THAT CLAIM, stated plainly:
what was executed is the lookup that gated signup, not POST /signup end to end,
which needs a GoTrue instance and a deployed edge runtime this container does not
have. The failure mode AC1 names is the lookup; it is closed.

SUPERSEDED SEEDERS DELETED: server/role-seeder.ts,
server/multi-location-role-seeder.ts, server/initialize-roles.ts - all three had no
importer and no npm script, all three were in docs/server-orphans-baseline.json,
which shrinks 146 -> 143 with exactly those three entries leaving.
server/rbac-initializer.ts is KEPT: it bridges System B and is not superseded by
this seed. Deleting the three dropped the tsc ratchet 315 -> 314.

Also corrected: signup's MISSING_ADMIN_ROLE message told the operator to "run the
RBAC seed", which was already the wrong instruction (seed:rbac fills System B) and
is now wrong in a second way; it names the migration.

TEST: server/tests/unit/role-catalogue-seed.test.ts, 9 tests, parses the migration
and checks it against all three consumers - the signup lookup, the ROLE_LEVEL
ladder, the dashboard registry - plus rbac-seeder.ts's template set. Guards: full
vitest suite green, check:migrations, check:server-orphans, check:phantom-cols,
check:edge-boot, check:shadowed-express all pass.

CORRECTED 2026-09-02 (WF-R-09): the empty permissions blob was NOT inert. navigation-permissions.ts derives every granular permission from the MODULE booleans in it plus the level, so '{}' expands to ZERO permissions at any level and a seeded COMPANY_ADMIN saw only the alwaysVisible sidebar sections. Migration 0073 fills the blob per department and level; it only touches a blob still empty, so a customised role is untouched.

userStories.title: Write roleLevel, role code and permissions into JWT app_metadata at every token issuance
userStories.description: As any authenticated user, my JWT must carry the claims the gates read. supabase/functions/_shared/rbac.ts getRoleLevel() reads app_metadata.roleLevel and defaults to 1; signup writes only tenantId, roleId, accessScope and isPlatformUser:false, and the only two updateUserById calls in the repo (supabase/functions/admin/index.ts) never touch app_metadata. mobile-auth computes roleLevel but only decorates the JSON response, not the signed token. Result: every user is level 1 on every gated edge function, including real platform admins.
acceptanceCriteria: Signup, password login (web and mobile-auth), OAuth callback and the assign-role mutation each persist roleLevel, role (code) and, if the decision in WF-R-01 says so, a permissions array into app_metadata via auth.admin.updateUserById.
Re-assigning a role refreshes the claim so the next issued token carries the new level; the limitation that a live token is not revoked is documented in the handler header.
getRoleLevel() returns the seeded level for a non-admin test account (verified with a decoded JWT in a unit test using a fixture user object, and manually against staging).
isPlatformAdmin() is true for a platform admin account without a manual dashboard edit; the code path that sets isPlatformUser is named in the story notes.
The five edge functions that already gate on level (erp-integration, monitoring-clients, device-monitoring, blog-agents, dashboard-widgets) behave correctly for a level-4 and a level-8 test user.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: supabase/functions/signup/index.ts:184-191; supabase/functions/_shared/rbac.ts:57-79; supabase/functions/mobile-auth/index.ts:314-380 (response-only enrichment). dependsOn: WF-R-01. FILED 2026-09-02.

DONE 2026-09-02 (WF-R-03). The claims the gates read are now written at every point
that sets a role, plus a self-healing backfill for the ones that cannot be hooked.
New module: supabase/functions/_shared/role-claims.ts.

THE ARCHITECTURAL FACT THAT DECIDED THE DESIGN, and it is not what the story
assumed. The gates DO NOT DECODE THE JWT. `_shared/auth.ts` requireAuth calls
GoTrue's auth.getUser(jwt), which answers with the CURRENT
auth.users.raw_app_meta_data. So a claim written now takes effect on the next
request - bounded by the AUDIT-005 auth cache TTL, not by the token's expiry - and
re-assigning a role does NOT require the user to sign in again. The corollary is
the whole problem: web sign-in is supabase.auth.signInWithPassword straight from
the browser (client/src/hooks/useSupabaseAuth.ts:414) and web OAuth is
exchangeCodeForSession (client/src/pages/AuthCallback.tsx:129), both entirely
between the browser and GoTrue with NO SERVER HOOK to attach to. "Write it at
token issuance" is therefore not implementable for two of the four paths named in
AC1; the claim has to be written where the role is SET, or on the next
authenticated request.

WHAT WAS WIRED:
- signup: buildRoleClaims before createUser, spread into the app_metadata the user
  is created with. One extra read, no extra write.
- admin invite (POST /admin/users): inviteUserByEmail puts everything in
  USER_metadata, so an invited user reached the gates with an EMPTY app_metadata -
  no tenantId either. Now writes both once the role is known.
- admin role change (PUT /admin/users/:id): syncRoleClaims when roleId changes.
- mobile-auth: it computed the level and put it in the JSON RESPONSE ONLY, which
  the iOS app reads but no gate does. It now persists it as well.
- requireAuth: ensureRoleClaims backfills a bag with no roleLevel. This is the only
  place guaranteed to run for web and OAuth users, and for every account that
  existed before this story. It fires at most once per user (GoTrue then answers
  with the claim); a per-instance attempted-set stops a user with no role_id from
  paying two `users` lookups per request. Never throws - a user who cannot be
  enriched keeps the level they would have had, and is never denied auth.

TWO PREDICATES WERE DEAD CODE, both the same shape and both found by reading rather
than by a guard. `_shared/auth.ts` requirePlatformAdmin compared app_metadata.role
against the LOWERCASE string 'platform_admin' while the claim carries the role CODE,
which is uppercase - so that half could never fire and the whole check rested on an
isPlatformAdmin flag nothing wrote. blog-agents had the identical comparison. Both
now match case-insensitively and accept level 8.

NOTHING SETS isPlatformUser TRUE (AC4's named path). signup writes false;
mobile-auth mirrors users.is_platform_user, which no INSERT or UPDATE in
supabase/functions/ or server/ ever sets true; the only code that derives it from
level 8 is server/middleware/supabase-auth.ts:367, which is the EXPRESS middleware
and therefore dev-only under the getApiUrl architecture. So in production that flag
is false for everybody, permanently. supabase/functions/security/index.ts:64 gates
on `!isPlatformUser && roleLevel < 8` - it was denying every user including real
platform admins, because both halves were false, and it starts working with this
story purely because roleLevel is now written. isPlatformAdmin (the claim this
story adds, derived from level >= 8 OR roles.can_access_all_tenants) is a different
key and is written; isPlatformUser is left alone rather than quietly redefined.

PERMISSIONS ARE ALWAYS WRITTEN, EVEN EMPTY. loadPermissions treats a non-empty
array as authoritative and anything else as "ask the database", so [] is the
correct representation of a role whose roles.permissions has not been authored yet
- which is every role, since migration 0072 seeds '{}' on purpose per
docs/rbac-decision.md. Always writing the key also means a stale non-empty list
cannot outlive a role change. When the catalogue gains permissions the claim
carries them with no code change.

VERIFIED: server/tests/unit/role-claims.test.ts, 25 tests, driving the real module
against a fake PostgREST/GoTrue pair rather than a call-recording mock - the
interesting behaviour is WHICH KEYS get written. It asserts the pre-fix bag (the
exact four keys signup used to write) reads as level 1 and the post-fix bag reads
as the seeded level, that flattenRolePermissions agrees with the flattenPermissions
the gates use, that a failed write leaves the user authenticated, and that each of
AC5's five functions decides correctly for a level-4 and a level-8 claim. The five
thresholds are READ OUT OF THE SOURCE, not typed into the test, so one that moves
changes the expectation with it - which is how the story's own premise turned out
to be off: device-monitoring gates at 3, not 5, so a level-4 manager is admitted
there and refused by erp-integration. Every wiring assertion was confirmed absent
from the pre-fix files with `git show HEAD:<file>`.

SCOPE OF THE VERIFICATION, stated plainly: no request was made against a deployed
GoTrue or a deployed edge runtime, so AC3's "manually against staging" and AC5's
"test user" halves are NOT done. What is proven is the module's behaviour and the
predicate each gate applies to the bag it now receives.

check:edge-rbac now advises tightening its baseline for signup and mobile-auth. DO
NOT: they are the sign-in paths and must stay open to all roles. The heuristic fires
on a metadata field name (app_metadata?.permissions), not on a gate. Guards run:
check:edge-boot, check:edge-rbac, check:phantom-cols, full vitest suite, tsc
ratchet holding at 314.

userStories.title: Build a Deno-side scope helper and apply it to the nine core list endpoints
userStories.description: As a sales rep, technician or warehouse associate, I should see my own records by default; as a manager, my team or location; as a district or area manager, my region; as an executive, the company. Today business-records, deals, service, tasks, invoices, meter-reads, purchase-orders, equipment and proposals filter by tenant_id only, so a level-1 user gets every record in the tenant. The two purpose-built engines (server/middleware/hierarchical-query-builder.ts and server/middleware/scope-middleware.ts) are Express-only and have no live callers, and production serves every one of these endpoints from an edge function.
acceptanceCriteria: A new shared module under supabase/functions/_shared exports a scope resolver (own / team / location / regional / company / platform) that takes the caller AuthContext and returns the user-id set or location-id set to filter on, mirroring the tier rules in scope-middleware.ts and reports/_hierarchy.ts.

Team scope resolves via users.manager_id (direct reports) and users.team_id; location scope via users.primary_location_id; regional scope via locations.region_id; company scope returns no filter; platform bypasses tenant when can_access_all_tenants is set.
The list handlers of business-records, deals, service, tasks, invoices, meter-reads, purchase-orders, equipment and proposals call the helper and apply its filter unless the caller is level 7+.
docs/edge-rbac-baseline.json openToAllRoles shrinks by those nine entries; npm run check:edge-rbac and npm run check:phantom-cols pass.
A unit test per endpoint proves a level-1 fixture caller receives a narrower query than a level-7 caller.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: per-endpoint table in the audit (all nine filter on tenant_id only; deals and business-records accept an optional ownerId no caller sends); supabase/functions/reports/_hierarchy.ts already ports the rule set for reports and is the pattern to reuse. dependsOn: WF-R-01, WF-R-03. FILED 2026-09-02.

DONE 2026-09-02 (WF-R-04). New module supabase/functions/_shared/scope.ts, applied
to nine list endpoints. Before this, every one of them filtered on tenant_id and
nothing else, so a level-1 sales rep listing quotes got every rep's pricing -
dealer cost and margin included - and a technician's queue was the whole company's
tickets.

THE TIER LADDER (docs/rbac-decision.md): L1-2 own, L3-4 team, L5-6 region, L7-8
company and platform, read off the WF-R-03 roleLevel claim. An explicit
accessScope/territoryScope claim may NARROW what the level allows - a company admin
deliberately scoped to one location is a real configuration - but never widen it,
or the claim becomes an escalation for anyone who can write their own metadata.

DEGRADATION NARROWS, AND IT WILL FIRE FOR EVERY LEVEL-5 USER TODAY. Location and
region scope need users.primary_location_id / users.region_id / locations.region_id
and NOTHING IN THE TREE WRITES ANY OF THEM: the admin invite sets role_id and
team_id only, and the one file that ever assigned a manager (server/auth-setup.ts)
is an orphan. WF-R-08 is the story that fills the org structure. Until it does, a
tier that cannot be answered falls back to the next NARROWER one and records what
was asked for in `degradedFrom`, because guessing wide is a cross-territory leak
and guessing narrow is a manager seeing less than they should. A lookup that throws
degrades to `own` for the same reason. reports/_hierarchy.ts made this call for
reports; this applies it everywhere else.

TWO TABLES HAVE NO OWNER COLUMN AND ARE SCOPED THROUGH THE CUSTOMER. invoices
carries `sales_rep`, which is an E-Automate NAME STRING, not a user id - filtering
on it would compare a person's name to a uuid and match nothing - and `equipment`
has no owner at all, being a customer's asset. Both are scoped by resolving the
accessible companies (owner_id / assigned_sales_rep) to an id list and filtering
customer_id against it. That list is capped at 500, because ~500 uuids is already
19KB of URL and PostgREST sits behind proxies that refuse it; past the cap the
filter NARROWS rather than widening - invoices falls back to created_by, equipment
to nothing at all, since it has no user column to fall back to. In practice the cap
will not bite while the org structure is empty, since regional degrades to team.

UNOWNED ROWS ARE VISIBLE ABOVE `own` SCOPE. A lead nobody owns yet, a ticket nobody
has picked up, an imported meter reading with no technician - hiding those is how a
shared queue silently empties. At `own` scope they are excluded, because own means
mine.

THE STORY NAMED TWO ENDPOINTS THAT DO NOT LIST. "service" is the knowledge and
embeddings function; the ticket list is in `service-tickets`. "meter-reads" is the
email/photo intake pipeline for submissions; the readings list is in
`meter-readings`. Both real lists are scoped; the two functions the AC named are
not, and would have been the wrong place.

AC4 CONFLATED TWO DIFFERENT CONTROLS, and the honest answer changed what I built.
It asked for openToAllRoles to shrink by these nine, but check:edge-rbac measures a
ROLE GATE - whether a user may call the endpoint at all - and every role must be
able to open /deals. Gating them on a level is exactly the lockout SEC-EDGE-002
warns about. So the guard gained a THIRD class: `rowScoped`, for a function every
role can reach whose ROWS are narrowed to the caller. openToAllRoles 202 -> 194 with
8 entries moved; proposals is the ninth and was already in `gated`, so it does not
appear in the new list. Fixing that classifier turned up two defects of its own,
both instances of a lesson CLAUDE.md already carries. It read COMMENTS, so a note
in signup saying a row is "required for downstream tenant/role resolution"
classified a sign-in path with no gate as restricted; comments are stripped now,
LINE BY LINE, because a `/*...*/` scan over a whole file matches the first `/*`
inside a string or regex literal and blanks everything to the next `*/` - which
swallowed monitoring-clients' real platform-admin gate on the first attempt - and
because hasRoleOnlyPlatformAdminCheck decides from a +/-3 line window that a
collapsed comment shifts. Second, a bare `app_metadata?.permissions` counted as a
gate, so mobile-auth - which WRITES that claim for WF-R-03 and enforces nothing -
was reported as restricted; the signal now requires the permissions to be TESTED.
Net effect on classification: no function moved from gated to open except those two
false positives, verified entry by entry against the previous baseline.

VERIFIED: server/tests/unit/scope-resolver.test.ts, 28 tests, driving the real
resolver against a fake PostgREST that evaluates the or()/in() expressions rather
than recording them - a call-counting mock would pass on a module that filtered the
wrong column. It covers the ladder, the claim-cannot-widen rule, a level-1 vs a
level-7 caller on each endpoint, the regional resolution when the org structure IS
populated, the degradation when it is not, the throw path, the customer-scope
overflow in both fallback shapes, and id quoting (an id carrying a comma cannot
break out of an in-list). The per-endpoint tests read the scoped COLUMNS out of
each handler's own source, so a handler that stops calling the helper or starts
scoping the wrong column fails here. One real bug the tests caught before commit:
degradedFrom reported the intermediate tier of a two-step degrade rather than the
one that was asked for.

SCOPE OF THE VERIFICATION: no request was issued against a deployed PostgREST, so
the filter strings are asserted as built rather than as executed. Guards: full
vitest suite (259 files, 4619 passing), tsc holding at 314, check:edge-boot,
check:edge-rbac, check:phantom-cols, check:edge-paths, check:routes,
check:shadowed-express.

WORTH KNOWING FOR WF-R-05 ONWARD: check:phantom-cols resolves a column literal
against the nearest preceding .from(), so a helper that takes a query as a callback
argument makes its columns look like columns of the CALLER's table. The first cut
of scope.ts did that and reported three phantom `locations` columns that were
really `users` columns. Two explicit query chains beat one clever one.

userStories.title: Apply tier scoping to the sales surface: leads, companies, quotes, contracts, leases, commission
userStories.description: As a SALES_REP I should open /leads, /crm/deals, /quotes and /commission-management and see mine; as a SALES_MANAGER my team; as a DISTRICT_MANAGER my region. The ten sales edge functions (deals, quotes, proposals, deal-desk, pricing, commission, contracts, leases, pipeline-config, sales-pipeline) plus companies and leads contain no requireRoleLevel or scope filter at all, and the list pages (LeadsPage.tsx, CrmDealsPage.tsx, ProspectsPage.tsx, CustomersPage.tsx) never send an owner filter.
acceptanceCriteria: companies, leads, quotes, contracts, leases, commission and pipeline-config list handlers apply the WF-R-04 helper (deals and proposals are covered by WF-R-04 itself).
business-records and companies scope on owner_id / assigned_sales_rep, not created_by (the current ownerId param maps to the creator).
The list pages default to "My records" for level 1-2, "My team" for level 3-4, and expose a level-gated toggle to widen; the toggle only offers scopes the server would grant.
A level-1 fixture user receives only their own deals from GET /deals and only their own leads from GET /companies?recordType=Lead; a level-4 manager receives their direct reports’ records too.
docs/rbac-landscape.md moves these functions out of the no-role-check bucket.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: grep -c requireRoleLevel across the ten sales edge fns = 0; supabase/functions/business-records/index.ts:286-314 maps ownerId to created_by; client/src/pages/LeadsPage.tsx:300 sends no owner param. dependsOn: WF-R-04. FILED 2026-09-02.

DONE 2026-09-02 (WF-R-05). Six more sales handlers scoped (companies, leads,
quotes, contracts, leases, commission), plus a caller-chosen scope that can only
narrow, plus the list-page toggle.

THE FINDING THAT MATTERED MOST IS A BUG WF-R-04 SHIPPED YESTERDAY. `companies` and
`business_records` are NOT the same table and do not have the same columns.
`companies` has 37 columns and names one user, `created_by`; `business_owner` is
free text for the CUSTOMER's proprietor. `owner_id` and `assigned_sales_rep` -
which WF-R-04 filtered `companies` on, and which AC2 here asks for by name - belong
to `business_records`, the canonical table `companies` duplicates (CRMX-002).
Confirmed in the Drizzle declaration AND in the 0000 DDL. So the account list would
have answered 42703 in production, and `accessibleCustomerIds` - which resolves the
customer set for invoices, equipment and contracts - was querying the wrong table
too. Both fixed. Every one of those three functions resolves its `customer_id`
against `business_records`, so that is where ownership lives.

WHY NO GUARD CAUGHT IT, AND THE GUARD THAT DOES NOW. check:phantom-cols reads
column LITERALS handed to PostgREST, but applyUserScope takes the column names as
arguments and assembles the or()/in() expression inside _shared/scope.ts at
runtime - the blind spot CLAUDE.md names as "runtime-assembled names". My own
module defeated the guard. It now also reads the literals passed to
applyUserScope/applyCustomerScope and resolves them against the nearest preceding
.from(), which is the same rule it already applies everywhere else. Verified by
reintroducing the bug: it reports both columns, on the right line, as `(scope)`.
That is the check to run after applying the helper to any further table.

AC2 CANNOT BE SATISFIED AS WRITTEN and the honest answer is recorded in the code.
It asks business-records and companies to scope on owner_id/assigned_sales_rep
"not created_by". Those handlers serve `companies`, which has neither, so they
scope on the creator - a WEAKER control, labelled as one in both files and in
docs/rbac-landscape.md. The `ownerId` query param stays mapped to created_by for
the same reason; the story's own evidence line calls that a defect, and it is,
but the fix is moving the handler onto business_records, which is CRMX-002's
migration, not this story. `leads` DOES query business_records and is scoped on
owner_id/assigned_sales_rep properly.

UNOWNED ROWS ARE NOW A DELIBERATE THREE-WAY CHOICE, because one rule does not fit.
Default: visible above `own` scope (a lead nobody owns must stay in the shared
pool). `includeUnowned: true` for the two companies-backed handlers, because those
lists arrive by import with no creator and excluding them would EMPTY the primary
CRM screen for every rep rather than narrowing it. `includeUnowned: false` for
commission, because a calculation belonging to nobody is a broken row, not shared
work.

COMMISSION IS THE SHARPEST ONE. GET /commission/calculations was every
authenticated member of the tenant reading every colleague's gross commission,
quota attainment, adjustments and payout date, filtered only by an `employeeId`
query param the caller picks. Scoped on employee_id now; a manager still sees their
reports, because the user set is the resolved tier's rather than a hardcoded self.

?scope= AND THE TOGGLE (AC3). resolveScope takes an optional requestedScope and
runs it through the SAME clamp as the metadata claim, so it can only narrow: a
level-1 account hand-writing ?scope=company still gets `own`. Threaded through all
fifteen scoped handlers. On the client, client/src/lib/record-scope.ts mirrors the
ladder and decides what the toggle OFFERS - own for L1-2, team for L3-4, the widest
they hold above that - and RecordScopeToggle renders NOTHING below level 3, where
there is one tier and no choice to make; a disabled control there only invites a
support ticket. Wired into the two shared tables rather than the four pages:
BusinessRecordsDataTable serves LeadsPage, ProspectsPage and CustomersPage, and
CrmDataTable serves CrmDealsPage. The scope is part of the QUERY KEY because two
scopes are two result sets. Client and server are locked together by
server/tests/unit/record-scope-parity.test.ts - a drift there is not a hole, since
the server clamps regardless, but it is a toggle that silently does nothing, which
is harder to diagnose.

PIPELINE-CONFIG IS NOT SCOPABLE AND WAS NOT SCOPED. AC1 names it, but
`pipeline_stages` and `pipeline_templates` are tenant-wide CONFIGURATION - the
board every rep shares. There is no per-user ownership to filter on and applying
one would empty the board. deal-desk, pricing and sales-pipeline are likewise not
per-user record lists.

VERIFIED: server/tests/unit/sales-scope.test.ts (26) and record-scope-parity.test.ts
(9), both reading each handler's own source for the columns it scopes on, plus an
assertion against the real schema that `companies` has no owner_id and
`business_records` does - so a future reader cannot "fix" AC2 back into a 42703.
Full suite 261 files / 4654 passing, tsc holding at 314. One concurrent run showed
a single failure that did not reproduce in isolation: the guard battery was
rewriting docs/edge-rbac-baseline.json while a test read it. check:edge-rbac
openToAllRoles 194 -> 188, rowScoped 8 -> 14. AC5's doc update is a new "Progress
against that" section in docs/rbac-landscape.md carrying the per-function table and
both caveats.

SCOPE OF THE VERIFICATION: no request against a deployed PostgREST, and the toggle
was not exercised in a browser - the filter strings and the offered tiers are
asserted as built.

userStories.title: Apply tier scoping to operations: tasks, purchase orders, warehouse operations, equipment lifecycle
userStories.description: As a WAREHOUSE_ASSOCIATE I should see the operations assigned to me and my location; as an OPERATIONS_MANAGER my location; as a DIRECTOR_OPERATIONS the company. Today tasks, purchase-orders, warehouse-operations, equipment and equipment-lifecycle filter by tenant_id only, so a level-1 associate and a level-4 manager have byte-identical API access to approve POs and transition equipment.
acceptanceCriteria: tasks scopes on assigned_to / created_by for level 1-2 and on team membership for level 3-4; warehouse-operations scopes on assigned_to and the location of the operation; purchase-orders scopes on created_by and location for level 1-3 and is unscoped for level 4+ (approvers must see the queue).
equipment and equipment-lifecycle scope by the location of the customer record for level 1-4 and by region for level 5-6.
Write endpoints that change status (approve, receive, transition) reject callers whose scope does not include the row, not only callers below a level.
npm run check:edge-rbac shows all five functions gated; a unit test per function proves the narrowing.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: supabase/functions/purchase-orders/index.ts, warehouse-operations/index.ts, equipment/index.ts, equipment-lifecycle/index.ts contain no role or scope check; supabase/functions/tasks/index.ts:24 documents assigned_to as an optional caller-supplied filter. dependsOn: WF-R-04. FILED 2026-09-02.

DONE 2026-09-02 (WF-R-06). The new capability here is AC3, and it is the one that
matters: until now every scope was a LIST FILTER, which narrows what a caller can
browse and does nothing about a write aimed straight at an id.

WHAT THAT WAS HIDING. `POST /purchase-orders/:id/approve` HAD NO GATE AT ALL - not
a level check, not an owner check - so any authenticated member of the tenant could
approve or reject any purchase order in it. Approve, reject, submit, receive and
the update branch were all reachable by id alone; so was a warehouse operation's
status, an equipment stage transition, and another person's task. A list filter
would not have touched any of them.

`rowInScope(row, columns, scope)` is the answer: a pure predicate over a row the
handler has ALREADY fetched to check its tenant, so it costs no extra round trip.
Its null rule matches applyUserScope - unowned work is shared work above `own`
scope - because a queue whose unassigned rows nobody may act on is a queue that
never moves. `unscopedAtLevel(scope, n)` is the second primitive, for an endpoint
whose ladder is not the default: purchase-orders is unscoped from level 4 rather
than 7, because an approver has to see every order waiting on them, including ones
raised outside their team. That widening is written at the call site where a reader
will find it, not buried in the resolver.

Approve and reject now require level 4. That is a real behaviour change and the
right one: AC1's own premise is that approvers are level 4+, and the same fact is
why the list stops being scoped there.

THREE THINGS THE ACs ASKED FOR THAT THE SCHEMA CANNOT EXPRESS, all recorded in code
rather than faked:
- "warehouse-operations scopes on assigned_to AND THE LOCATION of the operation":
  `warehouse_operations` has 13 columns and none is a location. Scoped on
  assigned_to only; a test asserts the column is absent so nobody adds a filter on
  a column that is not there.
- "equipment and equipment-lifecycle scope BY THE LOCATION OF THE CUSTOMER record":
  `business_records` has no location FK - its `territory` is free text - so
  ownership of the account is the only scoping available. Both go through
  accessibleCustomerIds.
- "by region for level 5-6": region scope still degrades to team, because nothing
  writes users.region_id. WF-R-08.

warehouse-operations' OTHER FIVE BRANCHES (/warehouses, /inventory, /transfers,
/bin-locations, /picking-list) were deliberately not scoped: WF-L-03 established
that six of the seven tables they read exist in no Drizzle schema and no migration,
and that they have no caller in any client tree. Scoping a branch that cannot run
would be theatre. Only the live `GET /` board list and its status PATCH are scoped.

A REGRESSION THIS CAUGHT IN AN EXISTING TEST, worth recording because the fixture
was wrong rather than the code. warehouse-operations-board.test.ts seeded an
operation with NO assigned_to and asserted a level-1 caller could list it and
change its status. Both now correctly fail - and the create branch in the same file
defaults an unassigned operation to the caller, so a row with no assignee is not a
shape this code produces. The fixture was updated to a real row, its fake db taught
the or()/in() the filter uses, and two cases added that drive the handler and prove
a level-1 caller gets 403 with nothing written, and does not see the row in the
list either.

VERIFIED: server/tests/unit/operations-scope.test.ts (22) covers the two new
primitives directly - including that an empty string is unowned rather than an
owner id, and that a missing row is refused - plus the wiring on each of the five
functions. One assertion is worth naming: for every rowInScope call on
purchase-orders it walks back to the fetch that produced the variable and checks
the SELECT actually asked for the column, because a row check against a column the
select omitted is silently always false. Behavioural coverage is the eight
warehouse-board tests, which run the real handler. Full suite 262 files, tsc
holding at 314. check:edge-rbac: all five of AC4's functions are in `rowScoped`,
openToAllRoles 188 -> 186.

SCOPE OF THE VERIFICATION: no request against a deployed PostgREST. The
purchase-order, equipment-lifecycle and task guards are asserted from source and
from the primitives' own behaviour, not by running those handlers; only
warehouse-operations is driven end to end through a fake.

userStories.title: Apply tier scoping to service: tickets, technicians, meter reads, dispatch
userStories.description: As a FIELD_TECHNICIAN I should see only tickets assigned to me; as a SERVICE_SUPERVISOR my crew; as a SERVICE_MANAGER my location; as a REGIONAL_SERVICE_MANAGER my region. supabase/functions/service/index.ts has no technician or assignee filter anywhere (every .eq is tenant_id or id), and service-tickets, technician-management and technicians apply none either. The sidebar hides analytics from technicians, but the API does not.
acceptanceCriteria: service and service-tickets list handlers apply the WF-R-04 helper using assigned_technician_id for level 1-2 and the technician roster of the caller’s team or location for level 3-4.
technician-management and technicians list handlers return only the caller’s team for level 3 and their location for level 4.
meter-reads and meter-readings scope by the equipment’s customer location for level 1-4.
Ticket status transitions (assign, close, void) check that the ticket is within the caller’s scope; a technician cannot close another technician’s ticket.
A seeded FIELD_TECHNICIAN JWT receives only their own tickets from GET /service/tickets in a unit test.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: supabase/functions/service/index.ts (20 .eq calls, none on an assignee column); supabase/functions/service-tickets/index.ts and technician-management/index.ts have no role check. dependsOn: WF-R-04. FILED 2026-09-02.

DONE 2026-09-02 (WF-R-07). Service tickets, both technician rosters and the
meter-read review queue are scoped, and the ticket write paths check the row.

AC5 IS THE ONE THAT IS ACTUALLY PROVEN, and it is proven by running the handler
rather than by reading it. server/tests/unit/service-scope.test.ts drives
supabase/functions/service-tickets/ against a fake PostgREST that evaluates the
or()/in() expressions, with a claim bag carrying roleLevel 1 and role
FIELD_TECHNICIAN - what migration 0072 seeds. It gets tk-mine and not tk-theirs.
The three write guards were confirmed by DELETING them and re-running: exactly
those three tests fail, the other seven pass, so they are testing the guard rather
than the fixture. Also covered: a manager sees their crew plus the unassigned
queue, a company admin is unscoped, and a caller with NO level claim reads as level
1 rather than as unscoped - failing open there would undo the whole line of work.

TICKET WRITES (AC4). Assign, close and void all arrive at the same PATCH, and
nothing checked whose ticket it was, so any authenticated member of the tenant could
close, reassign, delete or write an audit-trail update onto anybody's. All four
paths now go through one helper. A ticket that does not exist returns null from it,
so the handler keeps answering its own 404 - a 403 on an unknown id tells the caller
which ids are real.

THE ROSTERS. `technicians.user_id` is the link to `users`, so the roster scopes
through the same ladder: a supervisor sees their crew, a manager their location. A
technician sees their own row plus contractors with no user_id, which are unowned
and therefore shared. That is safe to narrow because the screens that need the whole
roster - dispatch and assignment - are level 3 and above.

TWO AC PREMISES WERE WRONG AND THE CODE SAYS SO RATHER THAN COMPLYING:

`service` has no ticket list. AC1 asks it to filter on assigned_technician_id, but
that function is knowledge search: its `/search` returns resolution notes from
CLOSED tickets across the tenant, which is the entire point of a knowledge base -
learning from a colleague's repair. Narrowing it to your own tickets would delete
the feature, so it is deliberately left cross-technician and a test asserts that,
with the reason, so nobody "fixes" it later.

The meter-read queue is scoped by CUSTOMER, not by reviewer. AC3 asks for "the
equipment's customer location"; `business_records` has no location FK (its
`territory` is free text), so account ownership is what this can express. More
importantly `meter_read_submissions` names two users and neither is an owner -
`reviewed_by_user_id` is whoever already triaged the item, so scoping on it would
show a reviewer the queue they had cleared and nothing still waiting. That is the
inverse of what a review queue is for. `meter_readings` itself stays on
technician_id/created_by from WF-R-04, which is a better answer than a location
column that does not exist.

VERIFIED: 13 tests in service-scope.test.ts, ten of them behavioural. Full suite
263 files, tsc holding at 314. check:edge-rbac openToAllRoles 186 -> 183, rowScoped
16 -> 19 (meter-reads, technicians, technician-management). Guards: check:edge-boot,
check:phantom-cols, check:shadowed-express.

SCOPE OF THE VERIFICATION: no request against a deployed PostgREST. service-tickets
is driven end to end through a fake; the roster and meter-read changes are asserted
from source plus the primitives' own behaviour.

STILL OPEN, and it is the same line in every one of these stories: region and
location scope degrade to team because nothing writes users.region_id or
users.primary_location_id. AC2's "their location for level 4" therefore resolves to
their team today. WF-R-08.

userStories.title: Build the tenant org-structure admin: invite user, assign role, set manager, location, region and team
userStories.description: As a COMPANY_ADMIN, I need to invite a user, give them a role, and place them under a manager, at a location, in a region and on a team, because the scoping in WF-R-04 filters on users.manager_id, users.primary_location_id, users.region_id and users.team_id and nothing populates any of them. The roles, role-management, user-management, users-team, user-assignments, locations, teams, territories, sales-territories and rep-capacity edge functions all exist and have zero callers; RoleManagement.tsx’s only mutation (POST /rbac/seed) returns 501 in production.
acceptanceCriteria: A routed admin page (gated to level 5+ in client/src/lib/navigation-permissions.ts) lets a COMPANY_ADMIN create a user, assign an existing role, and set manager, primary location, region and team.
The same page (or a companion) creates locations rows and regions rows and assigns a region to a location; teams rows carry a manager and a location.

Each write goes through an edge function that survives WF-R-01 (user-management, locations, teams or their replacements); the functions used leave docs/unreferenced-edge-fns-baseline.json and the unused duplicates are deleted.
Assigning a role triggers the WF-R-03 claim refresh.
npm run check:edge-rbac passes for every function this story makes reachable (level 5+ gate applied).
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: docs/unreferenced-edge-fns-baseline.json lists locations, teams, roles, role-management, user-management, users-team, user-assignments, territories, sales-territories, rep-capacity; supabase/functions/rbac/index.ts:300-312 returns RBAC_SEED_NOT_PORTED; shared/schema.ts users carries role_id, team_id, manager_id, primary_location_id, region_id. dependsOn: WF-R-01, WF-R-02, WF-R-03. FILED 2026-09-02.

DONE 2026-09-02 (WF-R-08). `/admin/org-structure` (routed, level 5+) is the page
that fills the tree WF-R-04 through WF-R-07 scope on. Until it, NOTHING wrote
users.manager_id, users.primary_location_id or users.region_id - the admin invite
set role_id and team_id and stopped, and server/auth-setup.ts, the one file that
ever assigned a manager, has no importer. So location and region scope degraded to
team for every user in every tenant, which is the caveat every one of those five
story notes carries.

WHERE THE WRITES LIVE, AND WHY NOT WHERE THE STORY SUGGESTED. AC3 offers
user-management, locations or teams. None was the right home:
- `user-management` and `users-team` are unreferenced DUPLICATES of the users CRUD
  the `admin` function already serves.
- `locations` had real CRUD but no caller, no proxy entry and no gate of its own -
  and four phantom columns (address_line1, address_line2, country, postal_code;
  the real ones are address/city/state/zip_code), so its create would have 42703'd
  the first time anyone called it. It had never been exercised.
- `teams` is not about org teams AT ALL. That edge function serves PROJECT teams -
  tasks, projects, time_entries - and shares only the word. The AUDIT-031
  collision shape, and adding org endpoints to it would have buried a second
  domain inside the first.
So the tree lives in `admin`, which is already reachable, already proxied per path
and already behind checkAdminPermission. All three duplicates are deleted;
docs/unreferenced-edge-fns-baseline.json 82 -> 79.

A DEV-ONLY 404 CLOSED ON THE WAY PAST. `/admin/user-management` is a routed page
calling `/api/admin/users`, and NO Express router owns that prefix - routes-registry
mounts /api/admin/knowledge-base, /subscriptions and /seed and nothing else, since
routes-admin-workflows was deleted by QUALITY-002. So the page worked in production
and 404'd in dev, and nobody had connected the two. Four scoped proxy entries
(/users, /locations, /regions, /teams) make dev match prod. Scoped per path
deliberately: a bare '/api/admin' entry would swallow the three prefixes Express
does own and take them from working to 404, which is the trap CLAUDE.md names.

AC4 CAME FOR FREE, and that is worth recording rather than glossing: assigning a
role through this page hits `PUT /api/admin/users/:id`, which WF-R-03 already wired

stories are locked together rather than merely adjacent.

TWO DESIGN DECISIONS IN THE ENDPOINTS. Delete is a SOFT RETIRE (is_active=false):
users.primary_location_id, users.region_id and users.team_id carry no FK
constraint, so a hard delete would leave people pointing at an id that resolves to
nothing and scope them to an empty set without saying why. And a placement cleared
in the UI is written as NULL, not '': an empty string scopes a user to a location
id that matches nothing, which looks identical to a real location with no members.

ONE FIELD THE UI DOES NOT OFFER. `teams` has no `code` column - name, department,

userStories.title: Close the /api/me fail-open default and return the role code
userStories.description: As a user whose role_id is unset or whose roles row is missing, I currently receive every module permission at level 1 from supabase/functions/me/index.ts (allModulePermissions() in the fallback branch), which grants the L1 tier of sales, service, finance and reports to an unassigned account. The same function never returns role.code, which is what the dashboard layout and the sidebar need.
acceptanceCriteria: The fallback role object in supabase/functions/me/index.ts sets every module to false, matching defaultRolePermissions() in client/src/hooks/useSupabaseAuth.ts.
The role object returned by /api/me includes code and level from the roles row.
A user with no role sees only the alwaysVisible sections (dashboard, settings) in the sidebar.
A unit test covers both the no-role and the found-role branch shapes.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: supabase/functions/me/index.ts:95-96 and :129-138 (allModulePermissions fallback); grep -c code in that file = 0. dependsOn: none. FILED 2026-09-02.

DONE 2026-09-02 (WF-R-09). The fallback is closed, the role code is returned, and a
LOCKOUT that closing the fallback would otherwise have caused is fixed in the same
change.

THE FAIL-OPEN. supabase/functions/me/ answered an account with no resolvable role -
role_id unset, or a roles row since deleted - with EVERY module at level 1, which
expands to 13 granular permissions across sales, service, finance and reports. A
MISSING ROLE WAS THE MOST PERMISSIVE STATE THE SYSTEM HAD. The client's
defaultRolePermissions() has always been all-false; the two disagreed and the
server was the side failing open. Both fallback branches now match it.

THE PART THAT WOULD HAVE BROKEN EVERYTHING, found while checking AC3. The sidebar
derives every granular permission from the MODULE booleans plus the level -
expandLegacyPermissions({sales:true,...}, 7) is 109 permissions, and
expandLegacyPermissions({}, 7) is ZERO. Migration 0072 seeded all 45 roles with
permissions = '{}' on purpose, deferring the vocabulary to WF-R-03. So on a fresh
database a seeded COMPANY_ADMIN already had no permissions at all, and closing the
fallback would have left every user - placed or not - with the same empty sidebar.
Migration 0073 fills the blob: level 7+ gets every module, below that the modules
come from the role's department (sales -> sales/products/reports, service ->
service/products/inventory/reports, finance -> billing/finance/purchasing/reports,
operations -> inventory/purchasing/products/reports, it and hr -> system/reports,
platform and admin -> everything). The LEVEL then decides how far each module
reaches, which is what expandLegacyPermissions already does - that is why IT_ADMIN
and HR_MANAGER hold `system` (admin.user.view at level 4) and a sales manager does
not. It is a starting point an administrator can narrow, not a policy.

The migration only fills a blob that is STILL EMPTY, so an operator who has
customised a role keeps it. Verified on a real PostgreSQL 16: 0072 then 0073
applied twice, 45 roles, 0 still empty, and a hand-edited SALES_REP blob survived a
third run untouched.

THE CODE, AND WHERE THE LIVE DEFECT ACTUALLY WAS. `/api/me` never returned
role.code. It also HAS NO CALLER in any client tree - it is in
docs/unreferenced-edge-fns-baseline.json - so the fail-open above was real but not
reachable from the web app, and fixing only that function would have changed
nothing anybody sees. The path a web session takes is useSupabaseAuth querying
`roles` through PostgREST directly, and its select named `id, name, level,
permissions, can_access_all_tenants` - no code. usePermissions reads
`role?.code || role?.name`, so every user's effective role code was their role's
DISPLAY NAME ("Company Administrator"), which matches no key in
DEFAULT_ROLE_LAYOUTS - those are codes. EVERY ROLE THEREFORE GOT THE DEFAULT
DASHBOARD LAYOUT, and the twelve role layouts in dashboard-widget-registry.ts have
never been reachable. Both sides are fixed: the edge function returns code, and the
client selects code and department.

VERIFIED: server/tests/unit/me-role-shape.test.ts, 13 tests driving the real
handler for both branches, plus the client select and the migration. Four of them
FAIL against the pre-fix function, confirmed by reverting it. The lockout claim is
measured rather than argued: the test asserts expandLegacyPermissions({}, 7) is 0
and the seeded COMPANY_ADMIN blob is above 50. Full suite and tsc below; guards
check:migrations, check:edge-boot, check:phantom-cols, check:nav, check:orphans.

SCOPE OF THE VERIFICATION: no deployed request and no browser run, so "the sidebar
shows only alwaysVisible sections" (AC3) is proven through the pure function the
sidebar uses rather than by rendering it.

LEFT ALONE DELIBERATELY: normalizePermissions still expands a legacy `['*']` array
to every module. docs/rbac-decision.md rules wildcards out of the granular
vocabulary, but that is about `sales.*` matching a gate; an explicit `['*']` blob is
an operator saying "everything", and silently narrowing it would be the opposite of
this story.

DONE 2026-09-02 (WF-S-07). RLS on the five CRM core tables, and Contacts.tsx no
longer reaches a table from the browser.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY OPEN. `companies` and `business_records` appeared in NO policy
file, and Contacts.tsx read `companies`, `company_contacts` and `users` straight
from the browser with the anon-key client. The only thing between one tenant and
another's account list, lead list and staff directory was an
`.eq('tenant_id', tenantId)` written in that file - a filter the CALLER supplies.
Anyone with a valid tenant JWT and curl could ask PostgREST for the rest.

drizzle/rls/crm-core.sql applies the existing apply_tenant_rls template to
companies, business_records, company_contacts, deals and users. deals is in for the
same reason business_records is - the third leg of the CRM core, and it carries
pricing.

VERIFIED AGAINST A REAL POSTGRESQL 16, all four policy directions, with a
stand-in auth.jwt() reading request.jwt.claims the way GoTrue sets it:
- SELECT: as tenant t1, each of the five tables returns 1 of its 2 rows, and a
  read of the other tenant's row BY NAME returns 0.
- INSERT naming another tenant: "new row violates row-level security policy".
- UPDATE re-parenting a row to another tenant: same rejection - that is the
  WITH CHECK half of the template, and without it a row could be moved out.
- DELETE of another tenant's row: no-op, the row survives.
- A session with NO tenant claim at all sees 0 rows.
- service_role still reads everything (BYPASSRLS), which is what keeps the edge
  functions working.
Applied twice; the second run is silent, so it is idempotent. One trap worth
recording: the first INSERT test failed on "permission denied for sequence", not on
the policy, because the fixture table used `serial` while the real tables are
`varchar PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()`. A sequence grant is not an RLS
result and I re-ran it on a uuid-keyed table rather than claim the insert policy
worked.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT COVER, and AC4 asks for it in writing because overreading it is
the easy mistake: every edge function uses the service-role client, which holds
BYPASSRLS. RLS constrains DIRECT client reads only. It is a backstop against a
missing tenant filter reached through PostgREST, not a second check on the API -
the API's isolation is still the tenant_id filter each handler writes, and CR-010
tracks the x-tenant-id override separately. Recorded in docs/rbac-landscape.md and
in the policy file's own header.

TWO LIVE DEFECTS FOUND WHILE MOVING THE PAGE, neither of them the security one:
- The users query selected `first_name, last_name` and the mapper read
  `u.firstName` / `u.lastName`, which are undefined on a raw PostgREST row. Every
  contact owner rendered as an email or as "Unassigned". /api/users already returns
  camelCase, so moving to it fixes the blank.
- The contact create set `owner_id: filters.contactOwner` - THE LIST FILTER. A
  contact created while the list was filtered by a colleague was assigned to that
  colleague, and one created with the filter on 'all' was assigned to the literal
  string 'all'. The server defaults owner_id to the caller, so the key is simply
  gone. Two more keys went with it, preferred_channels and favorite_content_type,
  both of which were always written as null.
The writes also stop sending a client-chosen tenant_id: an insert that names its
own tenant is only as good as the client that sent it, and that is the write half
of the same hole the reads had.

VERIFIED: server/tests/unit/crm-core-rls.test.ts, 11 tests over the policy file,
the template it relies on (the UPDATE WITH CHECK and the GRANT, both of which are
easy to lose), and the page. The zero-direct-reads assertion walks all of
client/src/pages rather than checking Contacts.tsx alone, so the next page to reach
for the browser client fails it. Full suite and tsc below; guards check:edge-boot,
check:nav, check:orphans, check:fabricated, check:a11y-names, check:raw-fetch.

ONE THING THE FIRST RUN GOT WRONG, worth repeating because CLAUDE.md already warns
about it and I did it anyway: the absence assertions matched the COMMENT explaining
why the line was removed. Comments are stripped before those two checks now.

SCOPE OF THE VERIFICATION: the policies were proven on a scratch database with
tables shaped like the real ones, NOT against the deployed Supabase instance - and
the file is an operator step (psql -f), not part of db:migrate, so applying it to
production is a human action that has not happened. The page was not run in a
browser.
