userStories.title: Fire deal.stage_changed from the stage-move endpoint the UI actually calls
userStories.description: As a sales manager, a deal reaching Closed Won must trigger automation. The only workflow dispatch for deal.stage_changed lives in the PATCH /api/deals/:id stage_id branch of supabase/functions/deals/index.ts, and no client ever sends stage_id there. Both the Kanban board (EnhancedPipelineBoard.tsx) and the deal page (DealDetail.tsx) post to POST /api/pipeline-config/deals/:id/move, which sets status won, probability 100 and writes deal_stage_history, then records an automation row with status skipped that nothing reads. Closed Won therefore fires nothing, on any host.
acceptanceCriteria: supabase/functions/pipeline-config/index.ts move handler calls dispatchWorkflowEventSafe with deal.stage_changed, the same dedupe key shape as the deals function, wrapped in try/catch.
A unit test asserts the event fires with the target stage id on a move; the parity test for the condition evaluator still passes.
The dead branch in supabase/functions/deals/index.ts is removed or documented as the direct-API path only.
pipeline_automation_logs rows are either read by the runtime or the write is removed, so no write-only log remains.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: supabase/functions/deals/index.ts:898-919; client/src/components/crm/EnhancedPipelineBoard.tsx:431; client/src/pages/DealDetail.tsx:274; grep dispatchWorkflowEvent supabase/functions/pipeline-config/index.ts = 0 hits. dependsOn: none. FILED 2026-09-02.
CLOSED 2026-09-02.

CLOSED WON FIRED NOTHING, ON EITHER HOST, FOR EVERY USER - and the workflow runtime
was live the whole time. dispatchWorkflowEventSafe now runs in the /move handler of
supabase/functions/pipeline-config/, which is what EnhancedPipelineBoard.tsx:431 and
DealDetail.tsx:274 both post to. Same `stage:<deal>:<stage>` dedupe key as the deals
function, so the two paths cannot enrol one move twice.

THE PAYLOAD NAMES BOTH STAGE IDS. COP-E02's two vocabularies meet exactly here: the
board speaks legacy deal_stages ids and the canonical model is pipeline_stages, so
the event carries stageId (legacy), canonicalStageId, fromStageId,
fromCanonicalStageId, stageName, isClosedWon and isClosedLost. A consumer that had
to guess which id space it was given would be the next COP-E02.

AC3 - the deals-function branch is KEPT and documented as the direct-API path. It
fires only when a caller sends stage_id to PATCH /api/deals/:id, which no client
tree does, but an API client patching stage_id directly is a legitimate path and
should still trigger automation. The dedupe key is what makes keeping it safe.

/transition DISPATCHES TOO, even though it has no caller in any client tree. A
stage-mover that does not dispatch is the exact defect this story is about, and
leaving one behind would recreate it the day something calls it.

AC4 - THE STORY'S PREMISE NEEDED CORRECTING, and the correction is the interesting
part. pipeline_automation_logs is NOT unread: executePendingAutomations walks it and
really does execute create_task and update_deal_field. It selects status='pending'.
The /move recorder wrote every row with status='skipped', so those particular rows
were write-only while the /transition rpc's rows were executed - two writers, one
reader, and only one of them matched. The approval row was worse than write-only: a
row saying "recorded for the approval workflow (CRMX-008)" reads like the approval
was handled when nothing had happened.

So recordStageMoveAutomations is now evaluateStageMoveAutomations: same evaluation,
same counts in the response, no inserts. Flipping 'skipped' to 'pending' was the
alternative and I did not take it - that would start a second automation engine
executing on the UI's hot path, with approval semantics I cannot validate, when the
runtime that actually arrived is dispatchWorkflowEvent. approvalRequired rides on
the event instead.

STILL NOT ENFORCED, named rather than logged: a stage_transitions rule with
requires_approval does not block the move. It never did - the old code recorded the
requirement and moved the deal anyway. That is now a comment in the code instead of
a database row that looks like enforcement.

A TEST DEFECT AND A REAL ONE, from the same failing assertion. The first run
reported fromStageId as the TARGET stage. The handler read deal.stage_id after the
update, which happens to work only because PostgREST hands back a fresh object -
a property of the client, not of the code - and my fake returned shared references.
Both are fixed: the handler captures fromStageId before the update, and the fake
returns copies like PostgREST does. Worth remembering that a fake sharing row
objects will pass code that a real client would break, and vice versa.

FOUND AND FIXED ON THE WAY: check:unwritten-tables could not see
`INSERT INTO public.pipeline_automation_logs` in drizzle/functions/
pipeline-config.sql, because its raw-SQL writer regex had no room for a schema
qualifier. So the moment the TypeScript writer went away, a table with a real
producer - a SQL function, which is precisely the "some external thing fills this"
case the guard exists to ask about - was reported as unwritten. The regex now
accepts an optional public. prefix. The baseline is unchanged at 39, so nothing
else was hiding behind it; this was one true negative restored, not a shrink.

userStories.title: Mark Won / Mark Lost on the deals table must move the stage, not only the status
userStories.description: As a rep, marking a deal won from the table must put it in the Closed Won column. CrmDealsPage.tsx patches status and actualCloseDate only, so the board (which groups strictly by stageId) keeps the deal in its old column while the table shows Won.
acceptanceCriteria: CrmDealsPage.tsx resolves the tenant’s closed-won and closed-lost stage ids from /api/pipeline-config/board and calls the move endpoint.
After marking won from the table, the deal appears in the Closed Won column on the board without a refresh (query invalidation).
Because WF-C-01 landed first, the same action fires deal.stage_changed.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: client/src/pages/CrmDealsPage.tsx:176-231; client/src/components/crm/EnhancedPipelineBoard.tsx:392-393. dependsOn: WF-C-01. FILED 2026-09-02.
CLOSED 2026-09-02.

Mark Won / Mark Lost now resolve the tenant's closing stage from
GET /api/pipeline-config/board and post to /pipeline-config/deals/:id/move. That
endpoint sets status, probability and actual_close_date from the STAGE'S OWN FLAGS
and fires deal.stage_changed (WF-C-01), so this is one call rather than a patch
plus a move - and the client stops deciding what "won" means.

THE SAME DEFECT WAS IN A SECOND PAGE and the story only named one. DealDetail.tsx's
Won/Lost buttons did the identical PUT { status, actualCloseDate }, one file away
from a moveStage mutation that already did it correctly. Both are fixed. This is
AUDIT-019's sibling-page rule again: when a page writes a field the board reads
from somewhere else, grep for the other page that writes it too.

REFUSING BEATS FALLING BACK. If the pipeline has no Closed Won stage, both pages
now say so and write nothing. A silent fallback to the old status patch would
recreate the exact disagreement this story exists to remove, and a pipeline with no
closing stage is a configuration problem rather than something to paper over.

AC2 needed no work, which is worth recording so nobody adds a redundant
invalidation: EnhancedPipelineBoard keys its board query as [apiEndpoint, 'board',
...], TanStack matches by prefix, and afterMutate already invalidates
['/api/deals']. The column the deal left and the one it lands in both refresh. What
was broken was never the invalidation - it was that stageId did not change, so
there was nothing to refresh TO.

isClosedWon / isClosedLost HAVE ALWAYS BEEN ON THE BOARD RESPONSE. DealDetail's
StageOption interface simply did not declare them, so the page had no typed way to
ask which stage "won" meant and patched a status instead. A missing field on an
interface is enough to make a page invent its own vocabulary.

The test is source-level rather than rendered, deliberately: what broke was WHICH
ENDPOINT the button calls, and a component test mocking apiRequest asserts the same
string with more machinery. It checks both pages, and it is comment-stripped
because both files now explain the old behaviour in prose - the absence-assertion
trap this repo has hit three times. Verified to fail on the pre-fix pages (5 of 6
red) and pass after.

ONE TEST DEFECT WORTH THE NOTE: the first version of the "no bare status write"
assertion was /status:\s*'won'/, which matches the TYPE ANNOTATION
`(status: 'won' | 'lost')` in the FIXED code - so the fix failed its own test. It is
anchored on what follows the literal now. An absence assertion has to distinguish a
value from a type.

userStories.title: Request Approval from the Quote Builder into Deal Desk
userStories.description: As a rep blocked by the margin or discount guardrail, I need an in-product path to ask for an exception. DealDeskDashboard.tsx lists requests and posts decisions; nothing in client/src creates a request, and QuoteBuilder.tsx never references deal-desk. A rep who hits the 409 from the proposals send guardrail has nowhere to go.
acceptanceCriteria: When the guardrail blocks send for a non-manager, QuoteBuilder.tsx shows Request Approval, which POSTs to /api/deal-desk/requests with the proposal id, effective discount and margin, and the matched rule chain.
DealDeskDashboard.tsx shows the new request without a manual refresh.
The request row carries the proposal id in a real column (add related_proposal_id if absent) so WF-C-04 can read it back.
grep for /api/deal-desk/requests in client/src shows a POST caller.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: client/src/pages/DealDeskDashboard.tsx:127-144; supabase/functions/proposals/index.ts:1905-1957 (guardrail). dependsOn: none. FILED 2026-09-02.

DONE 2026-09-02 (WF-C-03). QuoteBuilder's guardrail banner now carries a Request
Approval button that POSTs to /api/deal-desk/requests.

WHAT THE GAP ACTUALLY WAS. The send gate blocked a non-manager and told them to
"save as draft and request manager approval" - and NOTHING in client/src had ever
created a deal-desk request. DealDeskDashboard lists requests and posts decisions;
the create side had no caller at all. So the instruction in the toast named an
action the product did not have. The toast now names the button, which is on the
pricing banner where the violation is already displayed, and the button saves the
quote itself so a rep does not have to know that a request needs a proposal id.

AC3 ASKED FOR A COLUMN THAT ALREADY EXISTS. It says "add related_proposal_id if
absent". approval_requests has `quote_id`, which is the same thing under the name
this schema uses - a proposal IS the quote here - so no column was added. A second
id column for the same relationship is how the two come to disagree.

THE CHAIN IS BUILT SERVER-SIDE, and that is the decision worth recording. The
obvious shape was to match rules in the browser and post the chain with the
request. It is the wrong one: approval_chain is a client-supplied answer to WHO MAY
APPROVE THIS, and the decision handler reads its LENGTH as the number of steps - an
empty chain makes the first decision final. So POST /requests now matches the
active rules itself when the body carries no chain, reusing evaluateApprovalRule,
which check-approval already had and whose own comment says chain building
"belongs in the actual request-creation flow". A test posts an explicit empty chain
and asserts the server overrides it.

FOUR SMALLER CALLS INSIDE THAT:
- A matched rule with NO approvers still produces a step. The rule matched, so
  somebody has to look at it; dropping the step would shorten the chain and make
  an earlier decision final - the same failure as an empty chain, arrived at
  quietly.
- The SLA is the TIGHTEST matched rule's, not the first: a request that has to
  clear two rules is due when the sooner of them says it is.
- original_margin and proposed_margin are written. Both are real columns and
  neither was, so a reviewer saw a discount request with no margin on it - the
  number the policy is actually about.
- Steps come out in the rules' own priority-then-order sequence, so the chain
  matches the order the rules list shows.

VERIFIED: server/tests/unit/deal-desk-request-approval.test.ts, 15 tests. Nine drive
the real edge function against a fake PostgREST and cover the chain (two rules
matching, none matching, an inactive rule ignored, a no-approver rule, the SLA
minimum, and the caller-supplied chain being overridden); six read the quote
builder. The three chain tests were confirmed to FAIL against the pre-fix handler
by reverting the insert to `body.approvalChain || []`.

ONE EXISTING TEST NEEDED UPDATING, and its own title said how. AUDIT-037's
deal-desk-real-columns.test.ts pinned the WHOLE assignment expressions
(`sla_deadline: body.slaDueAt`, `approval_chain: body.approvalChain`) for a test
whose subject is that the COLUMN NAMES are right. Moving the value off the body
broke both. They now pin the column name and the body alias separately, which is
what the test is actually about.

ONE FIXTURE TRAP worth recording: deal-desk reads `app_metadata.tenant_id`, snake,
while most functions read `tenantId`. A camelCase claim in the fixture produced
"No tenant ID found" and a 400 that looked like a handler bug.

SCOPE OF THE VERIFICATION: no deployed request and no browser run. The button is
asserted from source; what is exercised end to end is the handler.

NOT DONE HERE: notifying the approver. approval_requests has a notifications_sent
column and nothing writes it; that is a notification path this story does not
build, and inventing one would have been the larger half of WF-C-04.

userStories.title: An approved Deal Desk request unblocks the original rep’s send
userStories.description: As a rep whose exception was approved, I must be able to send. Approval only updates approval_requests.status; the send guardrail in the proposals function trusts body.approved, which QuoteBuilder.tsx sets from the sender’s own isManager flag. A manager self-approves; a rep with an approved request still cannot send. Three approval models coexist (approval_requests, the PriceApprovals.tsx pricing approval, and the self-declared flag).
acceptanceCriteria: On final approve, the deal-desk function stamps the proposal (pricing_approval_id and pricing_approved_at) and the send guardrail accepts that stamp for the original sender.
A manager sending their own under-margin quote is unchanged (regression test).
A unit test proves an approved request unblocks a non-manager sender and a rejected one does not.
PriceApprovals.tsx is repointed at approval_requests or retired, so one approval model remains; the decision is recorded in the story notes.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: supabase/functions/deal-desk/index.ts:513-560; supabase/functions/proposals/index.ts:1905; client/src/components/quote-builder/QuoteBuilder.tsx:211,476. dependsOn: WF-C-03. FILED 2026-09-02.

DONE 2026-09-02 (WF-C-04). An approved deal-desk exception now unblocks the rep who
asked for it, and the bypass is decided by the server rather than by the sender.

THREE THINGS WERE WRONG AT ONCE, and the middle one is the sharp one:
1. Approving only moved approval_requests.status. Nothing touched the proposal, so
   an approved rep was still blocked - the story's premise.
2. The guardrail's bypass was `body.approved`, which QuoteBuilder set from THE
   SENDER'S OWN isManager flag. The server asked the caller whether the caller was
   allowed. Anyone able to post JSON could send any quote at any margin, and the
   feature the flag existed for did not work either.
3. `isSalesOnlyRole` matched role names ENDING in 'sales_rep', so
   ACCOUNT_EXECUTIVE and SOLUTIONS_CONSULTANT - individual contributors at levels 3
   and 2 in migration 0072 - matched nothing and skipped the guardrail entirely.
   It is a LEVEL check now (below 4, the same line purchase-orders draws for
   approving an order), with the string kept only as a fallback for a token issued
   before WF-R-03 started writing the claim.

Migration 0074 adds proposals.pricing_approval_id and pricing_approved_at, applied
twice to a real PostgreSQL 16 (second run all NOTICEs, index present). A column
rather than a join because the guardrail runs on every send and the alternative is
a query into approval_requests for a row that usually is not there. Both `proposals`
declarations carry it: the table is declared TWICE, 46 columns in shared/schema.ts
and 52 in shared/quote-proposal-schema.ts, and check:phantom-cols resolves the
ambiguity to whichever it sees - adding the column to one of them reported the
OTHER as phantom, which is how I found the duplicate.

THE STAMP IS CLEARED ON REJECT AND ON REQUEST_CHANGES, not only written on approve.
An exception that swung back is an exception that no longer holds, and leaving the
stamp would keep the quote sendable forever after one approval. It is written only
on a FINAL approve: a request part-way through a multi-step chain is in_review, not
approved.

AC4, AND THE ANSWER IS NEITHER OF THE TWO IT OFFERS. PriceApprovals.tsx reads
`price_change_approvals`, which is a DIFFERENT object - a catalogue price-change
request, not a quote discount exception - so repointing it at approval_requests
would conflate two things. But it is also written by NOTHING: two reads in the
pricing edge function and no insert anywhere in the tree, so it is a permanently
empty queue rather than a competing model. There were never three approval models;
there were one working model, one self-declared flag, and one empty screen. The
page is retired (redirects to /deal-desk, gate kept on the old path per AUDIT-019's
rule), and its notification badge and dashboard widget went with it - both were
already in docs/orphan-files-baseline.json, which shrinks 104 -> 102. The endpoint
stays; the pricing function has live endpoints beside it.

VERIFIED: server/tests/unit/pricing-approval-unblock.test.ts, 20 tests. The stamp
half is driven END TO END against the real deal-desk handler - approve stamps,
a part-way approve does not, reject and request_changes clear it, a request naming
no quote does nothing. The gate half drives a new pure module,
supabase/functions/proposals/_send-gate.ts.

WHY A PURE MODULE, since it is a seam and seams deserve a reason: proposals/index.ts
imports zod and pdf-lib from esm.sh and vitest cannot load either, which is exactly
why a dozen siblings in this tree already carry a header saying their logic was
split out for that reason. Left in index.ts the decision could only ever be asserted
by READING the file, and this is the security-relevant part. So needsPricingApproval
and hasPricingApproval live in _send-gate.ts and index.ts calls them. The round trip
- approve through the deal desk, then ask the gate - is tested across both halves.

ONE EXISTING TEST NEEDED UPDATING. PROD-014's pricing-edge-shape.test.ts read the
badge and the widget from disk to assert the endpoint returned the keys they
destructure. With both deleted it could not even load. The endpoint half is kept -
the mapping still matters to whoever calls it next - and the consumer half is now a
check that the three files are gone.

SCOPE OF THE VERIFICATION: no deployed request. What is NOT driven end to end is
PATCH /proposals/:id/status itself, for the esm.sh reason above; the two ends of the
chain are each exercised and the seam between them is one function call, asserted
from source.

userStories.title: Capture how the deal is paid (cash, lease, finance) and create a lease or a contract accordingly
userStories.description: As a rep closing a deal, the lease-or-payment check must be a step, not a memory. Proposal acceptance (the /p/:token respond flow and the internal status change) always calls createContractFromProposal and never creates a lease, regardless of proposalType; paymentTerms on the proposal schema is never read; leases has proposal_id, business_record_id and contract_id columns that nothing fills automatically; payment-processing and subscriptions have no client caller.
acceptanceCriteria: The quote and proposal builder capture an explicit acquisition type (cash, lease, finance) and, for lease or finance, the funding partner, term and monthly payment; the field is persisted on proposals.

On acceptance, a lease-type proposal creates a leases row pre-filled from the proposal (proposal id, business record, monthly payment, term, first payment date) and links it to the contract; a cash proposal creates the contract only.
LeaseForm.tsx opens pre-filled from ?proposalId= for manual correction.
A unit test over the accept handler covers cash, lease and finance.
The deal record shows acquisition type and, when present, the lease.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: supabase/functions/proposals/index.ts:822-850, :936-965, :2001-2010; shared/quote-proposal-schema.ts:204 (paymentTerms unread); leases columns per shared/schema.ts:2817-2819. dependsOn: none. FILED 2026-09-02.

WF-C-05 done.

The defect. Both accept paths - the public /p/:token respond and the internal status change - called createContractFromProposal and nothing else, whatever the proposal said. `leases` carried proposal_id, business_record_id and contract_id columns that no code filled, and `proposals.payment_terms`, the only nearby field, was written by nothing and read by nothing. So a leased fleet was indistinguishable from a cash sale the moment the customer clicked Accept, and the lease that has to exist for billing, renewal and end-of-term never did.

AC1. Five nullable columns on `proposals`: acquisition_type (cash|lease|finance), funding_partner, finance_term_months, finance_monthly_payment, first_payment_date. Migration 0076_wf_c05_proposal_acquisition.sql came out of `npm run db:generate`, and this is the second real proof the COP-M00 tooling works on live work - though it exposed a wrinkle worth recording below. The quote builder captures them in a "How it's paid" card on the Pricing step; the finance fields appear only for lease or finance, and switching back to cash sends nulls rather than leaving a stale term on the row. payment_terms is deliberately NOT reused: net_30 is when an invoice falls due, not whether the customer ends up owning the machine.

AC2. Acceptance now carries acquisition_type onto the contract, and for lease or finance drafts the `leases` row and writes contracts.lease_id back. A cash proposal creates the contract only, and so does a proposal that states nothing - the honest default, not a guess.

THE RULE THIS HOLDS, which is WF-C-09's from one story earlier: `leases` has eleven NOT NULL columns, five of them dates and amounts. A lease is drafted only when the proposal actually states a term, a monthly payment and a first payment date. Short of that there is NO lease and a reason naming exactly what is missing - not today's date and a 36-month default nobody agreed to, which is the fabrication WF-C-09 removed from the contract path. Everything the draft does derive follows arithmetically from those three stated values: total = monthly x term, last payment at month term-1, end at month term. addMonths clamps to the end of a shorter month, so 31 January plus one month is 28 February and not 3 March. The row lands as 'pending' because it is a draft for the rep to correct, and a failed lease never fails an acceptance the customer already made.

AC3. LeaseForm opens pre-filled from ?proposalId=. It derives the draft with planLeaseFromProposal - the SAME function the server runs, via shared/lease-draft.ts, the Node/browser twin of the Deno copy - so the rep cannot see an end date or a total the server would have computed differently. When the proposal's terms are incomplete the form pre-fills what it can and shows the server's own reason rather than inventing the rest.

AC4. server/tests/unit/proposal-acquisition.test.ts, 27 tests: cash, lease and finance; each missing term individually and together; zero and negative terms; a proposal with no account; the derived schedule; the month-end clamp; and an assertion that no current-year date appears anywhere in a declined plan. The row is checked column-by-column against the REAL Drizzle `leases` table via getTableColumns - no phantom column, every NOT NULL column without a default filled, both enum values legal - and then INSERTED into a real PostgreSQL 16 `leases` table to prove it, coming back as 24750.00 over 60 months from 412.50, ending 2031-10-15. The twins are locked comment-stripped.

AC5. DealDetail shows the acquisition type and, when there is one, the lease number, payment x term, lessor and status. The deals edge function reads the lease through contracts.lease_id rather than by proposal, because a contract is what a lease attaches to. Both rows render only when the fact exists, so a deal with no stated acquisition shows neither rather than "Cash" by default.

MIGRATION TOOLING NOTE, worth knowing before the next hand-journalled migration. db:generate emitted seven ALTER TABLEs, not five: it also re-emitted pricing_approval_id and pricing_approved_at from WF-C-04's 0074. The cause is that 0074 and 0075 were both hand-journalled with a COPIED snapshot, so the last snapshot predated their schema and drizzle-kit diffed against it. Those two lines were dropped from 0076 (0074 already adds them, idempotently) and the generate wrote a correct fresh snapshot, so the next one starts clean. The general point: a hand-copied snapshot does not just fail to record your change, it makes the NEXT generate re-emit somebody else's.

Verified: migration applied twice to PostgreSQL 16 (second run skips all five with a NOTICE), columns land as varchar(20)/varchar/integer/numeric(10,2)/timestamp. 4869 unit tests pass, tsc holds at 308, npm run build succeeds in 36s, and the full guard battery is clean - migrations, edge-boot, edge-paths, edge-rbac, phantom-cols, spread-insert-keys, routes, shadowed-express, dup-tables, orphans, server-orphans, nav, a11y-names, fabricated, no-mocks, no-static-posture, no-random-metrics, sql-string-tables, unwritten-tables, phantom-tables. eslint on QuoteBuilder.tsx is unchanged at its 21 pre-existing findings; LeaseForm.tsx and DealDetail.tsx are clean.

userStories.title: The contract record carries its deal, proposal, lease and start date
userStories.description: As anyone downstream of sales, I need the contract to know where it came from. contracts has tenant_id, customer_id, status and nine descriptive columns, and no deal_id, proposal_id, lease_id, acquisition type or start-by-acceptance date; deals has no contract_id. The spine from deal to installed unit breaks at its first link.
acceptanceCriteria: contracts gains deal_id, proposal_id, lease_id and acquisition_type via a generated migration; deals gains contract_id.
createContractFromProposal fills all of them; existing rows are back-filled where a proposal already references the customer and a won deal exists (script under scripts/ with a dry-run flag).
GET /api/contracts?dealId= and GET /api/deals/:id return the linked contract; DealDetail.tsx shows it.
Contract start_date is set by acceptance in WF-L-08, not at creation; this story leaves it null and documents why.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: contracts columns from shared/schema.ts (12 columns); deals columns (no contract_id). dependsOn: WF-C-05. FILED 2026-09-02.
CLOSED 2026-09-02.

Migration 0070 adds contracts.deal_id / proposal_id / lease_id / acquisition_type
and deals.contract_id, with four foreign keys and two indexes.
createContractFromProposal fills deal_id and proposal_id (the deal id is threaded
out of upsertDealForProposal, which already ran immediately before it and already
returned it) and writes the deals.contract_id back-link so the join works from
either end.

THE SUBSTANTIVE HALF WAS AC4, AND IT IS BIGGER THAN "LEAVE start_date NULL".
createContractFromProposal set start_date to today and end_date to today plus 36
months - a term nobody had agreed to. The END date is the damaging one:
contracts.tsx drives its "expiring soon" badge off it, and
supabase/functions/contract-renewal builds its ENTIRE queue by filtering
`.lte('end_date', ...)`. So every accepted proposal manufactured a contract that
would appear as a renewal three years out, with a term no customer had signed. Both
columns are nullable now and neither is written at creation; a null end_date does
not match those filters, which is the right answer for a term that is not yet
agreed. Existing rows keep whatever dates they have - correcting those is an
acceptance question (WF-L-08), not a back-fill.

acquisition_type is declared and left NULL. WF-C-05 is the story that captures how
a deal is paid, and defaulting it to 'cash' or 'purchase' would be inventing the
commercial terms of every contract in the system.

VERIFIED AGAINST A REAL POSTGRES, not asserted. Per COP-M07 this container ships
PostgreSQL 16, so migration 0070 was applied TWICE to a database holding the
pre-migration shape: idempotent (the second run is all NOTICE ... skipping), all
four FKs created, both NOT NULLs dropped, and a contract with no term inserts.

THE BACK-FILL WAS RUN AGAINST THAT DATABASE TOO, over four seeded shapes.
scripts/backfill-contract-links.mjs (npm run backfill:contract-links, --dry-run by
default). There is no stored trace back to the proposal, so the match is
reconstructed from what createContractFromProposal used at the time - it set
customer_id from proposal.business_record_id and nothing else. Customer alone would
link every contract a customer has ever had to one proposal, so a candidate must
ALSO be the only accepted proposal for that customer, accepted before the contract
and within 24 hours of it, because the contract was written in the same request as
the acceptance. Confirmed on the scratch database: the unambiguous row linked, the
customer with two accepted proposals was reported and skipped, the one accepted
eight days earlier was excluded, the already-linked row was untouched, and a second
--apply is a no-op. Attaching a contract to the wrong deal is worse than leaving it
unattached: it moves revenue onto the wrong rep's number and puts the wrong account
in WF-P-04's Needs Ordering queue.

GET /api/deals/:id READS BOTH DIRECTIONS. It prefers deals.contract_id and falls
back to contracts.deal_id, because the two sides are written together but a
back-fill can leave one behind, and a detail page that shows nothing because only
one direction was populated is the kind of gap nobody reports. There is a test for
each direction. GET /api/contracts takes ?dealId= and ?proposalId=.

DealDetail.tsx shows the contract number only when the deal produced one, and
deliberately does NOT show the term: start and end are null until acceptance sets
them, and rendering "N/A" for a date nobody has agreed to reads as missing data
rather than as not-yet.

userStories.title: Purchase-order line items are silently dropped: phantom table plus key mismatch
userStories.description: As a buyer, the lines I enter on a PO must be saved. PurchaseOrders.tsx posts an items array; the create handler in supabase/functions/purchase-orders/index.ts reads lineItems, so every line is dropped at 201. Separately, the line-items sub-resource (19 references) reads and writes purchase_order_line_items, which no schema or migration declares; the real table is purchase_order_items, itself declared twice with different shapes (shared/schema.ts and shared/equipment-schema.ts).
acceptanceCriteria: The create handler accepts the shape the page sends (or the page sends lineItems); a created PO round-trips at least one line (unit test on the handler payload).
grep purchase_order_line_items over supabase/functions returns 0; every reference targets purchase_order_items.

The duplicate purchase_order_items and purchase_orders declarations are resolved to one (the shape migration 0000 created, then any later conversion, read in journal order); npm run check:dup-tables shrinks by two.
Columns the receiving logic needs (inventory_item_id, part_number, unit_of_measure) are added by a generated, idempotent migration or the handler is cut to the columns that exist.
npm run check:phantom-cols and npm run check pass.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: client/src/pages/PurchaseOrders.tsx:95-110 (items schema); supabase/functions/purchase-orders/index.ts:761 (lineItems), :79-1345 (purchase_order_line_items x19); shared/schema.ts:6858-6883 and shared/equipment-schema.ts both declare purchase_order_items. dependsOn: none. FILED 2026-09-02.
CLOSED 2026-09-02.

THE DEFECT WAS PRODUCTION-ONLY, and that is the part worth carrying forward.
/api/purchase-orders is NOT in crmProxies, so dev is served by Express
(routes-purchase-orders.ts, registered at routes-registry:401 through
domains/warehouse) - and that handler reads `req.body.items` correctly and saves
every line. Production hits supabase/functions/purchase-orders/, which read
`body.lineItems` and priced each line off `item.unitCost` while the page sends
`unitPrice`. So a buyer entering three lines got a 201, a purchase order with no
lines, and a subtotal of 0 WRITTEN ONTO THE ORDER AS FACT - and every developer
who tried it locally saw it work.

FOUR DEFECTS, not the two the story names:
  1. The `items` / `lineItems` key mismatch (the page's array was never read).
  2. The subtotal derived from those unread lines, so `subtotal` and
     `total_amount` were both wrong even when a caller did use `lineItems`, since
     it priced off `unitCost` and the page sends `unitPrice`.
  3. `purchase_order_line_items` x19, a relation in no schema and no migration.
  4. A column vocabulary belonging to NO table in this repository -
     quantity_ordered / unit_cost / total_cost / quantity_received - where
     purchase_order_items has quantity / unit_price / total_price /
     received_quantity. Repointing the table name alone would have turned a
     42P01 into a PGRST204 and changed nothing for the user. `item_code` was the
     other half: a real column the function never wrote, and the exact field the
     page sends as `itemCode`.

ONE VOCABULARY, ONE PLACE. supabase/functions/purchase-orders/_line-items.ts holds
the table name and the column mapping. The row builder existed THREE times before
(the line-items POST, the PO create, the PO update) and had already drifted - the
update copy honoured quantity_received where the other two hardcoded 0. Accepted
input is deliberately wide (the page's names, the function's historical names, and
snake_case) because this module is what finally makes the two vocabularies agree;
narrowing it would break a caller that works today.

Two judgement calls in it. `total_price` is taken from the caller when sent and
derived from quantity x unit price otherwise: deriving unconditionally discards a
negotiated line total, trusting unconditionally lets a page bug write a total that
disagrees with its own quantity and price, and the column is what the vendor is
asked to invoice. And `quantity` is ROUNDED, because the column is `integer NOT
NULL` and PostgREST answers 22P02 on a fractional value rather than truncating.

A FAILED LINE INSERT NOW FAILS. The old code did `await admin.from(...).insert(...)`
and discarded the result, so the response was 201 whatever happened - which is how
this survived. It answers 500 naming the purchase order that WAS created, so a
retry does not silently make a second one.

MIGRATION 0067 adds the six columns the function has always written
(inventory_item_id, part_number, manufacturer_part_number, unit_of_measure, notes,
last_received_date) plus the FK the PostgREST embed
`inventory_item:inventory_items(...)` needs - without it those selects answer
PGRST200. Safe to add because the column is new and therefore entirely NULL, and
inventory_items.id is `varchar PRIMARY KEY`, matching. `updated_at` was NOT
re-added: 0001 dropped it deliberately, so the writes were removed instead.

WATCH WHAT db:generate EMITS. It wrote EIGHT statements that were not this change -
proposals.total_dealer_cost, total_margin_percentage, discount_reason,
discount_reason_note, share_token, share_expires_at, customer_feedback and
proposal_templates.template_content - every one already applied by 0042, 0043, 0045
or 0047. They re-appear because the snapshot chain is behind (COP-M00), and shipping
them as bare ADD COLUMN would have FAILED on any database that ran those migrations.
The file was cut to its own six statements and rewritten idempotent + table-guarded
in the 0064/0065/0066 idiom; the snapshot drizzle-kit wrote alongside it records the
proposals columns as present, which closes that drift for the next generate. Read
every generated migration for statements you did not cause.

AC3 (dup-tables shrinks by two) - shared/equipment-schema.ts held the PRE-0001 shape
of both tables: uuid columns, product_id / description / serial_number / updated_at
on the items, expected_delivery_date / notes on the orders. 0001 converted the
columns to varchar, dropped those four and added line_number / item_description /
item_code, and shared/schema.ts is what tracked it. shared/drizzle-schema.ts had
ALREADY resolved the collision in schema.ts's favour by skipping both by name, so
the equipment-schema shapes had no migration behind them and anything written
against them addressed columns that do not exist. Deleted, with a note in their
place. 14 -> 12.

--update-baseline REWRITES docs/duplicate-tables-baseline.json's NOTE from a
template and silently dropped AUDIT-035's scope-correction history. Restored by
hand, with a warning added to the note itself. Check the note, not just the list,
after running that flag on any baseline.

DELIBERATELY NOT ABSORBED: `npx tsx scripts/check-phantom-columns.ts` reports four
`projects` entries (actual_budget, estimated_budget, project_manager, tags) as
fixed. They were already stale on a pristine tree - verified by stashing this
story's changes and re-running - so they belong to whoever owns
supabase/functions/projects/, not to this commit. The baseline is left untouched.

server/tests/unit/purchase-order-line-items.test.ts: 11 tests. The three handler
ones drive the real default export against a fake Supabase client whose tables are
Maps with genuine state, so "the line was saved" is asserted by looking for it
afterwards, and they assert the COLUMN NAMES on the stored row - writing right
values under wrong keys is exactly what happened before. Verified to FAIL on the
pre-fix index.ts (3 failed / 8 passed) and pass after.

userStories.title: Receive against a purchase order from the UI, with partial receipts and inventory movement
userStories.description: As a warehouse associate, I need to receive a shipment against a PO. POST /purchase-orders/:id/receive exists and adjusts inventory_items quantities, but it runs over the phantom line-item table (WF-P-01) and PurchaseOrders.tsx has no Receive action; the only downstream action from approved is Release to Warehouse.
acceptanceCriteria: PurchaseOrders.tsx gains a Receive action on approved and ordered POs that records quantity received per line, with partial receipts allowed.
The status logic (partially_received / received) in the receive handler is covered by a unit test.
Receiving a line flagged as serialized hands off to WF-L-04 to capture serial numbers; non-serialized lines move inventory_items.quantity_on_hand and quantity_on_order.
Receiving an approved PO creates an accounts_payable row linked by purchase_order_id (add the FK; today purchase_order_number is free text).
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: supabase/functions/purchase-orders/index.ts:497-640; shared/schema.ts:6641 (accounts_payable.purchase_order_number varchar). dependsOn: WF-P-01. FILED 2026-09-02.
CLOSED 2026-09-02.

NOTHING IN THE PRODUCT HAD EVER SET received_quantity. POST /:id/receive existed on
the edge function and moved inventory, but the only action offered on an approved
PO was Release to Warehouse, which navigates to /warehouse-operations?orderId= and
records nothing. So the endpoint had no caller, and after WF-P-01 it was also the
only place that would have noticed the phantom line-item table.

THE ARITHMETIC IS NOW A PURE MODULE, which is what AC2 actually needs: every
decision used to be inline in the request loop, so none of it could be tested and
the Express half could not share it. supabase/functions/purchase-orders/
_receiving.ts holds planReceipt, statusAfterReceipt, serialCaptureRequired,
inventoryMovements and buildPayableFromReceipt; 19 tests cover them.

THREE RULES, each a decision rather than an implementation detail:

  OVER-RECEIPT IS APPLIED AND REPORTED, not clamped and not refused. A vendor
  really does ship 11 when you ordered 10, and refusing the receipt leaves the
  warehouse holding stock the system says does not exist; clamping loses the same
  stock more quietly. The excess lands and comes back in `overReceipts`, and the
  toast says so.

  A SERIALIZED LINE DOES NOT MOVE BULK INVENTORY. inventory_items.is_serialized
  already exists, so this is backed by real data rather than guessed. Those units
  become equipment rows with serial numbers (WF-L-04); adding them to
  quantity_on_hand as well would count them twice. The line still records its
  received quantity and comes back in `requiresSerialCapture`, so the receipt
  reports what is outstanding instead of a clean success. That is the AC3 handoff -
  a named boundary, not a stub.

  STATUS IS DERIVED FROM ALL THE LINES, never from the receipt just applied. The
  test that pins this hardest: an order whose first line was completed earlier and
  whose second is completed now is `partially_received` if a third is outstanding.
  Computing from the receipt would call the larger of two partials "received".

BOTH HOSTS, and this is the one that mattered. /api/purchase-orders is NOT proxied,
so Express serves dev and the edge function serves production - the split that let
WF-P-01 drop every line item in production while dev looked fine. Receiving is
worse to get wrong, because the disagreement would be about stock levels and a
payable rather than about a form. Nothing under server/ imports from
supabase/functions at runtime, so the module is DUPLICATED to
server/services/purchase-order-receiving.ts and
server/tests/unit/purchase-order-receiving-parity.test.ts compares the two as text
from the first export onwards. That is this repo's established answer (quote-math,
gpt5-prompts, ssrf, crm-list-query are all the same shape). The module takes
PostgREST's snake_case row keys and the Express caller maps its Drizzle rows before
calling in; making it bilingual was the alternative and it is worse, because a
bilingual version cannot be compared as text, which is the only thing keeping the
copies honest.

AC4: migration 0069 adds accounts_payable.purchase_order_id with an FK and a
(tenant_id, purchase_order_id) index. purchase_order_number was free text and
always had been, so nothing could join a bill back to its order - and nothing
created one from a receipt either. The payable is raised ONCE PER ORDER, not once
per partial receipt, hence the lookup first. Two judgement calls in it, both
recorded in the module: the row is an EXPECTED bill, not the vendor's invoice, so
bill_number is derived as `<PO number>-RECEIPT` because the column is NOT NULL and
inventing a vendor's own numbering would be worse than a derived one that says
where it came from; and net 30 is a DEFAULT, not the vendor's terms, because
vendors.payment_terms is free text and nothing parses it.

A PAYABLE FAILURE DOES NOT FAIL THE RECEIPT. The stock has physically arrived and
the line quantities are already committed by that point, so answering 500 would
tell the caller none of it happened. It comes back as `payableError` and the toast
shows it.

THE TWO HOSTS DISAGREE ABOUT THE DETAIL KEY, which the dialog has to survive:
Express returns { ...po, items } and the edge function { ...po, lineItems }. The
dialog reads both rather than picking one, because picking one breaks the other
environment silently - the PA-021 shape.

FOUND, NOT FIXED: the page's Submit and Approve buttons call
PATCH /:id/status, which only Express has. The edge function serves /submit,
/approve and /reject and no /status, so both buttons 404 in production. That is
WF-P-05's ground (it owns the approval gate on both hosts) and folding it in here
would have mixed a permissions story into a receiving one. Worth knowing before
anyone tests approval against a deploy.

userStories.title: A purchase order knows which contract, deal and customer it is for
userStories.description: As purchasing, I need a PO to point at the contract it fulfils. purchase_orders has vendor_id and status and no contract, deal or customer column; the Book Order button on contracts.tsx passes ?contractId= and the PO page displays it as text and never sends it.
acceptanceCriteria: purchase_orders gains nullable source_contract_id, source_deal_id and customer_id via a generated migration; insertPurchaseOrderSchema and the edge create handler accept them.
PurchaseOrders.tsx sends contractId from the query string on create and shows the contract on the PO detail.
GET /purchase-orders?contractId= filters; the contract detail lists its POs.
npm run check:phantom-cols recognises the new columns.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: purchase_orders columns per shared/schema.ts:6786-6856; client/src/pages/contracts.tsx:610-617; client/src/pages/PurchaseOrders.tsx:482-489. dependsOn: WF-C-09. FILED 2026-09-02.
CLOSED 2026-09-02.

Migration 0068 adds source_contract_id, source_deal_id and customer_id to
purchase_orders, all nullable, plus the three foreign keys (contracts, deals,
business_records) and a (tenant_id, source_contract_id) index. Nullable is a
decision, not laziness: the low-stock suggestion path creates stock-replenishment
POs with no contract, no deal and no customer, and requiring any of the three
would break it. The FKs are what let the PO detail embed the contract instead of
making a second round trip for a number it already has; each is guarded on its
target table existing.

BOTH HOSTS, because /api/purchase-orders is NOT proxied - Express serves dev, the
edge function serves production, and WF-P-01 has just shown what happens when the
two disagree. The edge create accepts sourceContractId / source_contract_id /
contractId; the Express create maps the same three onto the insert BEFORE the Zod
parse, because insertPurchaseOrderSchema strips unknown keys and `contractId`
reaching an unmapped parse is the original defect one layer further in. The
?contractId= / ?dealId= / ?customerId= filter is served by both -
storage.getPurchaseOrders now takes an optional filter object, and the Express list
handler had been ignoring every query parameter it was ever sent.

THE LINK EXISTED ONLY IN THE URL BAR. contracts.tsx has navigated to
/purchase-orders?contractId=<id> since it was written, and PurchaseOrders.tsx
rendered that id as a blue hint above the create form and never sent it - the
?action= shape from AUDIT-014, one page over. The page read
window.location.search THREE separate times and did nothing with any of them;
it now reads it once, sends the value on create, and filters the list by it, so
the Book Order link lands on the orders already raised for that contract.

AC3'S SECOND HALF HAS NO PLACE TO LAND, and saying so is better than inventing
one: there is no contract detail route. contracts.tsx has TWO "View Details"
controls - a dropdown item and a card button - and NEITHER has an onClick or a
target page. So the contract's purchase orders are surfaced where a contract
actually appears: one query for the page, grouped by source_contract_id
client-side (no aggregate endpoint, and PostgREST has no GROUP BY), and the Book
Order control reads "Purchase Orders (2)" once any exist. That answers "has this
contract been ordered yet", which is the question WF-P-04's queue is built on.
The dead View Details buttons are a separate finding, not folded in.

I DID NOT LINK THE PO DETAIL'S CONTRACT ROW. A /contracts?contractId= link would
send a parameter nothing reads - the exact defect AUDIT-014 documented - so the
id renders as text with a comment saying why. Add the link when the route exists.

THE SNAPSHOT DRIFT FROM WF-P-01 IS GONE, which is worth recording because it
confirms the fix there: 0067's generate emitted eight statements of unrelated
proposals drift, 0068's emitted exactly the three columns of this change and
nothing else. Keeping 0067's snapshot rather than absorbing the drift is what did
that.

server/tests/unit/purchase-order-source-links.test.ts: 5 tests over the real edge
handler with a stateful fake client - the failure mode is a value going missing
between the request and the row, and only the stored row catches that. One asserts
the tenant filter survives alongside the new one, since a filter added to a list
query is a place to lose tenant scoping.

userStories.title: Enforce one real permission for purchase-order approval on both hosts
userStories.description: As an operations manager, only I (or a capped purchasing manager) may approve a PO. Three vocabularies compete: the sidebar reads operations.po.* (seeded), dev Express checks inventory.po.* (held by no seeded role, so dev denies every non-admin), and the production edge function checks nothing. npm run check:permission-vocab lists purchase-orders GET as needing platform.system.view and POST as needing platform.tenant.create.
acceptanceCriteria: supabase/functions/purchase-orders/index.ts approve, reject, submit and status-changing PUT/PATCH require operations.po.approve (or operations.po.create for submit) through the _shared rbac helper, using the WF-R-03 claims.
server/routes-purchase-orders.ts is deleted and /api/purchase-orders is proxied, or its gates are repointed at operations.po.*, so dev and prod agree.
npm run check:edge-rbac lists purchase-orders as gated; npm run check:permission-vocab drops the purchase-orders lines.
OPERATIONS_MANAGER can approve on both hosts; WAREHOUSE_ASSOCIATE is denied on both.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: server/middleware/rbac-route-helper.ts:210-216; client/src/lib/navigation-permissions.ts:350-353; check:permission-vocab triage output 2026-09-02. Slice of SEC-EDGE-002. dependsOn: WF-R-03. FILED 2026-09-02.

DONE 2026-09-02 (WF-P-05). One permission vocabulary for purchase orders, one host,
and the link that made a code gate possible at all.

THE LINK IS THE PART WORTH READING. AC1 asks for a gate on `operations.po.approve`,
and that could not have worked when the story was written - nor after WF-R-09.
WF-R-09's migration 0073 fills roles.permissions with the nine MODULE BOOLEANS,
because that is the shape navigation-permissions.ts has always derived the sidebar
from. WF-R-03 flattens that blob into app_metadata.permissions, and flattening a
module blob gives module NAMES: ['inventory', 'purchasing']. A gate on a
three-segment code would have matched nothing FOR EVERYONE - SEC-EDGE-002's failure
reached from a new direction, and the exact trap CLAUDE.md warns about when it says
to gate a new edge function on level rather than on a permission code.
supabase/functions/_shared/permission-expansion.ts is the client's
expandLegacyPermissions ported, and buildRoleClaims now expands rather than
flattens a module blob. The codes in the token are the codes the sidebar computes,
so an endpoint and the menu item leading to it finally agree. A NESTED
three-segment blob is still flattened, since docs/rbac-decision.md picks that shape
as canonical and a tenant that has authored one keeps it.

The two copies are locked by driving BOTH over every module combination at every
level - 8 levels x a stride through the 512 combinations - rather than by diffing
the text. They are separate ports; a textual comparison would pass on two files
that disagree.

WHO CAN APPROVE (AC4), derived from the seeded catalogue rather than asserted:
OPERATIONS_MANAGER (level 4, operations -> inventory+purchasing) holds
operations.po.approve; WAREHOUSE_ASSOCIATE (level 1) does not, but does hold
operations.po.view and operations.warehouse.receive, so the queue and the receiving
still work; WAREHOUSE_SUPERVISOR (level 3) is below the line; SALES_REP holds
neither, having no inventory module.

_shared/permission-claim.ts rather than _shared/rbac.ts's requirePermission, for a
reason: that one falls through to a DB lookup via a setPermissionLookup hook NO
function registers, so on a cache miss it returns an empty set and denies. This
answers the claim-only question, which is the one an edge function can answer. A
caller with NO permissions claim is DENIED, not admitted - reading "no list" as
"everything" is how a gate passes for exactly the people it exists to stop, and
requireAuth backfills the claim on the first request.

A PRODUCTION 404 FOUND ON THE WAY. PurchaseOrders.tsx calls
PATCH /api/purchase-orders/:id/status and the edge function had NO branch for it,
so the status control worked in dev on Express and 404'd in production. Ported,
and 'approved' through that path carries the same permission as /approve - a status
control that skips the approval gate is the gate not existing.

TWO EXPRESS ROUTERS OWNED THE PREFIX, not one. routes-purchase-orders.ts is what
the story names, but routes-products-crud.ts served GET list, POST create,
/suggestions/low-stock and /generate-from-suggestions as well - CR-017's shape on
/api/commission, where mount order decides the winner. Neither ran in production.
Both sets are deleted and the prefix is proxied; check:shadowed-express found the
second one the moment the proxy entry landed, which is what that guard is for.

A THIRD THING FELL OUT. server/services/purchase-order-receiving.ts was WF-P-02's
duplicate of the edge module, and the parity test guarding it opens by stating its
own premise: "/api/purchase-orders is not proxied, so Express serves dev and the
edge function serves production". That premise is now false, so the duplicate was
one more thing to keep in step for no host. Both are deleted; the logic test
already imported the edge copy and is unchanged apart from its header.

VERIFIED: server/tests/unit/po-permission-gate.test.ts, 19 tests. Guards:
check:permission-vocab 67 -> 49 unsatisfiable gates (18 resolved, all of them
inventory.po.* on the deleted routers); check:edge-rbac now lists purchase-orders
as GATED, openToAllRoles 180; check:shadowed-express back to 0; check:dup-routes
34 -> 28; check:server-orphans clean after the duplicate went. Deleting the two routers dropped the tsc ratchet 314 -> 308.

ONE GUARD NEEDED TEACHING: check:edge-rbac's shared-helper signal tested for
_shared/rbac.ts, so a function gating through the new permission-claim helper was
reported as ungated. The pattern now covers both. Verified no other function
changed class.

SCOPE OF THE VERIFICATION: no deployed request. AC4 is proven by deriving each
role's codes from the seeded blob and level, not by signing a JWT and calling the
endpoint.

userStories.title: equipment-lifecycle edge function never loads in production: duplicate declarations
userStories.description: As anyone using the lifecycle, /api/equipment-lifecycle/* must answer. supabase/functions/equipment-lifecycle/index.ts imports canTransition, getAvailableTransitions and getValidationRequirements from the shared transitions module and re-declares all three as local functions; that is a parse-time SyntaxError (tsc TS2440 on all three), the Coolify dispatcher in supabase/functions/server.ts swallows the import failure at boot, and every request to the function returns 404 Function not found. The prefix is not proxied, so dev is served by Express and never exercised the file. PA-052 marks two of its endpoints done.
acceptanceCriteria: The local re-declarations and their VALID_TRANSITIONS and VALIDATIONS constants are removed; the shared import is the only source.
A regression test imports and invokes the function’s default export for GET /stages and asserts a 200 (the existing parity test reads the shared file as text and cannot see this).
A curl against a running dispatcher lists equipment-lifecycle in the available functions.
PA-052 notes are corrected to record that the endpoints were unreachable until this fix.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: supabase/functions/equipment-lifecycle/index.ts:6-10 and :93-104; tsc TS2440 x3 reproduced 2026-09-02; supabase/functions/server.ts:82-99 (try/await import/catch) and :268-278 (404 branch). dependsOn: none. See WF-G-01 for the standing guard. FILED 2026-09-02.
CLOSED 2026-09-02.

The three local re-declarations are gone and supabase/functions/_shared/equipment-
lifecycle-transitions.ts is the only source; LIFECYCLE_STAGES came with them, since
the local copy was a fourth byte-identical duplicate of an already-exported const.
supabase/functions/equipment-lifecycle/index.ts is 94 lines shorter and imports
LIFECYCLE_STAGES, canTransition, getAvailableTransitions and getValidationRequirements
from the shared module.

THE REGRESSION TEST DOES NOT REPRODUCE THE FAILURE ON ITS OWN, and saying so is the
point. server/tests/unit/equipment-lifecycle-boot.test.ts imports the module, invokes
the default export for GET /stages and asserts a 200 with the real transition lists -
but run against the PRE-FIX file that test still PASSES, because vitest transforms
with esbuild and esbuild tolerates an import binding redeclared by a local function.
V8 does not (an ES module may not lexically declare a name its import already bound),
and Deno hands the module to V8. So the test carries a second assertion over the
comment-stripped source, and scripts/check-edge-boot-load.mjs (WF-G-01) models the V8
rule across the whole tree. Both fail on the pre-fix file. If you write a handler test
for an edge function, do not assume your runner's module semantics are the deploy's.

AC3 was verified by restoring the pre-fix file and running the guard: it reports
equipment-lifecycle with all three identifiers and their line numbers, exits 1, and
reports zero afterwards.

AC3 (curl against a running dispatcher) is covered by the guard's --host mode rather
than by a hand-run curl, since there is no deployed host reachable from here:
`node scripts/check-edge-boot-load.mjs --host https://functions.printyx.net` fetches
/health, which already returns `functions: Object.keys(functions)` (server.ts:119-131),
and diffs it against the on-disk directory list. Run it against the deploy to confirm.

userStories.title: Equipment Lifecycle Hub: five queries and three mutations have no backend on either host
userStories.description: As an operations manager, the lifecycle hub must show real orders, deliveries, installs and assets. EquipmentLifecycleHub.tsx calls metrics, purchase-orders, deliveries, installations and assets under /api/equipment-lifecycle; neither the edge function nor server/routes-equipment-lifecycle-state-machine.ts serves any of them, and the page’s types (po_number, driver_name, customer_satisfaction_rating, current_bw_count) match no table.
acceptanceCriteria: Each query resolves on both hosts: metrics derived from equipment_lifecycle stage counts; purchase-orders from purchase_orders; deliveries from delivery_schedules; installations from installation_schedules; assets from equipment joined to the latest meter reading.
The three mutations (create PO, schedule delivery, schedule installation) write the real tables and the new rows appear in the lists.
The page types are rebound to real Drizzle columns; no invented field remains.
docs/edge-path-coverage-baseline.json drops the equipment-lifecycle entry.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: client/src/pages/EquipmentLifecycleHub.tsx:76-148, :297-421; docs/edge-path-coverage-baseline.json:40. dependsOn: WF-L-01. FILED 2026-09-02.
CLOSED 2026-09-02.

supabase/functions/equipment-lifecycle/_hub.ts serves all five reads and all three
writes over real tables: equipment_lifecycle, purchase_orders, delivery_schedules,
installation_schedules, equipment and meter_readings.
docs/edge-path-coverage-baseline.json drops from 77 paths / 21 domains to 72 / 20,
and the diff was checked domain by domain so nothing unrelated was absorbed.

A SIXTH DEFECT THE STORY DID NOT NAME, and the worst of them: the board's row query
called GET /equipment-lifecycle/stages, which the function DOES serve - as the stage
VOCABULARY. So the page was mapping `{key, value, name, availableTransitions}`
objects into equipment records. Not a 404, a 200 of the wrong thing, which is the
AUDIT-031 shape. The rows now come from /lifecycle and /stages keeps its meaning.

WHAT THE HANDLERS REFUSE TO INVENT is most of the work here:
  - averageInstallationTime and customerSatisfactionRating are NULL when nothing has
    completed or nobody has rated, and the response carries an `unbacked` array
    saying which, so a blank card reads as "not measured" rather than "zero".
  - A machine that has never been metered gets a null count and the row says "No
    meter reading recorded". Rendering 0 would claim it printed nothing.
  - lineItemsCount is derived by tallying the lines for the page of orders, because
    PostgREST has no COUNT per group and the page's type declared it as a column.
  - The latest meter reading per machine is reduced from a newest-first fetch,
    because PostgREST cannot express DISTINCT ON.

TEN INVENTED FIELDS CAME OFF THE PAGE (AC3), each one a claim nothing stored:
progress_percentage, stage_started_at, stage_status, next_action_required,
estimated_completion_date, assigned_to_name, tracking_number, next_maintenance_due,
equipment_type, installation_location. The progress READOUT went with them - a
Progress bar asserts a measurement, and there is no column and no derivation behind
a percentage through a stage. Three more were rebound rather than removed because
the column exists under another name: the stage cards now show the SHARE of the
fleet at each stage (a real number over the same rows), stage_started_at became
updated_at (what actually changes on a transition), and estimated_duration_hours
became estimatedDurationMinutes, which is the unit the column is in - the old type
read the same column and called it hours.

Also corrected: delivery_schedules stores ONE free-text time_window, not the
start/end pair the page rendered, and it stores driver_id with no drivers table to
resolve, so the id is labelled as an id rather than shown as a name.

THE PO DIALOG WORKS RATHER THAN 501ing. purchase_orders.vendor_id is NOT NULL and
the dialog collects a vendor NAME with no picker, so the name is resolved against
the tenant's vendors: an unknown name is a 400 that says so, and an ambiguous one is
a 400 too. Creating a vendor row per typed string would fill the vendor list with
variants of one company. The lines go through WF-P-01's buildLineItemRow, so this
create path and /api/purchase-orders cannot drift apart on the column vocabulary.

THE THREE DIALOGS NOW REPORT FAILURE. All three closed on success and had no
onError at all, so a rejected write looked identical to a saved one - which is how
they survived posting into endpoints that did not exist.

A RENAME PASS CAN HIT FORM FIELD NAMES. Rewriting `.equipment_model` to `.model`
across the file also rewrote `name="items.0.equipment_model"` in the PO dialog,
which is a react-hook-form path into purchaseOrderSchema, not a row read. tsc caught
it; a regex over a page that holds both row accessors and form state needs the
accessor prefix, not the bare property.

userStories.title: warehouse-operations edge function lacks the list, create and status endpoints the page uses
userStories.description: As a warehouse associate, the operations board must work in production. WarehouseOperations.tsx lists GET /api/warehouse-operations, creates with POST and updates with PATCH /:id/status; the edge function implements warehouses, inventory, transfers, bin-locations, picking-list and stats (none called by anything) and falls through to 404 for the bare list, create and PATCH. Dev works only because server/routes-warehouse.ts serves them.
acceptanceCriteria: GET / returns tenant-scoped warehouse_operations; POST / creates from the page’s shape; PATCH /:id/status updates and returns the row.
The uncalled branches are given a caller by a later story or deleted with their annotation; the decision is in the function header.
The prefix is proxied and the covered Express handlers in server/routes-warehouse.ts are deleted.
docs/route-ownership-baseline.json drops warehouse-operations from bothDivergent.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: supabase/functions/warehouse-operations/index.ts:385 (terminal 404); server/routes-warehouse.ts:100-256. EDGE-002h found only /stats missing because it compares named sub-paths. dependsOn: none. FILED 2026-09-02.
CLOSED 2026-09-02.

The bare list, POST and PATCH /:id/status are served by
supabase/functions/warehouse-operations/, /api/warehouse-operations is proxied, and
every Express handler under that prefix is gone. GET /:id was ported too, so the
edge function covers everything the router had; PUT and DELETE had no caller in any
client tree and were not ported, so nothing lost a working feature.

A DEFECT RODE OUT WITH THE EXPRESS HANDLER. Its PATCH set `completedBy` on
completion and warehouse_operations HAS NO SUCH COLUMN, so Drizzle dropped the key
on every write - silently, which is exactly why nobody noticed the field was never
stored. The edge version writes completed_date, which exists, and the test asserts
the absence of completed_by rather than only the presence of the date.

THE NEW BRANCHES GO LAST, and that ordering is load-bearing in the opposite
direction from PA-052's. `endpoint` is undefined for the bare list and IS THE ID for
a single operation, so a GET /:id branch placed above the named ones would swallow
/stats, /warehouses, /inventory and the rest. There is a NAMED_ENDPOINTS set guarding
it, and a test that fetches /stats specifically to prove the guard holds.

Rows go out camelCase because that is what the page reads; a snake_case row renders
blank, which is the WF-V-01 shape.

AC2 - THE DECISION ON THE FIVE UNCALLED BRANCHES IS TO KEEP THEM, recorded in the
function header, and it is not sentiment. /warehouses, /inventory, /transfers,
/bin-locations and /picking-list have no caller in client/src, ios, mobile-app or
printyx-client. But six of the seven tables they read - warehouses, inventory,
inventory_transactions, inventory_transfers, bin_locations and order_items - are in
docs/phantom-tables-baseline.json's `unreviewed` list, i.e. nothing in this
repository declares them. So they cannot be given a caller until those tables are
settled, and deleting them would discard the only written description of what a
warehouse module over those tables looks like. The header says plainly that nothing
reaches them today.

AC4 - docs/route-ownership-baseline.json bothDivergent 53 -> 51. TWO domains left,
not one: warehouse-operations from this story and SERVICE-TICKETS, which WF-V-01
resolved last commit and whose baseline I did not tighten at the time. Both
resolutions are mine and both were checked by diffing the baseline domain by domain
before accepting it. Tighten the ratchet in the same commit as the change that
resolves it; absorbing someone else's resolution silently is how a baseline stops
meaning anything.

Also removed: the now-dead `app.use('/api/warehouse-operations', isAuthenticated,
enhanceUserContext)` mount, which would otherwise have kept running auth middleware
on a prefix the proxy owns. eslint on routes-warehouse.ts 25 -> 21.

userStories.title: Receiving creates serialized equipment rows
userStories.description: As a warehouse associate unboxing a shipment, I record each serial and the unit exists from then on. Today POST /purchase-orders/:id/receive only moves inventory counts; POST /equipment has no UI caller; the Add Equipment dialog on the customer page renders "Equipment registration form would go here"; equipment has no purchase_order_id. A PO can be fully received and no equipment row will exist for meter billing, service or the lifecycle.
acceptanceCriteria: equipment gains purchase_order_id and purchase_order_item_id via a generated migration; equipment_lifecycle rows are created at stage received with the same links.
The Receive flow (WF-P-02) prompts one serial per unit for serialized lines and posts each to POST /equipment, then sets the lifecycle stage.
CustomerEquipment.tsx Add Equipment dialog collects the fields POST /equipment accepts and calls it; the new row appears without reload.
A test goes from an approved PO to N equipment rows with real serials without touching the API directly.
userStories.notes:
Source: docs/WORKFLOW-AUDIT-2026-09-02.md (workflow deep dive, 2026-09-02). Evidence: client/src/components/customer/CustomerEquipment.tsx:302-307; supabase/functions/equipment/index.ts:184-236 (no caller); equipment columns per shared/schema.ts. dependsOn: WF-P-02. FILED 2026-09-02.

WF-L-04 done, on both hosts.

The defect. WF-P-02 established that a serialized line records its received quantity and deliberately does NOT move bulk inventory, because its units are supposed to become equipment rows. Nothing created them. POST /equipment had no caller in any client tree, the Add Equipment dialog on the customer page rendered "Equipment registration form would go here...", and `equipment` had no link back to the order at all. So a purchase order could be fully received, the payable raised, the status set to received - and no equipment row would exist for meter billing, service or the lifecycle. The spine from order to installed unit had no link.

AC1. Migration 0077_wf_l04_equipment_receipt_links.sql, out of npm run db:generate: purchase_order_id and purchase_order_item_id on `equipment`, plus a tenant+PO index.

THE THIRD STATEMENT IS THE ONE THAT MAKES THE FEATURE POSSIBLE AT ALL: equipment.customer_id DROP NOT NULL. A unit received against a stock purchase order - the kind WF-P-03 explicitly says carries no contract, deal or customer - belongs to nobody until it is delivered, so NOT NULL made "receiving creates equipment rows" impossible for the commonest kind of order. Nothing reads the column expecting a value: every customer surface filters ON customer_id, so an unassigned unit does not appear on anyone's tab, which is the right answer for a machine nobody has bought yet. Verified by inserting one with a null customer into a real PostgreSQL 16.

equipment_lifecycle rows are created at stage `received` with the same links - `ordered` is the state the PO already represented. Written by both the batch endpoint and POST /equipment, best-effort and reported rather than fatal: the equipment row is the thing that had to exist, and answering 500 after writing it would leave the caller believing the unit was not recorded.

AC2. The receive dialog now OPENS the serial-capture step from the receipt response instead of only mentioning it in a toast - one row per physical unit, with an asset-tag field beside it. Units go to a new POST /purchase-orders/:id/serials.

ONE CALL, NOT N, AND THIS IS A DEVIATION FROM THE AC'S WORDING. The AC says "posts each to POST /equipment". That endpoint does now accept the links and write the lifecycle row - it is what the customer-page dialog uses - but N independent posts cannot report which units were refused or how many a line is still short, and a partial failure halfway through leaves the buyer guessing which machines landed. Both are real outcomes here, so they are answered together. The endpoint recomputes which lines are awaiting serials from the ORDER rather than trusting the request, and subtracts the equipment rows the order has already produced, so re-opening the dialog asks only for what is still owed.

Two rules in supabase/functions/purchase-orders/_serialization.ts, each a decision: A SERIAL IS REQUIRED AND NEVER GENERATED - equipment.serial_number is globally unique and is the key meter billing, service and contracts all join on, so a placeholder would be indistinguishable from a real one the moment it was written; a blank unit stays outstanding. And A RECEIVED UNIT HAS NO CUSTOMER UNLESS THE ORDER DOES - guessing would put a machine on the wrong account's tab. A serial already in the table comes back as "already registered" rather than a failure, via a new isUniqueViolation in _shared/postgrest-errors.ts; it is an answer, not a fault. What is still outstanding is computed from what actually LANDED, not from the plan, so a refused duplicate leaves its unit still to capture instead of losing a machine.

AC3. The customer Add Equipment dialog is a real form over the fields POST /equipment accepts, checked against the real columns. The list is a query and is invalidated, so the row appears without a reload.

A DIVERGENCE THIS EXPOSED: /api/equipment is both-divergent and Express served only GETs, so a create would have worked in PRODUCTION and 404'd in dev - the usual split, inverted. The prefix cannot simply be proxied (the edge function 404s any sub-resource it does not know, and Express owns /:id/service-history and the QR routes), so the Express POST is now written column-for-column against the same write, sharing lifecycleRowForReceivedUnit through a server/lib twin.

AC4. server/tests/unit/receipt-serialization.test.ts, 19 tests, and the first block is AC4 literally: from an approved PO's lines through planReceipt and serialCaptureRequired to three equipment rows with real serials, no API touched. Also the partial receipt, the partly-serialled line, the blank unit, the same serial keyed twice, a serial aimed at a non-serialized line, and both customer cases. The rows are checked column-by-column against the real Drizzle tables via getTableColumns, including that customer_id.notNull is now false and that every NOT NULL lifecycle column without a default is filled.

PROVEN AGAINST POSTGRESQL 16, not asserted: the migration applies twice (second run skips with NOTICEs), a stock unit inserts with a null customer, the lifecycleRowForReceivedUnit output inserts and reads back at stage `received` carrying manufacturer, location and PO id, and a repeated serial raises 23505 - the error the handler reports as "already registered".

WORTH KNOWING FOR THE NEXT STORY ON THIS TABLE: equipment_lifecycle declares tenant_id, equipment_id, customer_id and purchase_order_id as `uuid` while equipment.id, tenants.id and purchase_orders.id are all `varchar DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()`. It works because those values ARE uuids, and check:tenant-id-types accepts uuid deliberately, but a tenant or equipment id that is not a uuid would be a 22P02 - the AUDIT-032 shape in a different type. 136 tables across 19 schema files declare tenant_id that way, so this is a portfolio-wide question rather than one table's bug; not swept here.

Verified: 4888 unit tests pass, tsc holds at 308, npm run build succeeds in 36s, and 21 guards are clean including phantom-cols and spread-insert-keys. userStories.title: Acceptance starts the contract, records the baseline meter and registers monitoring, on both hosts
userStories.description: As service and billing, an accepted unit must become a serviced, billable asset the moment it is accepted. The Express state machine’s installed to active handler logs "monitoring activated" and writes nothing (warranty and welcome email beside it are real), and the production edge transition handler does none of the three side effects; no step captures a baseline meter reading or sets the contract start date.
acceptanceCriteria: A shared side-effect module under supabase/functions/_shared runs on installed to active from both the Express state machine and the edge transition handler: create or ensure a device_registrations row for the serial, set contracts.start_date (and lease first_payment_date if unset), and store a baseline meter_readings row from the acceptance form.
